# <span id="_Toc507075902"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Introduction</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold"> </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075903"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">The Development of Proto-Daoism in Ancient China</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">At the heart of Lao Ziâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the most celebrated writing in Chinese history, is an ancient oral tradition that pulsated throughout Chinese culture. This river of knowledge carried advanced mystical understandings of nature and spiritual alchemy that transformed every system of the ancient world, from medicine, to politics, to the inner worlds of human beings. Though infusing every branch of human life, the wisdom of Chinaâ€™s ancient peoples continuously returns to one source-principle â€“ Dao.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The earliest evidence of this ancient wisdom tradition is found in the work of Chinese shamans â€“ wise men and women with a deep connection to the cosmic principles of the universe, the same principles underlying King Wenâ€™s elucidation of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yi Jingâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">I Chingâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) divinatory hexagrams, and the enigmatic poetry of Lao Ziâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Written history, artifacts, and even the etymology of written Chinese characters, show the prominence enjoyed by these shamans in ancient China, arising primarily from their talents in ritual and divination. The practice of divination was considered paramount to the success of endeavours and in determining the favour of â€œthe spiritsâ€? (shen ming) when emperors and high government officials had to make their most important decisions. Such practices appear in Confuciusâ€™ teachings and stories â€“ said to be preservations of early Zhou culture â€“ and are evidenced in the Confucian Classic of Rites (Li Ji) in mentions of divining by tortoise shell and divining stalks</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é¾œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç­–</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Great weight was given to reading â€œsignsâ€? that indicated the favour or disapproval of Heaven and foretold the outcomes of various decisions and events. If one had the favour of Heaven, they would be protected by â€œthe spiritsâ€? and allowed to succeed. If not, their paths would be blocked, seemingly good events would turn bad, and if by relentless effort the goal was reached, it would still result in unforeseen negative consequences.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     According to the ancient shamans, one element would determine whether a human being could obtain the favour of gods and spirits:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">virtue</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Book of History</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, in providing discourses from early kings on how the powerful might obtain â€œthe will of Heaven,â€? makes abundantly clear that only virtue will endear the gods and spirits. Nepotism, power, and sacrificial offerings are said to be of no avail if they are not accompanied by deep and sincere virtue.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Naturally, great sages were sought out by imperial hopefuls looking to find, or otherwise contort, a clear answer to the question: â€œWhat is virtue?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Confucius (551-479 BC) described and promoted virtuous conduct, refining its definition with descriptions and anecdotes of benevolence, righteousness, filial piety, etiquette, and loyalty. For Confucius, these virtues depended heavily on acting appropriately. While benevolence was considered of highest importance, one could also distinguish Confucian morality by its common thread of duty throughout. If one could fulfill their duties in acting appropriately towards others, taking oneâ€™s role within various power dynamics into account, they could approach the level of the noble â€œjunzi.â€? It should be understood, however, that acting appropriately was superior to obedience for Confucius. Righteousness, for example, was not simply a matter of prescribed actions, but entailed consideration of larger consequences. Loyalty was not simply obedience, but a matter of putting others needs before oneâ€™s own.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In Confuciusâ€™ profound writing on the guidelines and importance of music, we can see that he viewed social harmony much as he did musical harmony. When events and behaviours are timed correctly, harmonized in accordance with a central key, and adhere to the ceremony of interaction, society may function in concert to create flourishing symphonies of life. To quote from Confuciusâ€™</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yeu Ji</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, or</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of Music</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span id="_ftnref1"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[1\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn1) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œThe knowledge of music leads to the subtle springs that underlie the rules of ceremony. He who has apprehended both ceremonies and music may be pronounced to be a possessor of virtue. Virtue means realization (in one's self).â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref2"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[2\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn2)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While Confucius established a zeitgeist of self-cultivation throughout Ancient China, his inner endeavours were not without their own foundations, and Confucius was not without his own heroes of sagely wisdom. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Shang Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">volume of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of History</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) contains accounts of the the ancient kings and battles that ushered in the Zhou Dynasty (c. 1046-256 BC), founded by King Wen and King Wu. Documented conversations from this time illustrate the underlying foundational ideals of Confuciusâ€™ philosophy, as Confucian philosophy is known as an attempt to revive the ethics and culture of the early, or â€œWestern,â€? Zhou Dynasty (c. 1046-771 BC).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The Zhou Dynasty began when King Wu overthrew the earlier Shang Dynasty (1600-1046 BC), completing the campaign begun by his father, King Wen. King Wen is known as the author of the original explanations of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yi Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">I Ching</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) hexagrams, later added to by another one of his sons, the Duke of Zhou, who expanded briefly on the hexagramsâ€™ individual lines. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yi Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is considered the first book ever written in China, and was revered by Confucians and Daoists, alike, for its cryptic wisdom and efficacy in divination.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Though King Wen and Wu are held up as the ideal examples of rectitude, and responsible for the cultural stability and refinement that lead to the flourishing philosophical schools of the Spring and Autumn (771-476 BC) and Warring States (475-221) periods,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Book of History</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">suggests that King Wen and Wu in fact received a wealth of knowledge from the preceding Shang Dynasty by a wise advisor to King Zhou, the last king of the Shang Dynasty. This advisorâ€™s name was Ji Zi.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Ji Zi was a relative of King Zhou (King</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç´‚</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Zhou of the Shang Dynasty, not to be confused with the Duke of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å‘¨</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Zhou or the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å‘¨</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Zhou Dynasty), known during his lifetime as Emperor Xin. The earliest written record of Ji Zi appears in the â€œMing Yiâ€? chapter of Chinaâ€™s oldest extant book â€“ the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yi Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. In this chapter, the Duke of Zhou puts Ji Zi forth as as an illustration of light and intelligence being smothered or suppressed. The image of this chapter is that of Earth over Fire. Earth smothers fire, just as tyrants like King Zhou block wisdom and guidance from shining through and bringing a nation out of darkness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Accounts of Ji Zi appear in many ancient texts, including Confuciusâ€™</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Analects</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yue Ji</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of Music</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">),</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Zhuang Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  (</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Chuang Tzu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, within the earlier â€œInner Chaptersâ€?),</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Hanfei Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huainan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Mo Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, amongst others. However, it is the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of History</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">that describes the moment when Ji Ziâ€™s passed his ancient knowledge onto King Wu, allowing it to survive the falling Shang Dynasty and live on in the new Zhou Dynasty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In the chapter entitled â€œPatterns of the Flood</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ´ª</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç¯„</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€? (found in the Zhou Shu volume), Ji Zi explains to King Wu that the father of the ancient King Yu (2200-2100 BC), Gun</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é¯€ â€œGiant Fishâ€?), committed an affront to Heaven by damming up the flood waters, bringing chaos and turmoil to his people and himself.   King Yu reversed this by creating water channels which allowed the water to flow throughout the land, arriving where it was needed, rather than attempting to simply block it up at the source. According to Ji Zi, King Yu was able to determine the correct solution because Heaven bestowed upon him the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ´ª</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç¯„</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¹?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç–‡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å½?å€«æ”¸æ•˜ patterns of the flood, with its nine categories, the principles of which are expressed throughout all relations.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref3"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[3\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn3)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The Zhou Shu volume, in which this chapter appears, is believed by scholars to have been written earlier than the vast majority of the other chapters in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of History</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">; however, it is still dated only to the 4</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">th</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">or 3</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">rd</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">century BC. Thus, it is difficult to say whether â€œthe patterns of the floodâ€?</span> <span id="_ftnref4"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[4\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn4) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">were passed down through Ji Zi and King Wu, or appeared in this chapter as a result of their emergence during the â€œ100 Schools of Thoughtâ€? that developed between the 6</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">th</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and 3</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">rd</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">centuries BC. One indication that â€œthe patters of the floodâ€? may have existed earlier on is that they included the categories and principles of the five elemental phases. The five elemental phases seem to have emerged with the Yin-Yang School which is attributed to Zuo Yan (305-240 BC). Zuo Yanâ€™s use of these concepts, however, appears nearly 100 years after the Zhou Shu is now believed to have been written. This would suggest that teachings on the principles of the five elemental phases were already in circulation before Zuo Yan wrote of them, albeit in a less literary and expounded upon form, leaving the exact time of their emergence open to debate.  If the five elemental phases were written about before Zuo Yan, and their intellectual origins cannot be traced, it may be that knowledge of them had been quietly passed down to worthy students for several centuries.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The story of Ji Zi offers a key turning point in the development of Daoism, and lends credence to the theory that Lao Ziâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was in fact the tip of a cultural iceberg, one which lay in the same type of quiet obscurity that Lao Zi often celebrated in his depiction of sagesâ€™ interactions with society. Ji Ziâ€™s delineation of Heavenâ€™s principles for Humanity may have set the foundation for many of the 100 Schools of Thought, and preserved a thread of teachings on behaviour, divination, and moral ideals which became essential to later Daoist practices.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     What this account of Ji Zi may most vitally reveal, is that Daoism developed as an extension of Ji Ziâ€™s assertion that King Yuâ€™s father committed an affront to Heaven by damming up the floods. This damming of the floods brought chaos and turmoil to his people, while King Yu succeeded in every way by allowing the water to flow according to the principles and patterns of nature. In the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, Lao Zi explains that by effortlessness (wu wei), and following nature (zi ran), things fall into their proper alignment. Nature (â€œHeavenâ€?) does no harm, while the forces of life nurture all things if unobstructed. When these operations are obstructed, generally as a result of desire and force, the prevailing alignment becomes aberrant, and disorder begins.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Knowing that Gunâ€™s great crime was attempting to force and block the flow of water, and that â€œthe will of Heavenâ€? and favour of the spirits are bestowed upon those with virtue, it then follows that King Yuâ€™s virtue was evident in his understanding of the importance of effortlessness, of allowing nature to follow nature, and the importance of quelling the mindâ€™s desire to use force against the powerful currents between Earth and Heaven. With this virtue and wisdom, Yu brought the life-giving waters to his people, thereby averting disaster, and cultivating prosperity throughout the provinces.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These principles are also shown in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(traditionally dated c. 500 BC) to be of pervasive applicability, reaching throughout the universe and within every living thing. While Lao Zi speaks of the imperative cultivation of effortlessness, however, he also speaks of shaping and fashioning vessels to be outwardly harmonious, and inwardly empty. Just as Yu did not sit and allow the floods to overtake the provinces, Lao Zi does not suggest allowing emotions and desires to overtake oneself. Instead, they both speak of bringing harmony to what can be shaped, and fashioning emptiness. Within emptiness, the force of these currents will nourish, rather than disrupt, the growth and prosperity of all it touches.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The principles of effortlessness (wu wei, literally â€œwithout doingâ€?) and naturalness (zi ran, literally â€œas itselfâ€?) are also found in the realm of the physical body and the practice of acupuncture, which works by opening and unblocking the flow of energy that circulates throughout the bodyâ€™s energy-channels. Daoist meditation techniques that â€œempty the heart-mind,â€? in turn, open these same energy channels and allow qi (chi) to move vital essences throughout the bodily system. By allowing the channels and vessels of the body to relax and open, circulation increases and the bodyâ€™s systems can be harmonized and revitalized. This might also be achieved with medications, though rarely do such medications not bring unwanted, often dangerous, side effects. Daoists, on the other hand, have devised ways to open the pathways without disrupting the natural alignment necessary for long-term health and vitality. Whether using medicinal herbs, needles, massage (tuina), or moxibustion, the layout of the body is essentially being energetically irrigated according to the connections and principles of the five elemental phases, a sort of Feng Shui of the body, which ensures that the internal alignment will not be imbalanced by the treatment in the long run.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The wisdom of Chinese medical theory and Feng Shui could be said to have descended from the wisdom of King Yu, benefitting from the long veneration of his idea to work with the harmonious flow of nature â€“ to allow circulation and avoid the dangers of excessive build-up. Lao Ziâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">reads somewhat as an homage to this idea, and its influence can be seen throughout the text. Note the importance given to accepting direction from the harmonious flow of nature in chapters two through nine</span> <span id="_ftnref5"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[5\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn5) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Two</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the whole world knows the pleasing to be pleasing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This ends in despising</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When all know the good to be good</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the end there is â€œnot goodâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, existence and non-existence are born together</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Difficulty and ease result in each other</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Long and short are compared to each other</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Above and below are opposites of each other</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Noise and tone are harmonized by each other</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Front and back accompany each other</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages handle affairs with non-action</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They practice wordless instruction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the myriad things all take their places</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without responding</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Given life, but not possessed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Acted for, but not expected of</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Perfection is cultivated, and not dwelled upon</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Surely, what is not dwelled upon</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Does not leave</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[ie, trying to accumulate a positive persona through artificial means will only result in ruin\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Three</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Do not exalt the worthy</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the people will not fight</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Do not praise goods which are difficult to obtain</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the people will not steal</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Do not display what is desirable</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And their hearts will not be in chaos</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sageâ€™s government</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Empties the heart and enriches the stomach</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Softens the will and strengthens the bones</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People then remain uncontrived and without desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While the scheming do not dare to act</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Act by not acting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And everything will fall into place</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[ie, excessive desires only ruin peopleâ€™s happiness; therefore, the Sage reduces these desires and opens people up to appreciating what is truly valuable in life â€“ social harmony and inner peace.\] </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Four</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao is a container</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though used (filled) again and again</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is never full</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Profound!  As though the ancestor of all things</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Rounding the points</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Untying the knots</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Softening the glare</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unifying the dust</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Tranquil!  As though having a life of its own</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I do not know whose child it is</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It appears to have preceded the primordial ruler</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[Like King Yuâ€™s irrigation channels, the Dao spreads life giving energy throughout and so is never full.\] </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Five</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven and Earth are not (willfully) benevolent</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Than grass for dogs</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The hundred clans are treated no differently</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Than grass for dogs</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The gate of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To speak countless words is worthless</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is not as good as guarding balance within</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[Speaking countless unnecessary words, fabricating reality and accumulating artificial ideas, will not provide the understanding acquired by allowing situations to flow in their natural direction, thereby revealing themselves\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Six</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be a valley to the spirit and you will not die</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[Valleys are often river channels. Lying low, water is able to flow through them, between the mountains.\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Seven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven has longevity, Earth has continuit</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">y</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ã€€</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven and Earth have the power of longevity and continuity because they do not live for themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is how they can live for so long</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages leave themselves behind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And they end up in front</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet they persist</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is it not because they are without selfishness and wickedness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[ie, because sages remain empty (of ego) and take the low position, like the valley or water channel, life continues to flow through them\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Eight</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The highest excellence is like water</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in giving can be found in benevolence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in speech can be found in sincerity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in aligning can be found in order</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in professionalism can be found in competence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in action can be found in appropriate timing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>
