<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[When people are empty (of ego) and take the low position, like the valley or water channel, the above benefits are found in them, all of which, according to Daoists, require non-obstruction and flowing with nature\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline">Chapter Nine</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(as it appears in the earliest known copy of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, found at Guodian)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">To accumulate until full</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">Is not as good as coming to a stop</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">When rushing waters gather</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">Nothing can be long protected</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">When gold and jade fill the halls</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">Nothing can preserve them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">When fortune and wealth bring arrogance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">They bring the misfortune of their own loss</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">Having achieved the goal, withdraw yourself</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">This is the way of Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">\[Consider that hoarding wealth, rather than circulating it back into the economy, suffocates the economy that this wealth relies on. Hoarding power, rather than allowing rights and credit where it is due, will result in resentment and loss of power. Allowing wealth and power to flow outwardly in a natural course ensures their perpetuity.\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As these chapters show, the wisdom of Lao Zi benefitted greatly from the ancient veneration of King Yuâ€™s wisdom, while the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">functioned like a juncture point in one of King Yuâ€™s water channels, accumulating and spreading his wisdom throughout ancient China, and beyond.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075904"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Guan Zi, Jixia Academy, and Chu Kingdom</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Guan Zi, also known as Guan Zhong (720-645 BC), was a Prime Minister of Qi State and key advisor to Duke Huan, ruler of Qi State from 685-643 BC. By following Guan Zhongâ€™s advice, Duke Huan amplified the power and prosperity of Qi, and was recognized as Hegemon of the Zhou empire.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The works found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, attributed to Guan Zhong, are now generally believed to have, in fact, been written by scholars much later, during the 4</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">th</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">century BC at Jixia Academy in the state of Qi.</span> <span id="_ftnref6"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[6\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn6) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It should also be noted that these writings were not compiled into the complete</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">encyclopedia of 86 books until much later, around 10 BC.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is generally considered a Legalist text, which is a school of thought associated more closely with Qin State after the fall of the Zhou Dynasty (256 BC). Legalism had already gained much attention by 360 BC, however, after Duke Xiao of Qin followed the advice of his minister Shang Yang and implemented strict Legalist policies in Qin as of 363 BC. These policies gave Qin the power and might that allowed it to take on, and soon thereafter replace, the Zhou Dynasty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While Legalism argued that strict enforcement of laws would ensure order, the proto-Daoist texts within the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">act as a counterbalance to this position by pointing to deeper sources of social co-operation and harmony: inner peace and inner harmony â€“ the â€œtrue natureâ€? of human beings. This position is also in contrast to the combination of Daoism and Legalism found in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Four Canons of the Yellow Emperor (Huang Di Si Jing)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Four Canons</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, perhaps written somewhat earlier than the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, closer to 400 BC, resembles Lao Ziâ€™s philosophy that rulers must be frugal, modest, and humble. It advocates not over-taxing the citizens, nor killing captives, or forcing corvee labour. It also speaks of yin and yang, and touches on the natural interplay of these forces in nature. It does not, however, speak at any length on the subject of internal cultivation, beyond the general principle that a ruler should dwell in the absence of desire. Further, it advocates the invariable and merciless application of punishments. Overall,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Four Canons</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is closer to Legalism than the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Though the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Four Canons</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">may pre-date the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as an example of Daoist philosophy, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">not only adhere more closely to Lao Ziâ€™s philosophy, but also to the idioms, form, and style in which his proposals and prescriptions appear in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Such similarities, detailed throughout</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, show that these texts, rather than the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Four Canons</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, are the likely precursors of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, if any exist.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, along with all Warring States era Daoist texts, appear to have come from the culture of Chu State, located in the south of China, though they may have come to fruition at Jixia Academy. Jixia Academy, located in Qi State</span> <span id="_ftnref7"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[7\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn7) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(north of Chu, on the eastern coast), hosted scholars from many different states, and is said to have been instituted by Duke Huan of Qi, under whom Guan Zi served as Prime Minister. The academy was later revitalized by King Xuan, ruler of Qi from 319-301 BC.</span> <span id="_ftnref8"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[8\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn8) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is likely that Chu scholars were most active in Qi around 330 BC</span> <span id="_ftnref9"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[9\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn9) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">thanks to stable relations between Qi and Chu, a result of the rising power of Qin in the West, and so it may have been during this time that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">found their way into the scholarly lectures and conversations in Qi.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Considerable power shifts driven by Qinâ€™s expansion east and south would have encouraged Chu scholars to travel north-east to Qi around 330 BC. King Huiwen of Qin began exerting military pressure eastwards on Chu around 337 BC. Chu then absorbed Yue, to its east, in 334 BC. Qin later absorbed Ba and Shu to the west of Chu in 316 BC. This may have given Chu scholars further incentive to travel east and north, towards Qi, after 337 BC, though it wasnâ€™t until 278 BC that Qin successfully attacked the capital of Chu, forcing them to relocate it. In 313 BC, King Huiwen of Qin enticed King Huai of Chu to cut ties with Qi, so as to repair ties between Chu and Qin after a failed allied attack of several states against Qin. This cooling of the previous relations between Chu and Qi, following further threats from Qin, may have strained the camaraderie at Jixia Academy and driven Chu scholars out of Qi around 313 BC, suggesting that proto-Daoist writings coming out of Jixia Academy would have pre-dated this event.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<img src="Image00001.jpg" style="border-top-style:solid; border-top-width:0.75pt; border-top-color:#000000; border-right-style:solid; border-right-width:0.75pt; border-right-color:#000000; border-left-style:solid; border-left-width:0.75pt; border-left-color:#000000; border-bottom-style:solid; border-bottom-width:0.75pt; border-bottom-color:#000000; -aw-left-pos:0pt; -aw-rel-hpos:column; -aw-rel-vpos:paragraph; -aw-top-pos:0pt; -aw-wrap-type:inline" width="432" height="407" />

<span id="_ftnref10"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[10\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn10)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In 299 BC, when the prolific Daoist philosopher and storyteller Zhuang Zi (aka Zhuang Zhou; Chuang Tzu) was 30 years old (died at 45), and Meng Zi (aka Mencius) was 73 years old (died at 83), King Qingxiang of Chu came to power. King Qingxianâ€™s childhood tutor was buried with the earliest known excerpts of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, at Guodian. This timeline could put King Qingxianâ€™s tutor at Jixia Academy around 330 BC, while relations were relatively calm between Qi and Chu.</span> <span id="_ftnref11"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[11\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn11) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Further, the proto-Daoist texts in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">show a counter current to the (proto-)Legalism of Shang Yang. Shang Yangâ€™s ideas likely found their way into Jixia Academy after their implementation by Duke Xiao of Qin in 363 BC, and continued to influence scholars after his execution by Xiaoâ€™s successor, King Huiwen of Qin, in 338 BC.</span> <span id="_ftnref12"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[12\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn12) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If the Legalism in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Four Canons of the Yellow Emperor</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(circa 400 BC) predated the implementation of Shang Yangâ€™s policies (363 BC), it may be that Shang Yangâ€™s ideologies were simply a radical form of the prevailing philosophical climate, a climate that the authors of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">hoped to transform. Their words foresaw the consequences of too much rigidity and, thus, shared methods for cultivating inner peace and enlightenment in an effort to mitigate tyranny, violence, and the inevitable chaos that follows them. It, therefore, seems likely that the proto-Daoist</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts were first written down sometime after or during Shang Yangâ€™s lifetime, when Legalist ideas had gained considerable influence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">appear to be early developments of Daoist ideas, these ideas could very well have been kept secret within the Zhou capital in Zhou State</span> <span id="_ftnref13"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[13\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn13) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(north of Chu, surrounded by Han State), where Lao Zi is said to have lived around 500 BC.  As Chu began to implement the Zhou culture in its political and martial activities, with the inspired reforms of King Zhuang of Chu (ruled 613-591 BC), esoteric Daoist teachings would have slowly come to light, finding a welcome environment in Chuâ€™s combination of shamanic and scholarly culture. It may also be that the moral teachings of Zhou were gradually interpreted by Chuâ€™s shamanic elders and transformed into the Daoist teachings later attributed to Lao Zi in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. If we are to go by the traditional dating and authorship of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, however, Lao Zi seems to have been inspired by the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which would have been available to him as the Zhou imperial librarian. This is to assume, of course, that he was not personally instructed in the â€œart of the heart-mindâ€? while working amongst the empireâ€™s best in the Zhou capital. After all, Qi State was loyal to the Zhou empire, and so any traditions on the subtleties of leadership and internal cultivation that Guan Zi was privy to would have been accessible to a worthy student in the Zhou capital.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     After King Zhuang died, he was succeeded by kings whose adherence to the Zhou principles varied widely. However, history shows that King Huai (ruled 328-299 BC) respected these principles, and passed them on to his son, later known as King Qingxian, through an imperial tutor,</span> <span id="_ftnref14"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[14\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn14) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">suggesting that Chu scholars would have had incentive to develop and write on such subjects under King Huai.  These scholars would have travelled between Chu and the Jixia Academy in Qi to further their education and writing, and consequently their status as proficient teachers in Chu and Qi. Though Chu eventually fell to Qin in 223 BC, the region continued to preserve the rich Zhou-influenced culture that developed there during the reign of King Zhuang.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     King Zhuang of Chu (ruled 613-591 BC) was a particularly boisterous and ruthless leader until he met Zhou Minister Wang Sun Man, who admonished him that virtue and not bronze (a resource Chu had in abundance and used for weaponry) provides a king with true power.</span> <span id="_ftnref15"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[15\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn15) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This inspired King Zhuang to observe the Zhou rites, and make Chu a leading example of Zhou culture in matters of state and war.</span> <span id="_ftnref16"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[16\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn16) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">King Zhuang brought Chu from being viewed as a state ruled by â€˜barbariansâ€™ to later being lauded by Confucius (551-479 BC) as a true example of high culture, and proof of the prosperity that follows adherence to the Zhou Dynastyâ€™s evolved approach to politics. As a result of his social and cultural reforms, and the power that they afforded him, King Zhuang was named Hegemon of the Zhou Dynasty, a position held several decades earlier by Duke Huan of Qi (ruled 685-643 BC), Guan Ziâ€™s employer.</span> <span id="_ftnref17"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[17\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn17)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lao Zi is believed to have lived in Chengzhou during his service in the imperial library, the same place where King Zhuang was admonished by Wang Sun Man; however, it was 100 years after King Zhuangâ€™s rule that Lao Zi, aka Li Er, is said to have worked in the Zhou library, and instructed Confucius on Zhou rites. Nonetheless, we can see in King Zhuangâ€™s adoption of Zhou culture and the parallels between his behaviour and Lao Ziâ€™s teachings that Lao Zi was also influenced by the moral ideals of Zhou. For example, King Zhou punished his own son for breaching proprietary law (equality under the law), and showed mercy once his authority had been established. Zhuang also ensured that those holding positions of power in his kingdom were familiar with Zhou rites and ancient classics such as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of Songs</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. This influenced even Chu warriors to become proficient in Zhou rites and moral standards. When Chu defeated the Jin army, King Zhuang would not allow his troops to pile the bodies of the Jin soldiers as a victory celebration, but insisted they be buried in the same manner as their own troops. Following this burial, King Zhuang paid his respects by worshipping the God of the Yellow River.</span> <span id="_ftnref18"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[18\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn18) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This respect for oneâ€™s adversary is prescribed in Lao Ziâ€™s chapter 31:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Beautiful weapons are instruments of ill omen</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All creatures should despise them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, those who have Dao do not stay with them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The superior man (junzi) prefers to stay on the left</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But those who use weapons prefer the right</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Weapons are not instruments of good omen</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They are not instruments of the junzi</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If an attacker cannot be stopped, and weapons are used</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To be calm and unemotional is considered most important</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If victory is then won, do not be pleased</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For to be pleased with this would be to celebrate murder</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Anyone who celebrates murder</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is not capable of obtaining the will of the world!</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For auspicious matters they \[junzi\] stay on the left</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For ominous matters, they \[junzi\] stay on the right</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the low ranking officer is on the left</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the high ranking officer is on the right</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is said to observe the rites of mourning</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When many people are killed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is cause for sympathy and mourning</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Victory in war</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is also cause for the mourning rites to be observed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Though Lao Zi is believed to have worked in Zhou State, scholars ascribe Daoist thought mainly to the Chu region. This discrepancy is mitigated by the belief that Lao Ziâ€™s birthplace was in what is now Guoyang county, Anhui Province, in the north-eastern corner of the former Chu Kingdom.  We can also see, for example in DDJ31 above, that the author of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">subscribed to Chuâ€™s elevation of the left side over the right side,</span> <span id="_ftnref19"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[19\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn19) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">in contrast to the Zhou preference for the right over the left. Furthermore, after King Zhuang made Chu a stronghold of Zhou culture and scholarship, it follows that Daoist interpretations and expansions of this culture were likely to arise, especially alongside the potent shamanism and nature worship that Chu was formerly looked down upon for by the other Zhou states. Chu had a reputation for being culturally anarchistic, rejecting the authority and norms of the Zhou Empire, and absorbing from the various cultures that Chu Kingdom enveloped. It appears to have been this syncretism, infused with a pervading influence of Zhou culture, which gave rise to the Daoist school of thought, and provided a fresh approach to the Zhou teachings of Confucius, and, perhaps more significantly, a fresh approach to the rigid Legalist policies of the rising Qin powers. If only the Qin Legalists had taken heed of the Daoistsâ€™ guidance, the Qin Dynasty (221-206) might have lasted more than the 15 years it took for a rebellion to rise up and usher in the Han Dynasty. As Lao Zi states in chapter 76 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As with all things</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When plants and trees begin to grow</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They are flexible and pliant</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet, when dying</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They become dry and rotten</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, hardness and inflexibility are the approach of death</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While softness and pliancy are the approach of life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In 213 BC, the first emperor of the Qin Dynasty, Qin Shi Huang, ordered the burning of any books which might be used to prove his leadership unjust. Were it not for the 1978 AD discovery of a complete</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(including all 81 chapters) in a tomb sealed in 168 BC, the earliest known copy of Lao Ziâ€™s text to survive from this period would date from approximately 1 AD, in Yan Zunâ€™s commentary, and even this only contains the De (Virtue) volume, and not the Dao (Way) volume. In 1993, an earlier copy containing only fragments of roughly a third of the chapters was discovered in the tomb of King Qingxianâ€™s tutor, at Guodian, dated around 300 BC. Thus, it appears, Qin Shi Huangâ€™s purging of texts was so thorough that only two copies of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">from that time period, both buried in tombs, survive to this day.</span> <span id="_ftnref20"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[20\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn20)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Thankfully, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts survived, possibly because of their technical practicality and association with Guan Zhong.  This may have associated them with the Legalist school at the time, and spared them the fate of other philosophical texts.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075905"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Compiling the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">, circa 26 BC</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was compiled by Liu Xiang, beginning in 26 BC, and completed and submitted to the Emperor by his son, Liu Xin, around 6 BC. Though it was not compiled until this time, an existent corpus attributed to Guan Zi (Guan Zhong) was widely known to scholars by at least the time of Hanfei Zi, who wrote around 250 BC:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä»Šå¢ƒå…§ä¹‹æ°‘çš†è¨€</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ²»</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è—?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å•†</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç®¡ä¹‹æ³•è€…å®¶æœ‰ä¹‹</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Today, the people of the state all discuss good governance, and everyone has a copy of the works on law by Shang (Yang) and Guan (Zhong) in his house.</span> <span id="_ftnref21"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[21\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn21)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To compile an official encyclopedia of Guan Ziâ€™s teachings, Liu Xiang gathered 564 book bundles, including 389 from the imperial library, and the rest from various government officials,</span> <span id="_ftnref22"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[22\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn22) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">to be collated with the help of several scholars.  Over a period of two decades, they â€œeliminated 484 duplicate bundles to make the standard text of 86 books.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref23"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[23\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn23) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     There is no mention as to how many duplicates were found of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">or</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, but with 6.5 times more duplicate bundles than what eventually made up the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, it seems likely that these texts also had duplicates. It should be noted that Liu Xin had initially categorized the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as part of the Daoist school of thought,</span> <span id="_ftnref24"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[24\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn24) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">surely due in large part to the weight and content of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu, Bai Xin,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which scholars generally agree to be among the earliest texts included in the compilation.  Though the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was not categorized as a Legalist text until the Sui Dynasty (581-618 AD),</span> <span id="_ftnref25"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[25\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn25) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">it is generally categorized as such to this day.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Liu Xiang (77-6 BC) was a Confucian scholar and distant relative of Liu Bang (256-195 BC), founder of the Han Dynasty. He was, thus, also a relative of Liu Bangâ€™s grandson, Liu An (179-122 BC), who edited the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huainan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, an early compilation of Daoist thought, around 139 BC. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Liu Xin (Liu Xiangâ€™s son, who finalized the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">soon after his fatherâ€™s death) was a Confucian scholar, founder of the â€œOld Textsâ€? Confucian school, and the imperial librarian under Xin Dynasty Emperor Wang Mang.  Wang Mang leveraged his position and family connections in the Han Dynasty to briefly replace the Han Dynasty with the Xin Dynasty (9-23 AD), dividing the Han Dynasty into the â€œWestern Han (206-9 BC)â€? and â€œEastern Han (25-220 AD)â€? periods.  Liu Xin may have had a considerable influence on Wang Mang, who sought to restore much of the ancient Zhou Dynasty systems and Confucian rites.  While at the outset, Wang Mangâ€™s ideals seemed to be in line with Daoist counsel â€“ eliminating government excesses, sanctioning social equality, and abolishing slavery â€“ his approach to handling affairs proved gratuitously meddlesome, restrictive, and lacking flexibility, ultimately leading to discontent, chaos, and defeat.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075906"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Proto-Daoism in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As touched upon earlier, the proto-Daiost texts in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">often read as a repudiation of the surging Legalist philosophy that ushered in the Qin Dynasty. Legalism is characterized by a reliance on staunch adherence to laws, rewards, and punishments. It also values virtues such as righteousness and benevolence, but does not trust in them as Confucius and his followers did. Though Legalism appreciates a leaderâ€™s duty to display virtuous qualities in order to influence those below them, it holds reliable demonstrations of rewards and punishments as the primary determinant in human behaviour, provided these rewards and punishments match the likes and dislikes of their recipients. While this strategy has predictable short-term effects, the proto-Daoist philosophers point out its inability to bring about true transformation of the populationâ€™s inner virtue, a limitation that would in fact make the people more deceitful and beguiling, leading to further disorder, and distortions of their true nature. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 144-150, describes the situation as follows:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Affairs have suitable and unsuitable (solutions).  For example, it is suitable to use an ivory bodkin to untie (knots). What cannot be untied is then untied.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As for those who excel at improving situations, when the nationâ€™s people cannot figure out how to â€œuntieâ€? (a situation), they apply their skill but do not hold onto the situation without letting go. This would be unskillful, for it submerges the situation in laws and punishment. Such ability is not skillful. Attain trustworthiness (xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ä¿¡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) and then stop.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Humanityâ€™s true nature, the proto-Daoists explain, is the easiest and most trustworthy state of being that rulers can bring about, if the ruler first cultivates this simplicity, economy of desires, and sincerity of personality in himself. Allowing people to return to this natural simplicity would ensure an abundance of resources and communal harmony; while the power of the rulerâ€™s virtue, and that of his people, would eventually win the hearts of those in other states, ensuring strong alliances and pervasive loyalty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Relying on virtue rather than law may resemble Confuciusâ€™ approach to political order, however, a defining difference between Confucianism and Daoism is that Confucius advocated adherence to rules of conduct much as Legalists demanded adherence to laws. These adjustments, in the view of Daoists, were external and too easily fabricated, despite Confuciusâ€™ emphasis that virtue must come from within. Thus, the Daoists called for leaving off any externally imposed restrictions, and a realization, or re-awakening, of the true heart. Reaching to this true heart, all else will follow, just as water allowed to sit undisturbed will eventually purify, of itself.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The authors of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also try to impart that law is much greater than the rules and precepts decided by lawmakers. They explain that there are natural laws in the universe which govern the success or failure of all things, regardless of what the human powers that be may demand. For example, in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Purifying the Heart-Mind</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), lines 102-118, we find:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ for human beings.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There is something that governs them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Their laws, like rolling drums of thunder</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cannot incite themselves.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There is something always inciting them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What is this constant thing?  It is present at all times.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Looking for it with the eyes, it will not be seen.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Listening for it with the ears, it will not be heard.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Scattered throughout, it fills all under Heaven.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though not seen on the surface,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is collected in the harmonious shape of the face.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is known in the muscles and the skin.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dutifully, it comes and goes,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet no one knows its timing.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So small, it is (within) the square (of Earth).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So expansive, it is (exceeds) the circle (of Heaven).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Expanding and expanding, no one can reach its gate.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">goes on to explain the futility of ruling only with laws, and simply trying to gain control of a population by heaping more and more laws upon them. As lines 144-151 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">illustrate, this is like trying to untie a knot by continuing to pull at the string, rather than employing a bodkin (an analogy for a sage) to untie it.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">lines 34-37, even argue that people would be better off if â€œthe correct manâ€? simply stopped telling people how to act so that they could find the true righteousness and filial piety that reside in them naturally, and stop competing with each other over who displays these traits the most.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To connect with the highest law, the Way (Dao), the Daoists counsel finding peace and order within oneself so as to first see clearly from the vantage point of peace and order before trying to guide the world towards it. In doing so, these writers employ guidance which likely comes from a formerly obscure tradition of internal cultivation. Always looking to the source to see how things come about, the Daoists learned how to cultivate oneâ€™s kingdom by understanding how to cultivate oneself, and they understood how to cultivating oneself by looking at the source of every person:  Heaven and Earth. With a body as stable as the Earth, and a mind as vast as the Heavens, the Daoists sought transcendence of the seeming limitations of existence. Not only this, but they also found in Heaven and Earth the manifestations of Dao, and the laws by which all things proceed. The Daoists therefore modeled their behaviour on Heaven and Earth in order to achieve ultimate longevity, and advised kings to abide by these same principles in order to preserve their kingdoms. In</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Art of the Heart-Mind, lower volume</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), we find in lines 18-20:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages resemble Heaven during such times. They are without thought of self when sitting above all.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They resemble Earth during such times. They are without thought of self when supporting all.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for thought of self, it puts the world in chaos.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, we also find a contradiction of one of the Legalistsâ€™ greatest faiths: the ultimate power of rewards and punishments.  Lines 92-99 retort:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The ancient enlightened kingsâ€™ love for all under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Allowed the world to depend on them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The violent kingsâ€™ hatred of all under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Caused the world to abandon them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, rewards are not enough to demonstrate love,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And punishments are not enough to demonstrate fierceness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For this love will end with the rewards,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And this fierceness will end with the punishments.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Thus, it appears that the proto-Daoist</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts, though found in what is generally considered a Legalist compilation, were in large part written in response to the Legalist ideologies of Shang Yang, prevalent at the time it was most likely written, around 350 BC. The writersâ€™ attempts to warn Legalists of the imbalances that would result from such stringent adherence to their doctrines turned prophetic when the Qin Dynasty, bolstered by the Legalist policies of Shang Yang earlier on, swept all of China by 221 BC, and then fell in 206 BC, only 15 years after unification.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Much of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">contains advice more closely resembling that of Confucius and Lao Zi than the advice of Shang Yang. The writers of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">advise considering the welfare of the people as most important, and instilling righteousness, benevolence, frugality, and simplicity in them, rather than simply manipulating them with rewards and punishments, laws, and even poverty as Shang Yang does. While the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Shang and Xia), and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">are its only texts on Daoist internal cultivation, a great deal of the writings on statecraft in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">seem to heed Lao Ziâ€™s teachings in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, though they may have been transcribed at an earlier date. If we are to faithfully ascribe these writings to Guan Zi and Lao Zi, Guan Zi (720-645 BC) would have written his texts some 100 years before Lao Zi wrote the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Perhaps, as suggested earlier, the historical thread of these teachings goes back even further to the shamans and sages of the Shang (1600-1046 BC) or Xia (2070-1600 BC) Dynasties.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Because of Qin Shi Huangâ€™s order to burn all philosophical books in 213 BC, it is difficult to say with any certainty when the Daoist approach to government first appeared in writing. The influence of Zhou rites and culture on King Zhuang of Chu shows that such ideals for government, and virtuous rule, were in place long before Confuciusâ€™ time, even if fidelity to these ideals was not constant throughout the Zhou Dynasty. Confucius, who helped to revitalize these ideals, was likely a product of the zeitgeist of his time, realizing the precipitous nature of an empire losing its principles while its states had begun declaring themselves kingdoms. Though the virtuous rule touted in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is considered Confucian in many respects, Confucius was a teacher of Zhou culture, and the philosophy and rites of Zhou are what Li Er (aka Li Dan, Lao Zi) is said to have taught while working in the Zhou imperial library. Seeing this blend of Confucianism and Daoism in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, then, one has to question if this approach to government is not simply a product of studying Zhou culture, a subject which comprised the education of the nobility for hundreds of years prior to Confucius. That Confucius did not even leave his home state of Lu until he was in his 50s, and yet still knew so much about Zhou culture, shows that the influence of Zhou-centered education was widespread, and likely well documented until â€œthe burning of the booksâ€? during the Qin Dynasty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Another question raised by the seemingly Daoist centered approach to government in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, pertains to its relationship to Daoist meditation. Much of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and the proto-Daoist texts in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">use metaphors of pacifying the nation when describing how to bring about inner peace. These writings suggest that by bringing order and peace to oneself through non-effort, minimizing desires, and utilizing the course of nature, one will then understand how to bring order and peace to a nation. Though this process begins by finding inner peace, it is nonetheless difficult to say for certain if this approach to meditation inspired the corresponding approach to government, or if the corresponding approach to government enlightened the Sages as to its facility in cultivating the inner domain.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Much of the inter-textual analysis in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">focuses on the complementary relationship between the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and proto-Daoist</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts, as they expound in subtler and more overt ways on the same principles of statecraft and internal cultivation.</span> <span id="_ftnref26"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[26\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn26) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It appears, at times, that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">pre-supposed a familiarity with the concepts and principles in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and was written to clarify the relationship between statecraft and internal cultivation. At other times, it appears that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">describes, more esoterically, elements of statecraft that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts present more clearly as elements of internal cultivation. This, again, makes it difficult to determine which application of these principles came first â€“ the skillful application of Dao and De in statecraft, or internal cultivation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075907"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Internal Cultivation in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic"> </span>

## <span id="_Toc507075908"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Bai Xin (Purifying the Heart-Mind)</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though, at least, fragments of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">may predate them, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin, Xin Shu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">are the earliest available examples of Daoist methods for internal cultivation. Given its emphasis on more external matters of leadership, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">may be the earliest of these four texts.  Of the proto-Daoist</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is also closest to the language in some of the more definitive chapters of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, especially chapters one, two, five, and nine, offering important insights into how Lao Ziâ€™s subtleties would have been received by those privy to the early oral traditions from which they arose. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also dismisses the modern notion that early Daoists had no belief in the supernatural, unlike the Daoist religion and the rest of Chinese society at the time, when it explains in lines 41-44:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The success of an army follows good fortune, and the approach of virtue depends on the individual.  This is why it is said that omens and apparitions (gui) (arrive to defend) the righteousness of others. (Thus) an army must never lack righteousness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And in line 143:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To those who are righteous towards others, the spirits (shen, deities, gods) bring good fortune.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     If the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">pre-dates the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, it is also the first to prescribe a physical bearing for meditation, a technique given more emphasis in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">when it speaks of aligning the body. Lines 201-207 read:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Left, right, front, and back, (running) full circle, they return to the place (at the center).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Holding to a ceremonious outward appearance</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">åŸ·å„€æœ?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è±¡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), respectfully welcome that which approaches</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ•¬è¿Žä¾†</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è€…</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those today who seek its approach require this method to (invite) Dao.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without soaring (into the sky), without spilling over, the destined life-force (ming) will be extended. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Harmonize by returning to the center, where both body and pure nature (xing) are preserved.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be unified and without (doubt or) division.</span> <span id="_ftnref27"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[27\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn27) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  This is called â€œknowing Dao.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wishing to be enveloped by it,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">you must unify to the furthest extent, and solidify that which is protected within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     â€œHolding to a ceremonious outward appearance</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">åŸ·å„€æœ?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è±¡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), respectfully welcome that which approaches</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ•¬è¿Žä¾†</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è€…</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">),â€? means to take the appearance of someone welcoming a respected guest, and demonstrate refined conduct. Doing so, the posture would be upright yet relaxed and dignified. As the comment on this section in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦this posture should be calm and dignified, but not prideful and stiff, putting the ego aside and being open to the guest. In both meditation and welcoming guests, the mind should also be bright, open, and attentive (internally and singularly attentive for the case of Daoist meditation). Guests are not welcomed ceremoniously with dull and lethargic minds, nor inattentive minds.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The line preceding this also suggests a stable and centered posture, not leaning or asymmetrical:  â€œLeft, right, front, and back, (running) full circle, they return to the place (at the center)â€? (line 201).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In addition to this early description of physical positioning, this section offers what may be the earliest description of mindfulness, or â€œinner observation (nei guan)â€? in Daoist literature.  Lines 196-200 instruct: </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By rejecting what is close and chasing after what is far, how can one but squander their power? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said:  â€œDesiring to take care of myself, I must first know my true inner state, and become acquainted with the universe by examining within myself.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In this way, one can know the image, thereby knowing the tendencies of their true inner state.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing the tendencies of their true inner state, they will know how to nourish life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Notably, the focus of this excerpt is a quote (â€œthus it is saidâ€¦â€?) from an earlier source, one which was either an early version of Lao Ziâ€™s chapter 47,</span> <span id="_ftnref28"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[28\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn28) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">or likely to have influenced it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Also important is the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s early mention of the cultivation and preservation of â€œdestined life-force (ming)â€? and â€œpure nature (xing).â€? The cultivation of xing and ming plays a central role in later Daoist internal practices, and was mentioned early on in Zhuang Ziâ€™s (circa 350 BC) parables and fictional discourses. Whereas Zhuang Zi mentions xing and ming as important factors in the development of a Sage, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">differs in its more direct instructions for cultivating xing and ming. Given that Zhuang Zi never provides much in the way of defining xing and ming, or methods focused on their cultivation, it would appear that these topics were already understood by his contemporary audience, and so did not need reiterating. There may have been even earlier philosophical texts that would have shown the introduction of xing and ming cultivation into the cultural sphere at the time, which were lost, tragically, to the Qin Dynasty book burnings of 213 BC. Thankfully, however, the proto-Daoist</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts can provide a clear example of these early cultivation practices, and thus help to trace their influences to writings from this era.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

## <span id="_Toc507075909"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Xin Shu Shang and Xin Shu Xia</span></span>

## <span id="_Toc507075910"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">(Art of the Heart-Mind, upper and lower volumes)</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">illustrates the symmetry between methods of ruling the kingdom, and methods of cultivating the self. This connection is considered, by Daoist initiates, an esoteric undertone of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, emphasized in Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary around 200 AD. Scholars have long argued that such connections are largely imagination and fancy. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, however, makes very clear that this metaphor had been a part of the proto-Daoist tradition since at least the time of Zhuang Zi. The opening lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">read:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the body,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The heart-mind holds the throne of the ruler.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The nine apertures hold offices</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Of various public servants.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the heart-mind remains with Dao,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The nine apertures act reasonably;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When desires and euphoric feelings are plentiful,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The eyes donâ€™t see appearances</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the ears donâ€™t hear sounds.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said:  When those above lose the Way,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those below neglect their duties.</span> <span id="_ftnref29"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[29\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn29)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This connection is again made clear in lines 41-42:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When scattered, it is as though a rebellion rises up within you. When calm and still, order naturally arrives.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Force cannot widely establish such order.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wisdom cannot formulate all strategies.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As stated in my comments on the opening lines of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     What the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">immediately reveals about the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, is that the Sage is not only a wise counsel to the nationâ€™s presiding authority, but is also within, guiding the ruler â€“ the heart-mind â€“ towards sovereignty over â€œall under Heavenâ€? and â€œthe myriad thingsâ€? â€“ ie., the senses, emotions, desires, stress, impulses, and anything else which must be stabilized in order to preserve inner unity. When these things are disordered, confusion reigns, and the sovereignty of the heart-mind is imperiled. The Sage is to the ruler what the spiritâ€™s illumination is upon the heart-mind. She brings clarity, perception, and peace to the ruler. To invite the Sage, the ruler must first become stable and orderly, kind and genuine.  Then the Sage will find it safe to convene with him, seeing that the ruler is capable of giving up tyrannical power and instead following Dao. The art of the heart-mind is not simply a way to find peace, but a way to bring forth the spiritual intelligence â€“ the Sage.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">   </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yellow Emperorâ€™s Classic on Internal Medicine, Plain Questions (Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">contains, perhaps later,</span> <span id="_ftnref30"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[30\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn30) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">expansions of the administrative metaphor found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.  For example, in chapter eight of this text we find a more detailed illustration of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s opening lines:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Qi Bo repliedâ€¦ </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The heart holds the office of the ruler;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth spiritual intelligence.</span> <span id="_ftnref31"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[31\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn31)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The lungs hold the office of the grand tutor;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They bring forth order and moderation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The liver holds the office of the general;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth ambitions and planning.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The gallbladder holds the office of the rectifier;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth decisiveness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pericardium (enclosure of the heart) holds the office of minister and envoy;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth joy and pleasure.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The spleen and stomach hold the office in charge of grain storage;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They bring forth the five tastes (flavours).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The large intestine holds the office of transportation and distribution;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth change and transformation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The small intestine holds the office in charge of receiving bounty;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth things which have been transformed and processed.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The kidneys hold the office in charge of increasing power;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They bring forth ability and expertise.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The triple burner holds the office of regulating channels;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It brings forth pathways for water.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The urinary bladder holds the office of regional administrator;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Bodily fluids are stored in it, and when their qi has been transformed, they are brought forth.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All of these twelve offices must not lose their connection to each other.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, when the ruler is enlightened, the subordinates are peaceful.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivating life in this way, longevity ensues</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And until the end of the era, there will be no danger.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thereby all under heaven will greatly flourish.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If the ruler is not enlightened, the subordinates are endangered.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They seal up the paths of communication, and the body is greatly injured.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivating life in this way brings disaster.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Ruling the world in such a way endangers the ancestral heritage.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be careful of this!  Be careful of this!</span> <span id="_ftnref32"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[32\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn32)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As the heart-mind, which also houses the spirit, brings peace to the bodyâ€™s subordinate organs and functions, the art, or method, of the heart-mind is not only for the benefit of the mind, but also to generate the complete harmony of the physical and spiritual self. It is a method of ruling the body through the spirit. By dissolving internal forces that can destabilize the spirit, for example the energy of anger and its ability to wrest decision making power from the spirit, practices in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">aid in re-establishing homeostasis and thereby preventing myriads of illnesses. Given that Classical Chinese Medicine rightfully held prevention as superior to all other forms of treatment, the art of the heart-mind was duly revered as a deeply profound and enriching method of preventative health-care.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It should be noted that the modern equivalent term for</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">xin shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¿ƒ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è¡“</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) is</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">xin fa</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¿ƒ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ³•</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).  The shared meaning between</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">fa</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is method, or technique, while</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also means skill and art, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">fa</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also means law, principle, and dharma.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Fa</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">appears in the titles of a few other books in the Guan Zi, for example â€œPrinciples of Warâ€? (Bing Fa) and â€œPrinciples of Lawâ€? (Fa Fa).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The commentary included in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as part of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">offers a number of clarifications of Daoist concepts, such as the relationship between Dao and De, and the interchangeable use of Virtue (De) and attainment (de).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Virtue is the abode of Dao.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When things attain (Virtue), they live.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Being alive, they can know the office of Daoâ€™s essence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, Virtue (De) also means â€œattainment (de).â€? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for this attainment, it is called â€œattaining the causality.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The effortlessness of this (causality) is called â€œDao.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The abode of Dao is called â€œVirtue.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, between Dao and Virtue, there is no space.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For this reason, it is said â€œthey are not separate.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(XSS 113-121)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     That such an early commentary on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">exists shows its popularity at the time. Commentaries are most often written when a text has reached a considerable audience and thereby generated enough discussion that someone more familiar with the subject eventually seeks to address this audience, especially when that audience has spread beyond the reach of those immersed in the traditions from which the teachings arose. For example, detailed commentaries on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">did not appear for nearly 500 years after it was written, and commentaries on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huang Di Nei Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">did not appear for nearly 1000 years after it was written,</span> <span id="_ftnref33"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[33\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn33) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">despite the interest and questions that these texts were sure to have inspired.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s renown may also be evident in the writing of Confucian scholar Xun Zi (313-238 BC), who shows a great deal of influence from Daoist thought, though he is also critical of Lao Zi.</span> <span id="_ftnref34"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[34\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn34) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In his chapter â€œRemoving Obstacles,â€? (c. 250 BC), Xun Zi echoes the opening lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, referring to the mind as the ruler of the body (â€œand the host of spiritual intelligenceâ€?). He then continues in a fashion that further reflects the teachings of unification found throughout the proto-Daoist</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A mind that branches out in many directions knows nothing; a mind that is not level is not acute; a mind that is divided is doubtful and confused. But for a mind with focused scrutiny, the myriad things can come together in its understanding; for in oneself is a unity that runs though all categories.</span> <span id="_ftnref35"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[35\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn35)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As with the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">shows that body alignment, if not sitting meditation, was in fact part of the early heart-mind cultivation techniques. Whereas the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Upper Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begins by focusing on aligning the heart-mind so as to bring order to oneâ€™s â€˜inner kingdomâ€™, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Lower Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begins by stating, â€œWhen the bodily form is not aligned</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(æ­£</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">: straight, aligned, upright), Virtue does not approach.â€? So, just as one can bring peace and order to their nation by bringing peace and order to themselves, they can also bring peace and order to themselves internally by bringing peace and order (alignment) to their body, externally. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">further develops connections between internal and external government, focusing primarily on self cultivation as a means to establishing order in oneâ€™s kingdom, both literally and figuratively.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Added to this metaphor is that of governing the heart-mind and body according to the patterns of Heaven and Earth. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">summarizes these analogies by closing with the saying â€œFor what is above, study the Heavens; for what is below, study the Earth.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Most of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is found dotted throughout the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which appears to be either a redaction of the lower (â€œxiaâ€?)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, or to have developed out of the same oral tradition. The inclusion of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, regardless of its many similarities to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, was possibly due to it having many duplicates as a self-contained book, likely alongside the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.  The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, then, may have been collated by Liu Xiang, and assisting scholars, from a multitude of scattered book fragments on internal cultivation. This might explain why the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(book 49) is separated from the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(book 36),</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(book 37), and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(book 38), which appear consecutively in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. It might also explain the drastic reconfiguration of shared lines, variations in terminology, and why the sequence of these shared lines is more fluid in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, where ideas follow more readily from the developing support of their preceding lines. This sequence appears as follows, outlined by the line groupings in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">1)</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">     </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the body is aligned, the Virtue of Dao approaches and the body fills with qi.  The self is thereby transcended as the body and mind function like Heaven and Earth. (lines 1-20)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">2)</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">     </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This transcendence of self brings all things together and makes them peaceful in their unity.  Those who attain this unity within are blessed with an awareness of the causes of calamity and good fortune. (lines 21-31)</span>

## <span id="_Toc507075911"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Nei Ye (Internal Cultivation)</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">reflects the same internal cultivation tradition as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, while focusing more on physical longevity.
