This technique is the foundation, leading to later stages known as nei gong, and nei dan, both also briefly suggested in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. The heart-mind technique, aside from its role in nei gong and nei dan, is taught as a means to bring â€œspiritual intelligenceâ€? (shen ming) â€“ a facet of consciousness in which greater perception, and unity with Dao, are made possible by the spiritâ€™s illumination of the mind. Another benefit of cultivating â€œspiritual intelligenceâ€? is increased emotional-intelligence â€“ oneâ€™s capacity to recognize their own emotions and mitigate the negative effect of these emotions in their lives. Such negative effects might include limitations on impulse control, on oneâ€™s ability to differentiate sense and reality, and on self-actualization. Emotional intelligence is, of course, important for rulers, generals, and other leaders who must determine the reality of a situation before deciding appropriate courses of action or non-action. <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To understand shen ming (spiritual brilliance/spiritual intelligence), it helps to think of shen-spirit as a divine essence, rather than an entity in the way that spirit is understood in the West. Essential to consciousness, shen is often translated for Chinese medical purposes as â€œmind,â€? though it contains a wider applicability in Daoist traditions. Shen ming could be translated as spiritual enlightenment, though to avoid complicating the term with Buddhist notions of enlightenment, spiritual intelligence seems more fitting (</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ming</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">means literally â€œto see clearly,â€? and â€œthe illumination of the sun and moonâ€?).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The term shen ming is found elsewhere as referring to guardian spirits, â€œspiritual lights,â€? which act like emissaries from Heaven, protecting and developing those who cultivate â€œinner attainmentâ€? or â€œinner Virtue.â€? While early Daoist definitions of shen ming are elusive, its function resembles the ancient Chinese theory of the three yang-spirits (hun) and seven yin-spirits (po) that all people are said to be born with. The hun and po spirits are integral to life within the physical body, while loss of these spirits causes spiritual and physical illness. Shen ming, on the other hand, is not intrinsic to each individual, but comes and goes according to how one keeps their inner domain, like small birds taking rest where it is peaceful, or Daoist gods visiting the sanctity of a Daoist temple. A similarity appears between the shen ming guardians and the shen ming awakening, as they both seem to take up residence when a person is purified of emotions and cravings. For example, Heshang Gong comments on chapter 16 of the Dao De Jing:</span>

# <span id="_Toc507075912"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Guan Ziâ€™s Influence on the Guigu Zi (Ghost Valley Master)</span></span>

In perception we are ordinarily assailed by a stream of conceptualizing tendencies, which have their ultimate source in linguistic conventions and categorizing practices. <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€˜inner Virtueâ€™.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thereby, the energy of intention is settled;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Having settled, it returns to alignment.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Energy-breath then fills the body,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And oneâ€™s conduct is righteous and upright.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Note the nature of this conduct as it relates to Guigu Ziâ€™s ability to determine whether or not one cultivates their will:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To know if othersâ€™ energy is abundant or lacking, and if they cultivate the energy of their will, examine their peace and stability. Thereby, know their ability.</span>

# <span id="_Toc507075953"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">The Zen of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span></span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">    </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Chinese Buddhism, quiet openly, drew a great deal from the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Zhuang Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and thereby the cultural history that gave birth to these texts.  When Chan masters speak of emptiness, no-mind, no form, and no self, they seem to be speaking of the Dao itself and providing keys to the mysteries spoken of by Lao Zi centuries earlier.</span> <span id="_ftnref61"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[61\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn61)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     For example, in the Zen teachings popular with Japanese samurai, focusing largely on maintaining an empty and agile mind, we see a later development of teachings found in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 51-59:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the junzi does not dwell on what he likes, nor is he coerced by what he dislikes.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Tranquil, pleasant, and effortless, he abandons wisdom, and it abides in him as a result.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He responds, but does not initiate;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Moves but does not possess.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If one is excessively headstrong, they will err when adapting to changes.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, the ruler who has Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Remains in the state of not knowing.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He responds to things as though by coincidence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the Dao of tranquil means.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Though Buddhist teachings have oftentimes been the vehicle that brought these indigenous Chinese teachings back around to Chinese followers of Daoism, the Daoist precedence of their philosophical commonalities tends to be egregiously overlooked, to this day.</span> <span id="_ftnref62"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[62\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn62) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075954"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Oneness in Buddhism and the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When people today think of Oneness, they generally think of it in terms of the unity of all phenomena.  This is the understanding of unity commonly found in Buddhism, yet also put forth by Zhuang Zi in his chapter â€œThe Talisman of Complete Virtue.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucius replied: â€œDeath and life are both great matters, yet are not considered as changes (to Wang Tai).  If Heaven and Earth were to tumble over and sink into each other, he would not consider this any loss.  His focus is on that which is without any falseness.  He does not follow along with the changes of things, knowing that transformation is but their certain destiny.  Rather, he guards the source of these changes within himself.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Chang Ji asked: â€œWhat do you mean by that?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucius replied: â€œLooking at things from their differences, we find a liver and a gallbladder; a Chu State and a Yue State.  Looking at things from their sameness, the myriad things are all one.  As such, (Wang Tai) does not know what is meant for his eyes or ears, but simply allows his mind to float along in the harmony of Virtue.  Things are seen as one, and so he does not see loss. When he lost his foot, he considered it as leaving behind a pile of earth.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref63"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[63\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn63) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  </span>

# <span id="_Toc507075955"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Translating the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The translations and annotations for the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">make a case for retaining numerous characters that have been considered typos by various eminent scholars in the field. Annotations are provided where dispute of the translation is anticipated for this and other reasons, sometimes addressing the suggested changes, or otherwise simply providing support for the translation.  This is in an effort to provide readers with a translation of the original text as it was received in ancient times.  Though itâ€™s possible that the texts have numerous errors, I have tried to keep an open mind as to how these characters made sense to the early scribes and authors, finding this exercise, coupled with additional research, to reveal functional and relevant meanings for the original characters in all but one or two occasions.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(BX) begins by addressing matters of decorum and diplomacy; however, as soon becomes apparent, these strategies are not simply techniques to avoid conflict. Rather, they are offered by someone steeped in the Daoist Sageâ€™s tradition of cultivating longevity and spiritual evolution, seeking to impart this path to enlightenment upon those tasked with bringing peace and stability to Chinaâ€™s Warring States Period.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">bears many resemblances to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(DDJ), including its simultaneous outer and inner meanings when speaking of government.</span> <span id="_ftnref67"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[67\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn67) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is considered an early confirmation of Lao Ziâ€™s hidden metaphors for internal cultivation in methods of statecraft. However, these proto-Daoist texts in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">show that this metaphor was well established by the time the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was more widely circulated, around 200 B.C.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This ability to speak with simultaneous exoteric and esoteric meanings is evident in the first five lines of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Purifying the Heart-Mind (Bai Xin)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. The treatise begins: â€œTo  establish long-standing order: take peace and tranquility as your revered ancestor.â€? The essence of Daoist cultivation lies in longevity and a peaceful existence, attained by following nature and learning from, for example, the detachment of Heaven and patience of Earth. â€œTake peace and tranquility as your revered ancestor / yi jin wei zongâ€? teaches that the basis of this masterâ€™s diplomacy lies in the â€˜art of the heart-mindâ€™ â€“ an art which can ensure, and even be used to describe, the most skillful policy in all matters of government. This sentence can also be read â€œconsider silence as the origin,â€? or â€œconsider bringing peace to the world as a form of worship.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     How should one take peace and tranquility as their revered ancestor?  Line three reads:  â€œTreat opportune moments as precious jewels.â€? When appreciating a precious jewel, one may not even touch it, yet they will look at it deeply, considering its hues, and the hidden lines within it. If one wishes to shape such a jewel, they must find its soft and hard points so that their shaping of it neither destroys it, nor removes more than is necessary to reveal its full splendour.  Above all, they give it their full attention, and do not cast it aside. This is, as line four states, to treat the moment as â€œa matter of ceremony.â€? And in this harmony, one finds the path towards longevity, and peace (see line 5).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     â€œTreat opportune moments as precious jewels,â€? refers to opportunities, both immediate and seasonal, with the word â€œshi,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ™‚</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, season, timing.â€? This line may intentionally corresponds with the last several lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, on timing and cultivation, while also speaking of the external factors of planning and acting according to seasons of planting, growing, harvesting, and storing, whatever these steps may mean to oneâ€™s given endeavours.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œTreat political affairs as a matter of ceremonyâ€? is also reflected later on (lines 201-207) in regards to keeping an outward appearance of decorum during sitting meditation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If I am not ceremonious, who will see an advantage and not act on it? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While these lines offer external, actionable, guidance, they reveal the actions of someone who holds to his or her practice of keeping the heart-mind undisturbed, cautiously making sure that their mind does not become muddied with thoughts, and emotionally entangled.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem"> </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Evidently speaking as someone of high authority, the author explains here that leaders must conduct themselves, in these precious moments, in a calm and dignified manner so as to avoid setting a precedent for ungracious behaviour. After all, if those tasked with ensuring the greater good are impetuous and selfish, what more can be expected of those under them?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This circumstance provides a helpful model of what it means to be in accord with Dao. Encountering a situation of great potential gain or loss, the leader is not â€œthe first to move forwardâ€? but remains earnest and considerate. They suspend their personal goals to engender a climate of respect and rectitude. As Lao Zi says in DDJ77:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who can have in excess, and care for all under Heaven? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Only those who have Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And in DDJ67:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  I have three treasures</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Which I hold close and protect</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The first is kindness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The second is economy</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The third is not daring to be first (and take precedence over) the worldâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While not indicating any familiarity with the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">clearly illustrates Lao Ziâ€™s â€œthird treasureâ€? in lines 6-10. This sentiment of working harmoniously with others appears in the opening and closing remarks of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, showing the importance of social unity in its philosophy.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Similarities to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also appear between BX11-14 and DDJ2:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ Noise and tone are harmonized by each other</span> <span id="_ftnref68"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[68\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn68)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Front and back accompany each other</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages handle affairs with non-action</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They practice wordless instruction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the myriad things all take their placesâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     At first glance, it may appear that these authors discourage initiative altogether; however, as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">will soon make clear, their objective is accordance with Heaven,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¤© Tian, often equated, perhaps rightfully so, to the Western notions of Nature and its manifestations â€“ nature.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All areas of human life, internal and external, can thrive by according with nature, and so the early sages sought ways to fit into its patterns and ebbs and flows. Such logic follows that if people can learn to live as one with</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">each other</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, they will also thrive as one with nature; just as by cultivating harmony within oneself, harmony will naturally manifest itself in oneâ€™s life.</span> <span id="_ftnref69"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[69\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn69)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     It should be noted that the nature of human beings, according to Daoists, is qing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.1rem ;letter-spacing:0.27rem">é?œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:  silence, tranquility, stillness. It is this state to which all things return. While humans have powerful emotions, like rainstorms, these emotions do not last, and are followed again by tranquility. As these texts show, by cultivating tranquility, one can see things as they are, and thus act according to the time. So, by non-action, one knows the time; and when that precious timing arrives, it is embraced accordingly.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, for producing many flourishing things, nothing is greater than Heaven and Earth;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Here we see the emergence of a higher wisdom: the â€œclear visionâ€?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ˜Ž ming: enlightenment) that accompanies oneâ€™s ability to preserve Dao within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While, again, not indicating any familiarity with it, lines 15-18 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">show a striking correlation to the following lines from DDJ1, perhaps offering further insights into them:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ1:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Dao that can be told is not the Eternal Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The name that can be named is not the Eternal Name</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Named is the mother of the myriad thingsâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">BX15-20:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The true primordial strategy is the root from which life springs.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing its image, one apprehends its form.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reaching to its principles, one knows its nature.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Seeking its end, one knows its name</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, for producing many flourishing things, nothing is greater than Heaven and Earth.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For transforming many things, nothing can transform so many things as the sun and moon.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">calls â€œthe</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">åŽŸå§‹ primordial</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è¨ˆ strategy (that is)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¯¦ real,â€? the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">refers to as the Eternal Dao in the verse â€œThe Dao that can be told is not the Eternal Dao.â€? Both texts begin this discourse by setting apart the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">true</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao. As will be seen later, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also uses the term</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é?“ Dao much in the same way as Lao Zi.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The parallels continue:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ1:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Thus, always without desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observing its inner subtlety</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Always with desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observing its outer surfaceâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">BX17-18:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reaching to its principles, one knows its nature.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Seeking its end, one knows its name</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Despite the stark similarities in these verses, the differences in their terminology and shifted sequences of development suggest that both texts were written records of a shared oral tradition, rather than one directly influencing the other.  Their verse like qualities further suggest an oral transmission aided by these mnemonic devices.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 15-16 also shed light on DDJ35â€™s â€œby holding onto the great image, the world is put into motion.â€? The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">clarifies the meaning of â€œthe image,â€? here, as an indistinct sense of Dao, not yet revealing its principles. Holding to the image, then, is to â€œknow without knowing;â€? in other words, to know Dao, â€œthe true primordial strategy,â€? without intellectualizing it. Heshang Gong (c. 200 AD) comments on this line from DDJ35:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œBy holding onto the great image, the world is put into motionâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œHolding onto,â€? here, means holding close. â€œImage,â€? here, means Dao. The Sage holds the Great Dao close to him, and everything in the world shifts its heart to the way things once were. He governs his body, and Heaven sends down spiritual lights. (These spiritual lights go) back and forth between his body (and Heaven).</span> <span id="_ftnref71"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[71\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn71)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As such, Heaven does not twist its seasons in consideration of an individual thing.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">23</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">          </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ˜Žå?›è?–</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">äºº</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">äº¦ä¸?ç‚ºä¸€äººæž‰å…¶æ³•ã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven moves according to its own movements, and the myriad things arrange their own benefits.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage also moves according to his own movements, and the hundred clans arrange their own benefits.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For this reason, each of the myriad things all praise them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Preserving Dao within, Sages do not take counsel from the confused logic and surface understanding of those whose vision is blurred by desire, fear, ambition, and self-interest.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 19-26 present a backdrop of ideas concerning Heaven, Earth, and the Sage that the author of DDJ5 may have presupposed a familiarity with when stating:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven and Earth do not act benevolently</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The myriad things are treated no differently than ceremonial grass-dogs</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages do not act benevolently</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The hundred clans are treated no differently than ceremonial grass-dogs</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wang Bi, a 2</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">nd</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">century commentator on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, interpreted these lines to mean that all people are treated equally under the law, stating:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The myriad things are all governed together and managed in the same way. Thus, (Heaven and Earth) are not benevolent.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Ren, translated as â€œbenevolence,â€? carried a meaning, especially in ancient times, of diligent consideration for courtesy, manners, and hierarchies, following the culture of those who served in the court. One of the most significant contrasts between Daoists and Confucians was that Daoists had little value for complex and prescribed manners and courtesies which they felt must flow as a natural expression from peopleâ€™s sense of oneness with all things.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heshang Gong comments on the first line of DDJ5:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œHeaven bestows, and Earth transforms. It is not because of benevolence or mercy that they do this, but simply because it is in their nature (ziran).â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Ziran</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è‡ª</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç„¶</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) translates literally to â€œas itself,â€? and means â€œspontaneous, natural action.â€? The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">describes ziran, here, without using the term, in lines 24-25:  â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Heaven moves according to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è¡Œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">moves, follows) its own movements</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦â€?  This line precedes another helpful explanation, this time of â€œnot benevolent,â€? with â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">and the myriad things arrange their own benefits</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.â€? If Heaven was benevolent, it would arrange things on behalf of the myriad things, yet instead, it simply acts according to its nurturing nature (described in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as De, â€œVirtueâ€?), and this is enough for the myriad beings to arrange things for themselves. One might say that to give a fish is benevolent, but Heaven and the Sage are more like the lake itself. By simply acting according to their own nature, they provide all things the opportunity to reap these benefits.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     By the same token, we also see that Heaven and Earth are impartial; they are unaffected by partisanship or privilege.  The ancient texts taught that righteousness, virtue, and adherence to Dao will determine fortune.  Although:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">for producing many flourishing things, nothing is greater than Heaven and Earth; for transforming many things, nothing can transform so many things as the sun and moon  (BX19-20)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">those who contravene the Dao of Heaven may soon learn that</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">for causing urgency in people, nothing is more urgent than water and fire (BX21).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is part of the teachings on the â€œart of the heart-mind,â€? the integrity and stability described in lines 22â€“26 also allude to â€˜retaining the throne of the rulerâ€™ â€“ a metaphor in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(XSS) for not allowing the senses to wrest power from the heart-mind.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When names are corrected and laws perfected, the Sage is without further endeavours.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Impartial and unhurried, one can see what corresponds to reality, remove what is illusory, and further clarify the nature and shape of a given situation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Given the similarity between lines 22-26 and DDJ5 (see above), lines 27-29 appear to reflect the end of DDJ5, while lines 19-20 also reflect its middle lines.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The second part of DDJ5 reads:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  The gate of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is it not like a bagpipe?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Empty yet not finished</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It moves, and again more is pushed forth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">BX19-20:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, for producing many flourishing things, nothing is greater than Heaven and Earth. For transforming many things, nothing can transform so many things as the sun and moon</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ5:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To speak countless words is worthless</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is not as good as guarding balance within</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">BX27-32:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sageâ€™s method of government is to still the body and wait.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Things then arrive at their names, (showing what they are,) and naturally fall into place.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As these names naturally order themselves, those which do not fit are abolished.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When names are corrected and laws perfected, the Sage is without further endeavours</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Including lines 19-20 in this section, we see that all of DDJ5 is reflected in lines 19-29. The inexhaustible creative power of the â€œbagpipeâ€? (often translated as</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">bellows</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">)</span> <span id="_ftnref72"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[72\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn72) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is an illustration of the inexhaustible power of Heaven and Earth, described in BX19-21, while Lao Ziâ€™s disregard for attempts to inflate reality with words is described in BX27-32. Again, the drastically different sequences in which these same ideas appear suggests that both texts were written from their authorsâ€™ own contemplation of ideas circulating amongst their peers at the time.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ3 can also be better understood through BX27-29.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">BX27-29:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sageâ€™s (method of) government is to still the body and wait. Things then arrive at their names and naturally fall into place.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ3:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Therefore, the Sageâ€™s government</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Empties the heart-mind and enriches the stomach</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Softens the will and strengthens the bones</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People then remain uncontrived and without desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While the scheming do not dare to act</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Act by not acting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And everything will fall into place</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This passage from the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">has been a source of controversy, as many found it to suggest making the populace ignorant; however, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and commentators such as Heshang Gong, show that â€œthe Sageâ€™s (method of) governmentâ€? simultaneously refers to self-cultivation and meditation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also makes clear the interest of the ancient sages in â€œnames,â€? and these namesâ€™ true inclinations.</span> <span id="_ftnref73"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[73\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn73) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing these inclinations helps sages to understand the roles (also a facet of meaning in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œå??</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">namesâ€?) of various phenomena in the world. Giving names to things assigns their connection to other things. The use and origin of things is more open without their names. Imagine, for example, the way an animal sees the world without words, and how things are not so distinguished when they no longer have any names. As we understand how to use things, we differentiate them with names. This process is at the basis of wisdom, and so is the role of the Sage.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Further, this practice of seeing the true character of external things coincides with the practice of observing oneâ€™s own internal phenomena, such as cravings and emotions, which are brought to stability and order by practicing â€œthe Sageâ€™s method of government.â€? Such considerations can be seen in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter one:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  The Nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Named is the mother of the myriad things</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, always without desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observing its inner subtlety</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Always with desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observing its outer surface</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">These two were born together, yet differ in name</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Together, they are called Fathomless Mysteryâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage is unattached to outcomes. Ego is just a responsibility that they would happily divest themselves of, given the opportunity. <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 33-36 also correlate to DDJ3â€™s â€œsoftening the will.â€? Heshang Gongâ€™s comment on this line helps to illustrate the proximity of these ideas as they were understood in the proto-Daoist culture:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œSoftens the willâ€? refers to willfulness, stubbornness. As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">point out, softening oneâ€™s will to control reality is an important step towards seeing what things truly are. When scheming desires and emotions stop trying to control situations (â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">People then remain uncontrived and without desires, while the scheming do not dare to actâ€? â€“</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ3</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the â€˜heart of the heart-mindâ€™</span> <span id="_ftnref74"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[74\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn74) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">attains sovereignty, and a new, enlightened, perception of reality.</span>

Thus, it is better to soften oneâ€™s willfulness, and forcefulness, so as to â€œfollow the changesâ€? and do what is best for the time.</span> <span id="_ftnref75"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[75\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn75)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When there is abundance, (people are) generous; when there is little, (people are) studious.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(This causes) things to be in surplus, or insufficient.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">39</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">           </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å…µä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å‡º</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å‡ºæ–¼</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">äºº</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Deploying an army is to send it out towards others;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When others invade, they invade oneâ€™s own territory.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(However,) the success of an army follows good fortune,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is why it is said that omens and apparitions (arrive to defend) the righteousness of others.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Thus,) an army must never lack righteousness.</span> <span id="_ftnref76"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[76\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn76)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Outcomes are unpredictable, but even more so when sought greedily, without considering the rights of others. Thus, the Sage relies on righteousness, and so avoids unexpected misfortunes that might arise from seemingly successful ventures.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 37-44 go further into the dangers of arrogance, hinted at in the lines preceding, and made more explicit in DDJ9â€™s: â€œWhen fortune and wealth bring arrogance, they bring the misfortune of their own lossâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 37-38 show that the inclination of people is to take for granted when they have enough, and to be studious when their resources have been depleted. Note that the parallel structure running through lines 37 to 44 suggests that lines 37-38 are not simply a comment on the previous statement of â€˜doing what is best for the time,â€™ but also connect the discourse that follows them with the preceding considerations of consequence and appropriate action.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The ideas in lines 39-48 also show up in DDJ67:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ Through kindness, there can be courage</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Through economy, there can be generosity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Through not brazenly taking precedence over the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I can fashion vessels of longevity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Now, if one neglects kindness in courage</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Neglects economy in generosity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Neglects humility in being at the forefront</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They will die.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So, kindness in times of war brings victory</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And protecting it brings strength and stability</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven will bring its aid</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And kindness will be protected</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And in DDJ69:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the employment of an army, there is a saying:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œI dare not be the host, but I will be a guest</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I dare not advance an inch, but will step back a footâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called advancing without advancing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Misfortune has no greater cause</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Than not respecting an enemy</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By not respecting an enemy</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">How much do we risk destroying what is precious?...</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">45</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">          </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¼·è€Œé©•è€…æ??å…¶</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å¼·</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are forceful and arrogant, their strength is decreased;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">46</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">          </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¼±è€Œé©•è€…å‰?æ­»äº¡ã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are weak and arrogant, death and destruction await them;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">47</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">          </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¼·è€Œå?‘</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç¾©</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¿¡å…¶å¼·ã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When strong, humble, and righteous, this is true strength;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">49</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">          </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ˜¯æ•…é©•ä¹‹é¤˜</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å?‘</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å?‘ä¹‹é¤˜é©•ã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For these reasons, the excessively arrogant are humbled, and the excessively humble become arrogant.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By cultivating himself, but not over-estimating himself, the Sage invites good will, greater clarity, and greater opportunities for success.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The idea of arrogance leading to downfall appears in many chapters of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Notice, for example, the similarity between DDJ30 and lines 45-49.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Where troops gather, thorns and brambles appear </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following war, there is sure to be famine and misfortune</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Large armies are sure to bring sadness in the future</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim well, and then stop</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Do not dare to abuse power</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not boast</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not attack again</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not become arrogant</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not claim all the credit</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not abuse power</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Things thrive in their prime and then become aged</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œnot Daoâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If this were practiced throughout, all under Heaven could be provided for.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And not by prophesy or divination, but by how cautiously one follows (Dao), can you know fortune and misfortune.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing that success for all means lasting success, the Sage is careful to ensure that he remains with Dao, like a coachman takes care not to lose his carriage.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To understand how one follows the way of Dao when orchestrating affairs, we might turn to DDJ51:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  It actuates them but does not possess them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sets them in motion but does not expect of them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It extends their lives without ruling and controlling them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called Fathomless Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivating the Virtue of Dao, and the benefit to those who do, is referred to in DDJ54, where the term â€œVirtueâ€? can otherwise be read as its synonym and homonym:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¾— attainmentâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Cultivate this in the body and its Virtue will be true</span> <span id="_ftnref80"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[80\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn80)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivate this in the home and its Virtue will be plentiful</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivate this in the village and its Virtue will be long lasting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivate this in the nation and its Virtue will be abundant</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cultivate this in the world and its Virtue will be widespreadâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 62-63 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">offer an explanation of the closing lines in DDJ38,</span> <span id="_ftnref81"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[81\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn81) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">which also addresses putting more importance on divination than intrinsic virtue (De):</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Thus, when Dao is lost, virtue appears</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sageâ€™s spiritual intelligence is elusive, but real.  To focus on selfish endeavours would complicate his connection to the oneness of all, and so he places value on following Dao and lets its principles of renewal take care of his needs.    </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ37 also discusses inner stability and the nameless:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Dao is always effortless yet without inaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The simplicity of the nameless removes all desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the tranquility of desirelessness is established</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The world stabilizes itself</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 69-72 help to explain why the term â€œthe namelessâ€? is used to describe the ineffable, and begin a transition into a more overt discussion of self-cultivation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 65-72 speak to taking action when necessary and then releasing the grip of control. This theme holds the surface meaning of managing affairs while allowing the nature of situations of reveal themselves.  It also has implications pertaining to the heart-mind and the inner Sage of spiritual intelligence. When action is required, the heart-mind gives rise to thought and contemplation, but when understanding has been reached, the ruler (heart-mind) does not spin his wheels on the subject. Rather, the heart-mind returns to emptiness and practices the Sageâ€™s way of government, exemplified by Dao and â€œFathomless Virtue.â€? As explained in the ancient commentary section of the Xin Shu Shang:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œResponding to things as though by coincidence.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œadapting to the seasonâ€? â€“</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Like a shadow taking the shape of a form,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Or an echo responding to a sound.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, when things reach them, (the junzi) respond.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When these things move on, (the junzi) remain in place.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This means (the junzi) reverts back to emptiness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(XSS 215-221)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Our fear of losing something often gets in the way of obtaining it.  The Sage is not afraid of continuing on as he is, and so is not afraid of failing to obtain something new. This, paradoxically, affords him success in obtaining something that escaped others of the same abilities.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 73-75 travel deeper into the nameless, the ineffable, arriving at the â€œuntroddenâ€? purity in the â€œdepths of the heart</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(è¡·</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).â€? Such a description is reminiscent of what later Daoist teachings on cultivating the Internal Elixir (Nei Dan) referred to as the Mysterious Pass. Perhaps the clearest description of the Mysterious Pass is found in Li Daochunâ€™s (circa 1300 AD)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Collected works on Central Harmony</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(aka</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Book of Balance and Harmony</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, circa 1300 AD).  </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Mysterious Pass</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">çŽ„</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">é—œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, xuan guan) is the pass of the most mysterious, most subtle, of mechanisms... Why do none of the Nei Dan texts give the exact location of the Mysterious Pass? It is because it is difficult to describe, and no attempts to do so will succeed that they call it the â€œMysterious Pass.â€? Therefore, the Sages simply wrote of it with the single character, â€œcenter,â€? and had (students) understand that â€œcenterâ€? referred to the Mysterious Pass. So â€œcenterâ€? meant neither inside nor outside, upper nor lower.  It was not this sort of center.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When Buddhists say, â€œthinking neither good thoughts nor bad thoughts, see the face of your original self</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸?æ€?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å–„,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸?æ€?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æƒ¡,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ­£æ??éº¼</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ™‚,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é‚£ç®‡æ˜¯è‡ªå·±æœ¬ä¾†é?¢</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç›®</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">),â€? this is the â€œcenterâ€? of Chan Buddhism. When Confucians say, â€œwhen euphoria, anger, sadness, and pleasure have not yet come forth, this is called â€˜the centerâ€™,â€? this is the door of Confucians</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ­¤å„’å®¶ä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æˆ¶</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) â€“ their â€œcenter.â€? When Daoists say, â€œthe place where thinking does not arise is called â€˜the centerâ€™,â€? this is the â€œcenterâ€? of Daoism. This is how â€œthe centerâ€? applies to the three teachings.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When the Yi Jing (I Ching) says â€œtranquil and unmoving,â€? this refers to the â€œcenter.â€? â€œSensing and accomplishing,â€? is the employment the center.  Lao Zi says â€œArrive at supreme emptiness; embrace deep silence. Myriad creatures arise together. I thereby observe them returning.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The Yi Jing says: â€œReturning, see the heart of Heaven and Earth.â€? The Yi Jing hexagram â€œReturningâ€? shows one yang line arising under 5 yin lines. Yin is stillness (and silence). Yang is movement. At the extreme of stillness there is movement. This point (before) movement is the Mysterious Pass.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Put your mind to the place from which thinking arises. Persevering in this, the Mysterious Pass will naturally appear. Upon seeing the Mysterious Pass, the medicinal substance, firing process, timely operation, subtracting and adding, and final release through emergence of the spiritual embryo, collectively come from nowhere but this single opening.</span> <span id="_ftnref84"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[84\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn84)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">uses similar terminology to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and describes the pristine oasis found in the â€œheart of the heart-mindâ€? as such:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Within the center of the heart-mind, there is another heart-mind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In this heart of the heart-mind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There is a resonance (intent) which precedes words </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(lines 165-167)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While sayings such as â€œ(To value what is) beyond achievement is to value achievementâ€? likely carry an internal meaning meant to help one transcend the mind and find their way towards this Mysterious Pass, in characteristic proto-Daoist fashion, they carry additional wisdom in their surface meanings. Discovering and exploring the center of the heart requires a purity and sincerity that can easily escape those who seek renown, and so the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">teaches the importance of first abandoning this superfluous interest. This is reflected in the opening lines of DDJ2, often interpreted to mean that when someone is appreciated by all, they become full of themselves and thus no longer merit such praise. These lines, again, read:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When all know the beautiful to be beautiful</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This ends in ugliness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When all know the good to be good</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the end there is â€œnot goodâ€?â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Note, too, the understanding shared between line 78, and the end of DDJ77:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Heavenâ€™s Way diminishes what has excess</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And restores what lacks sufficiency</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The way of man, however, is not this way</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Diminishing what suffers lack</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And assisting where there is excess</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who can have in excess, and care for all under Heaven? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Only those who have Daoâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The phrase â€œ(what is) ç„¡æˆ? beyond achievementâ€? in line 79 suggests an appellation similar to â€œthe nameless.â€? The Dao encompasses all things and thus all names. It encompasses all achievements and is, thus, beyond all achievements. Dao encompasses all action and, in a sense, it</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">is</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">action; thus, it is beyond all actions, and said to be â€œwithout actionâ€? (wu wei).</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç„¡ Wu, withoutâ€? can therefore also be understood in these phrases similar to the way it is understood in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç„¡æ•¸</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">numberlessâ€? and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç„¡é™? limitlessâ€? when describing infinitude.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To borrow the conclusion from line 81, then:  In action, heed what is â€˜beyond action.â€™</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lao Ziâ€™s DDJ48 helps to clarify these lines further:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of learning requires daily accumulation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of Dao requires daily reduction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reducing and reducing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Until arriving at effortlessness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Effortless, yet without inaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Conquering all under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is best done without the endeavour to do so</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Perpetually, this endeavour will continue without satisfaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Even when all under Heaven has been conquered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These lines serve to show that, while anxieties and insecurities compel the mind to bolster the ego with thoughts of achievement and strength, we can also simply focus on removing these thoughts of achievement from our minds, and allow all things to unify in the emptiness therein.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can the self be without the (separation of) self (and other)?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Various replications of this compose the history of Heaven and Earth.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage is unencumbered by any need to be admired. He enjoys the long road of life, and does not try to win the race.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This imagery of the sun and moonâ€™s rise and decline was also used in Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">to caution against the error and consequences of arrogance.</span> <span id="_ftnref85"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[85\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn85) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">can be read here as making the same point by suggesting that the rise and fall of nations and rulers follows the rise in their self-satisfaction. Thus, the proceeding lines (89-96) provide guidance on avoiding this self-satisfaction.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 87-88 bring to mind DDJ7, which might be further explained by the lesson on restraint and longevity in lines 82-86:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven has longevity, Earth has continuity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven and Earth have the power of longevity and continuity because they do not live for themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is how they can live for so long</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages leave themselves behind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And they end up in front</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They do not cater to themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet they persist</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is it not because they are without selfishness and wickedness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">That they are able to fulfill themselves?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Parallels to this rise and fall are also apparent in DDJ2, as discussed above.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage does not wish to get caught up in narcissistic sentiments of his wisdom and perception.  He only wishes to keep his virtue and perceptions pure. Being taken in by otherâ€™s opinions about him, good or bad, will only diminish his ability to do this.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 89-96 counsel self-reliance and not giving undue power to external validation and the opinions of others. They are particularly evocative of DDJ13 in light of the question â€œCan the self be without the (separation of) self (and other)?â€? in line 87:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ13:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Favour and disgrace are both startling</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Appreciate the great worrying that both of these cause in your body</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ What does it mean to say â€œAppreciate the great worrying</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That (favour and disgrace) cause in your body?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The reason I have great worries is because I have a self</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If I did not have a self, what worries would I have?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, those who (govern) the self as the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And cherish it as such</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">On them the world can rely</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who (govern) the self as the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And love (care for) it as such</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To them the world can be entrusted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Good words and bad words can be used to manipulate the ego and steer oneâ€™s decisions according to the manipulatorâ€™s agenda. For a true leader, this is like giving the executive passwords to anyone who knows how that leader would like to view themselves.  Sages, therefore, took care to warn those with the virtue to lead of this common vulnerability for the safety of the masses who had vested their power in such leaders, knowing that a leader who is not capable of ruling themselves will have great difficulty ruling the world.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">     DDJ81 (â€œTrue words are not beautified; beautified words are not true words â€¦â€?) could also be compared to lines 89â€“96.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage sees the larger picture. In his wisdom and perception, he knows that he is only taking orders from the higher order. He does not establish anything, but only helps return things to the natural state of balance demanded by laws of harmony.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 97-101 are, in fact, largely supported by the theory of ether, held by Nikola Tesla, and also later held by Albert Einstein. Tesla quotes himself in a letter to the editor of the New York Times, April 21, 1908:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What I said in regard to the greatest achievement of the man of science whose mind is bent upon the mastery of the physical universe, was nothing more than what I stated in one of my unpublished addresses, from which I quote:  "According to an adopted theory, every ponderable atom is differentiated from a tenuous fluid, filling all space merely by spinning motion, as a whirl of water in a calm lake. By being set in movement this fluid, the ether, becomes gross matter. Its movement arrested, the primary substance reverts to its normal state. It appears, then, possible for man through harnessed energy of the medium and suitable agencies for starting and stopping ether whirls to cause matter to form and disappear. At his command, almost without effort on his part, old worlds would vanish and new ones would spring into being. He could alter the size of this planet, control its seasons, adjust its distance from the sun, guide it on its eternal journey along any path he might choose, through the depths of the universe. He could make planets collide and produce his suns and stars, his heat and light; he could originate life in all its infinite forms. To cause at will the birth and death of matter would be man's grandest deed, which would give him the mastery of physical creation, make him fulfill his ultimate destiny.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Einstein at first denied the existence of this ether, but later changed his position. In â€œEther and the Theory of Relativityâ€? (1922), Einstein wrote:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:normal">Recapitulating, we may say that according to the general theory of relativity, space is endowed with physical qualities; in this sense, therefore, there exists an ether. According to the general theory of relativity, space without ether is unthinkable; for in such space there not only would be no propagation of light, but also no possibility of existence for standards of space and time (measuring-rods and clocks), nor therefore any space-time intervals in the physical sense. But this ether may not be thought of as endowed with the quality characteristic of ponderable media, as consisting of parts which may be tracked through time. The idea of motion may not be applied to it</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What is this constant thing?  It is present at all times.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage recognizes order in harmony and thereby learns the laws and principles governing even the Imperial Emperor â€“ the â€œSon of Heaven.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 107-118 speak of the ineffability of Dao, a topic touched upon in many Daoist texts, including of course the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. This ineffability is said to manifest in the principles of harmony, noted throughout the myriad things, and likely suggested in DDJ1â€™s discussion of finding the principles of Dao in â€œouter surfaces.â€? Note too, the shared mention of an ever expanding gate (see line 118):</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  The Nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Named is the mother of the myriad things</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, always without desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observing its inner subtlety</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Always with desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observing its outer surface</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">These two were born together, yet differ in name</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 119-126 suggest an idea similar to the concept of interdependence in Buddhist philosophy, and also to the concept of origins mentioned earlier in lines 94-106. Just as listening is made possible by the ears, and observing is made possible by the eyes, all things depend on other things for their existence and operations. Awareness of this natural law is also evident when ancient Chinese texts speak of â€œnames.â€? This word suggests more than simply appellations, but also the full development and function of a â€œthingâ€? in the world, having reached a level of distinction from the things on which its existence depends. While a â€œname/mingâ€? describes physical characteristics, it also signifies function, much the same as a â€œtitleâ€? in English.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This maturation of â€œnamesâ€? can be seen in other lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, for example:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 16-18</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing its image, one apprehends its form;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reaching to its principles, one knows its nature;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Seeking its end, one knows its name.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 27-32</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sageâ€™s method of government</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is to still the body and wait.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Things then arrive at their names, and naturally fall into place. As these names naturally order themselves,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those which do not fit are abolished.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When names are corrected and laws perfected,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage is without further endeavours.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And, further down, in lines 130-135</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for men of highest wisdom,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Their mouths are without empty chatter,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And their hands are without empty gesturing.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As things arise, they are destined to be heard of,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And combined according to form and appearance.</span>
