<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Engineers know how to arrange things so as to bring about a desired effect. When the components of a structure are human beings, rather than things, it becomes more difficult to ensure a desired effect.  The Sage is adept at seeing through how people present themselves, into who they are.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">here discusses assigning the right people to various posts in government, and does so following an illustration of how all things arise according to underlying principles. The juxtaposition of these ideas alludes to the Daoist interest in â€œnamesâ€? as a description of functional relationships depending on the characteristics of interrelated things. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The advice in lines129-132, for sussing out candidatesâ€™ abilities, is mirrored in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guigu Zi</span> <span id="_ftnref89"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; font-style:italic; vertical-align:super">\[89\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn89) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span id="_Toc502792110"></span> <span id="_Toc503479128"></span> <span id="_Toc507075970"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When reason reaches (its objective), knowledge is effective. When knowledge is effective, chaotic energy does not cause turmoil within the breast. Thus, internally, energy is cultivated; and externally other people are understood. By cultivating the will, the heart-mind is effective. By understanding other people, (appropriate) divisions of labour are clearly perceived.</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span id="_Toc502792111"></span> <span id="_Toc503479129"></span> <span id="_Toc507075971"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If you wish (to know) the usefulness of others, you must first know their (ability to) cultivate the energy of the will. To know if othersâ€™ energy is abundant or lacking, and if they cultivate the energy of their will, examine their peace and stability. Thereby, know their ability.</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 127-132 may also evoke the statements of DDJ2:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Therefore, sages handle affairs with non-action</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the myriad things all take their places without responding</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Acted for, but not expected of</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Perfection is cultivated, and not dwelled upon</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Surely, what is not dwelled upon</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Does not leave</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The main difference here, however, is that DDJ2 refers to â€œthe myriad thingsâ€? which are left to define themselves and make their own way in the world, whereas the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">refers to political candidates, and how rulers can determine if they will use power responsibly. The intent seems to be that if rulers maintain their own inner stability and sincerity, rather than relying on written methods and strategies, they will make correct choices and allow appointees to carry out duties without interference, or danger to the nation. By taking this approach, the ruler acts as the human delegate of De, Virtue, nurturing an arrangement whereby the various counties can freely define themselves, and thrive according to their characteristic abilities.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, it is said:  â€œTo ferry across the river (requires) harmonious waters.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref90"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[90\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn90) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While the Sage is able to see beyond words, definitions, and mental constructs, they also know the value and power of words. It is through words that they are able to steer nations from potential disaster, simply by showing rulers that their definitions were wrong.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A common query often voiced in regards to the Lao Ziâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, is that â€œif the true Dao cannot be spoken (see DDJ1, line one), why did Lao Zi write 81 chapters on it?â€?  Lines 133-141 might help to answer this question, in saying that things which arise are destined to be heard of, and those who â€œreach the ultimate goalâ€? are thereby able to pass on their teachings.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When Lao Zi described Dao, he did so by speaking of the things that arose from it, such as nature, humanity, Heaven, and Earth. He did not attempt to define Dao, but rather only spoke of how it transcends the limitations of any definition. He simply contrasted definitions, or â€œnames,â€? with their opposites to show that Dao is both, and so neither.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Dao is â€œthe unbornâ€? â€“ it cannot yet be described. As DDJ4 states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Tranquil!  As though having a life of its own</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I do not know whose child it is</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It appears to have preceded the primordial ruler (God)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heshang Gong comments on DDJ1:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Eternal Name can only be like that of a child who has not yet spoken; like baby chicks which have not come out of their eggs; like a brilliant and precious pearl which is still within its oyster; like beautiful jade which is still between the rocks</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 142-143 refer to the commonly held belief that spirits hold much sway in orchestrating the success or misfortune of humans in the physical realm. Heshang Gong often referred to shen ming, or â€œspiritual lights,â€? as, for example, in chapter seven:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All people love (sages) like their own mothers and fathers. The spiritual lights (shen ming) protect them like a newborn child. Thus, they always remainâ€¦  Sages act with love towards people, and are protected by the spiritual lights. Is this not because they are fair, upright, and without selfishness?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">      We see here a spiritual equivalent to what Buddhists would ascribe to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">karma</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As line 143 states:  â€œTo those who are righteous towards others, the spirits bring good fortune.â€? While Daoists and Buddhists agree on the universal principles of balance, stretching through ones lifetimes in the case of Buddhism, it is still not uncommon to find references to agents of the spirit realm, meting out recompense and retribution, in Daoism.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Bring left and right to align in the center, and then stop.</span> <span id="_ftnref93"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[93\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn93)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When resolving conflicts, the Sage does not let his emotions direct his actions, but carefully observes a situation and the impulses of those involved. To avoid deepening the problem, he first identifies the opposing sides of the issue.  He can then work his way towards the larger issue by resolving the many smaller ones along the way.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 144-151 speak of using suitable actions to ameliorate a situation, and of not overusing the tools of power and prohibition. This lesson also appears in DDJ9:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To take hold and continue filling</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is not as good as coming to a stop</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If you obsessively refine a spear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It will not be long enough to protect you</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If gold and jade fill the court</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Nothing can hold onto them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When fortune and wealth bring arrogance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They bring the misfortune of their own loss</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When achievements are completed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Their recognition should continue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But the individual should withdraw </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the way of Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Note the common thread of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">holding on for too long</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(see BX line 148). The similarity here is also interesting in that the earliest copy of DDJ9, found at the Guodian tombs,</span> <span id="_ftnref94"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[94\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn94) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">did not refer to â€œholding,â€? while the edits made to later copies of this chapter reflect the lexicon found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Though DDJ9 is more lyrical, the same message is carried across, and lines 144-151 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">offer a more exact meaning to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s broader applicability.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The message in both texts can be traced back to an inner meaning of letting go rather than using force, and of unburdening the mind of worry and excessive thought. The Guodian copy of DDJ9 has the image of waters accumulating and then bursting forth and causing damage, rather than being allowed to circulate naturally and not build up a reservoir of trouble. This idea is discussed further in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s following lines, which look at an obsession with prohibitions.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What about (governing) the districts?  (As sure as) the sun and moon go on without stop,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">153</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">        </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ„•æ„•è€…ä¸?ä»¥å¤©ä¸‹ç‚º</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ†‚</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are alert and responsive will not cause the world to worry;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">154</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">       </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">åˆºåˆºè€…ä¸?ä»¥è?¬ç‰©ç‚º</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç­´</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who make longwinded speeches do not consider the myriad things in their plans.</span> <span id="_ftnref95"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[95\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn95) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is difficult to describe the method of creating rules and laws.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">157</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">       </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é ˆå?Œè€Œå‡ºã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">One gets close (to the goal), and can avoid (trouble).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage knows that words can be used to obscure the truth more easily than they can be used to reveal it.  Thus, he is careful about over-limiting things with definitions of true and false, right and wrong.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 152-159 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also warn of promoting rules and expectations without restraint, and might be best understood alongside DDJ57:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When aligned, the nation is well governed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When aberrant, the military is effective</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is by having no endeavour to do so</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That the world is conquered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">How do I know this to be the case? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By this:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When taboos are abundant in the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The people are extremely poor</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the people have an abundance of sharp weapons</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The nation grows dark</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When people have an abundance of skill and ingenuity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Irregular things flourish</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When laws and standards are increasingly publicized</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thieves and robbers abound</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus the Sage says:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I do nothing, and the people reform themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I love stillness, and the people regulate themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I do not endeavour, and the people enrich themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I am without desires, and the people are natural </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These lines from the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also echo the sentiment of DDJ81:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">True words are not beautified</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Beautified words are not true words </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The skilled are not argumentative</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The argumentative are not skilled</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who (pretend to) know do not remain open-minded</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The open-minded do not (pretend to) knowâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">160</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">      </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ•…æ›°ï¼šçŸ¥ä½•çŸ¥ä¹Žï¼Ÿ</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said:  â€œKnow!â€?  But what should you know? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To those who are cautious in venturing outwards, these (answers) naturally draw near.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing others is called â€œhelping across the riverâ€? (</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">jÄ«</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">165</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">       </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">çŸ¥è‹Ÿé?©</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å?¯</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç‚ºå¤©ä¸‹å‘¨ã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By knowing what is frivolous and what is necessary, one can bring the world into unison.</span> <span id="_ftnref96"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[96\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn96)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Internally, solidifying oneself into a unified whole, one may lengthen their lifespan.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Discussing the application of this principle reveals the way to rule all under Heaven.</span> <span id="_ftnref97"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[97\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn97)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Trying too hard to know can lead one away from their spiritual intelligence, and into the realm of pragmatic definitions, created to serve purposes that are no longer relevant. Better to just sit and wait, purifying the heart-mind of all â€œdoing,â€? until illumination arrives.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 160-167 provide an important historical backdrop for the development of Daoist internal cultivation. We see here the suggestion to first find inner stability and unity before attempting to assist the world (lines 166-167). This ties into earlier passages which warned of wielding excessive control. By first finding inner calm, leaders can avoid impetuous decisions that create even more dissent and disorder â€“ the exact opposite of a lawâ€™s intended effect. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">here, points out the confluence of these internal and external endeavours: </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Internally, solidifying oneself into a unified whole, one may lengthen their lifespan.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Discussing the application of this principle reveals the way to rule all under Heaven  (lines 166-167)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The parallels between BX160-167 and DDJ47 paint a picture of how these ideas were taught at the time:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ47:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without going out the door</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Know all under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without glancing out the window</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">See Heavenâ€™s Way</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The further out one goes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The less they know</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sage does not move</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet he knows</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He describes and names (things)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without seeing (them)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He brings about perfection</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without acting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     BX160-167 also tie into the ideas of DDJ57 (appearing in the commentary for lines 152-159, above), while showing a closer resemblance to DDJ65 in their guidance on knowledge and the connection between strategies for self-government and state-government.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ65:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The ancient masters who aligned society with Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Did not do so by enlightening the people</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But rather, fostered their simplicity </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Difficulty in governing people</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Comes from a wealth of wisdom</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Hence, when knowledge is used to govern the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This results in thievery from the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Not using knowledge to govern the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Blesses the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Understand the broader application of these two principles</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">There is an infinite understanding</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Which can be found in these principles</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(see BX line 167)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called Fathomless Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Fathomless Virtue, profound and far-reaching</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following it, things return back to their nature</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Arriving at great submission</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Note here, as well, the definition of Fathomless Virtue given in DDJ51, and the meaning it gives to self-government and state-government in DDJ65 and the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(from DDJ51)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  (Dao) actuates them but does not possess them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sets them in motion but does not expect of them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Extends their lives without ruling and controlling</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called Fathomless Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Some passages in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, such as chapter 65, are often confused with a tyrantâ€™s effort to stifle the populace with ignorance. However, it should be noted that the Sages practiced this heart-mind purification themselves, as described in DDJ20:  â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The crowd is joyous and buoyantâ€¦  I alone am like the clearness of still water.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€? What is taught here, rather, is to â€œdo not-doingâ€? within the deepest recesses of the heart-mind. At the basis of fabrication is tension and thinking.  To reach true naturalness, one must learn to give up these efforts, â€œknowing what is frivolous and what is necessaryâ€? (see BX165).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called Fathomless Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Fathomless Virtue, profound and far-reaching</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following it, things return back to their nature</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Arriving at great submission</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(DDJ65)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, it is said:  â€œWhen it is common to abandon argumentation and clever scheming,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind submits to the spirit, peace reigns throughout the body.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In lines 168 to 172, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">speaks of jing-essence in its original state as endowed by the Heavens  â€“  the basic seed of life. Just as the Daoist concept of De, Virtue, is that of an intrinsic perfection, this jing-essence from Heaven is uncorrupted and therefore holds the plan of Heaven within it. As lines 179-183 (below) show, when this jing-essence can genuinely expresses itself and individuals do not try to confine this expression within the limitations of intellect, this Heaven endowed jing-essence can bring them to the full expression of Heavenâ€™s plan in their lives, allowing them to be like the wind to the waves as their desires are suited to the plan of Heaven.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begins by discussing how (primordial) jing-essence is the basis by which common people develop into Sages, and later shows that purifying the mind of thoughts is necessary for the cultivation of jing (see NY88-104). The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also appears to imply clearing the mind in lines 160-167, and follows with this statement about the great transformative power of jing, suggesting that heaven packs qi and spiritual knowledge into jing, which is essentially â€˜un-packedâ€™ through heart-mind purification techniques. As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(ancient commentary section), lines 90-97 state:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What people occupy themselves with today is jing-essence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Getting rid of desires should be the priority.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">From this follows quiet stillness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quiet stillness brings about jing-essence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">From jing essence, singularity is established.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Singularity brings about illumination.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Illumination brings about spirit.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for spirit, this is reaching the treasure.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, it is said that those whose thoughts search the depths of essence can clearly perceive advantages and disadvantages.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 179-181 provide some degree of confirmation as to Lao Ziâ€™s intent when rejecting the Confucian approach to self-cultivation:  seeking a name as someone who has succeeded in attaining true virtues brings with it the consequence of backsliding in the cultivation of jing-essence â€“ the pure life-force endowed by Heaven (Nature) which is truly responsible for oneâ€™s ultimate potential and development.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As Heshang Gong comments on DDJ27:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œExcellent counting does not use counting devicesâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are excellent at finding a strategy to attain Dao simply guard Oneness within and do not shift from it. Their strategies are not numerous, and so they do not use counting devices to know them all.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For further reference on this approach please also see: DDJ19:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quit sageliness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Abandon wisdom</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the people will benefit one hundred fold</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quit benevolence, abandon right-conduct</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the people will return to caring for their parents</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quit cleverness, abandon profit</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And robbers and thieves will not exist</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">These three</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Are only ornamental, and not satisfactory</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, we have the following:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observe the natural state</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Embrace the unaltered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Minimize self-importance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And have few desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When there is overabundance in the nation, officials should not be appointed.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage finds nourishment in the simplicity of nature.  He knows that filling a room with too many things makes it uninhabitable, just as filling the mind with too many ideas makes it unaccommodating to a full and true experience of the present.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 184-189 may be the most complete reflection of DDJ9 in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Note, especially, the similarity between lines 184-185 and the beginning of DDJ9, as well as the similarity between line 186 and the end of DDJ9. Here is chapter nine again, for comparison:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To take hold and continue filling</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is not as good as coming to a stop</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If you obsessively refine a spear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It will not be long enough to protect you</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If gold and jade fill the court</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Nothing can hold onto them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When fortune and wealth bring arrogance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They bring the misfortune of their own loss</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When achievements are completed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Their recognition should continue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But the individual should withdraw </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the way of Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The connotations in this chapter are made abundantly more apparent by contrasting it with BX184-189. Tirelessly seeking reputation is like grinding down a blade. One can only do so for so long before they have nothing left to sharpen. Having a great and widespread reputation invites people to test and attack it, and if this doesnâ€™t destroy it, one can bring shame on themselves simply by â€œbelieving their own hypeâ€? and becoming arrogant. Thus, Lao Zi counsels to simply do marvelous things and then move on without demanding recognition. The Sage is content to remain undefined, like the Dao, rather than speaking of his or her strengths, achievements, or anything that may garner the admiration or sympathy of others. This is the Sageâ€™s way of both survival and enduring success.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 187-189 reflect on the importance of accepting when things are going well, and not trying to force extreme progress. For a ruler to preside over a nation with Dao, they must be wary of having too many desires, and also of powerful officials under them with too strong a desire for a great name. These shortcomings are at the root of disruptions to a harmonious balance, and are easily fostered when one is surrounded by success and abundance. As Lao Zi remarks in DDJ77, â€œWho can have in excess, and care for all under Heaven?  Only those who have Dao.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao encompasses the vastness of Heaven,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao is right there, within everyone and everything, every moment and every circumstance. By training the mind to look within and notice the heart-mindâ€™s many activities, one can begin to rein in its many affairs and consolidate focus. They can then move forward in a positive and meaningful direction.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 190-200 reflect ideas that run through DDJ70, 71, and 72, and which might be summarized as follows:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While people seek to make great names for themselves, Dao surpasses all yet is known to so very few. Such names are external, existing in the minds of others, whereas Dao is found within, in emptiness, seemingly non-existent.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In the same way that Dao is not acknowledged by those who chase after renown, the virtue of those who live by Dao goes unnoticed. They are simply natural, and seemingly â€œnothing special,â€? not seeking to display their progress for others; instead, they work on themselves in obscurity.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 196-200 read, remarkably, almost like a paraphrase of DDJ47. Here is that chapter again:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without going out the door, know all under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without glancing out the window, see Heavenâ€™s Way</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The further out one goes, the less they know</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sage does not move, yet he knows</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He describes and names (things) without seeing (them)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And brings about perfection without acting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">appears to suggest that the Sage transcends time and space to see physical things and circumstances, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">explains that what is perceived is internal. Comparing these two texts reveals an early Chinese tradition of mindfulness. A central practice of mindfulness is to observe oneâ€™s inner state, and pay attention to phenomena such as emotions, urges, and feelings by becoming aware of their â€œarising, abiding, declining, and ceasing.â€? As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said:  â€œDesiring to take care of myself, I must first know my true inner state,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And become acquainted with the universe by examining within myself.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In this way, one can know the image, thereby knowing the tendencies of their true inner state.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing the tendencies of their true inner state, they will know how to nourish life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     DDJ47 states this as:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Therefore, the Sage does not move, yet he knows</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He describes and names without seeing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And brings about perfection without acting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     â€œHe describes and names without seeingâ€? may refer to closing the eyes and looking inwards at what has no shape or sound, referred to vaguely in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, line 199, as â€œthe image.â€? As explained in the commentary above, on</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">line 16, â€œthe imageâ€? is essentially another term for Dao. Here, â€œthe imageâ€? is shown to encompass a meaning similar to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">dharma</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.  As with the term â€œDao,â€? dharma can mean a principle of cosmic order, a way of living, and/or phenomena. While phenomena seem separate, they are empty of independent existence; they are illusory, and simply a part of the one principle. Phenomena such as feelings, emotions, thoughts, ideas, beliefs, mental and social constructs, etc., when allowed to reveal their â€œnames,â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref102"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[102\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn102) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">eventually simply disappear, returning to the one principle â€“ emptiness; Dao.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As part of Daoist mindfulness practice throughout the day, one can pay attention to the movement of the qi (energy-breath) as it is affected by emotions. The Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen, chapter 39, describes these movements as follows:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The hundred diseases are generated by qi.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When one is angry, their qi rises</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When euphoric, their qi relaxes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When sad, their qi dissipates</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When fearful, their qi descends</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When cold, their qi collects</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When over-heated, their qi leaks out</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When startled, their qi is chaotic</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When exhausted, their qi is wasted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When pensive, their qi is knotted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While it takes time to dissolve the internal triggers that set our emotions off and put the heart-mind at risk of usurpation, by noticing, for example, the rising qi of anger, one can see the roots of their reactions and employ the energy-moderating power of the lungs</span> <span id="_ftnref103"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[103\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn103) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">to even out their qi.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Buddhist teacher Pema Chodron (1936-present) reveals that the path outlined in BX190-200 continues to this day:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">"If your everyday practice is to open to all your emotions, to all the people you meet, to all the situations you encounter, without closing down, trusting that you can do that â€“ then that will take you as far as you can go. And then you'll understand all the teachings that anyone has ever taught."</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wishing to be enveloped by it,</span> <span id="_ftnref105"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[105\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn105) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">you must unify to the furthest extent, and solidify that which is protected within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Aligning the body helps to align the heart-mind and perceptions, connect the nerve path-ways and improve the circulation of vital essences. This enables the unhindered intuitive response of the bodyâ€™s movements and the innate functions of the internal organs. The Sage understands the importance of following the natural laws of harmony, and so is mindful of the natural harmony of his body.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This section of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is amongst the clearest descriptions of meditation from texts of this time, including parables in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Zhuang Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. â€œA ceremonious outward appearanceâ€? (line 204) suggests an upright yet relaxed and dignified posture. â€œRespectfully welcome that which approachesâ€? suggests that this posture should be calm and dignified, but not prideful and stiff, putting the ego aside and being open to the guest. In both meditation and welcoming guests, the mind should be bright, open, and attentive (internally and singularly attentive for the case of Daoist meditation). Guests are not welcomed ceremoniously with dull and lethargic minds, nor inattentive minds. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also points out that, with the busy life and busy minds of most people, â€œthose today who seek its approach require this method to (invite) Daoâ€? (line 205). </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Line 204 counsels simplicity and inner balance in this practice, and warns against â€œsoaringâ€? and â€œspilling over.â€? A similar sentiment can be seen in DDJ15:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Who, by the power of their stillness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can make clouded water slowly become clear?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their serenity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can sustain this progress until life slowly arises?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who maintain this Dao do not desire fullness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is because they are not full that they can remain covered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And not let what is new come to an end</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 205 and 201 describe an inward gathering of energies, which the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">suggests includes the energy of thoughts, and a â€œreturning to the centerâ€? â€“ a singularity of mind and attention, not scattered on myriad interests, but focused on the present. DDJ5 refers to this with the lines â€œTo speak countless words is worthless. This is not as good as guarding the center.â€? Such descriptions resemble the practice of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">stabilizing jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, (especially) lines 135-150.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 205-207 give very useful and succinct instructions on what to do once these initial stages have taken place. In this process, â€œleft, right, front, and back, running full circle, they return to the place (at the center)â€? (line 201). This is the blending of yin and yang into Oneness. The place at the center could also refer to the lower-dantien, considered the bodyâ€™s center of gravity, and located about two finger-widths behind and below the navel. Gathering focus to the center resembles advice often found in Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary. For example, compare line 206 with the following comments by Heshang Gong on DDJ1, and DDJ10:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thus, always without desires, observing its inner subtlety</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The â€œsubtlety,â€? here, means the key. People who maintain the absence of desire will be able to observe the key to Dao. â€œThe keyâ€? is Oneness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œ(Is a) multitude of gates, all leading to the subtlety withinâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven can return to the Heaven within itself, and dispense energy-breaths which are either potent or weak.  Eliminating strong emotions, abandoning desires, and guarding balance and harmony within:  this is called â€œknowing the gate-key to the door of Dao.â€?             </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(DDJ1)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All the names together are One. Referring to Oneness, it is said:  â€œIn a unified consciousness, there is no (doubt or) division.â€? (DDJ10)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     If lines 206-207 were to precede lines 201-205, the sequence of ideas in this section (unifying to the fullest extent, returning, and preserving ming) would be the same as in DDJ16: </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Arrive at supreme emptiness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Embrace deep silence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Myriad creatures arise together</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I thereby observe them returning</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So many things blossoming</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And each returns back to its roots</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Returning to the roots is called silence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This means returning to oneâ€™s destiny-life-force (ming)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Returning to oneâ€™s destiny-life-force is called eternalityâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Quite significantly, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">refers to both pure nature (xing) and destiny-life-force (ming), whereas the DDJ does not mention xing in any of its chapters. Xing and ming later become perhaps the most fundamental, and mysterious, elements of Daoist meditation texts. Ming, more literally translated as â€˜destinyâ€™, and â€˜mandateâ€™, has particular meanings associated with the life-preservation practices of Daoist cultivation â€“ an association made especially clear in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 204 and 205.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The importance given to â€œthe timing of Heavenâ€? in this section of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">reveals yet another level of depth in this text, showing that it truly is an early ascendant of Daoist â€œInternal Alchemyâ€? <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The greatest enlightenment of all enlightenment is not loved when people refuse each other.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I have witnessed opposition, and the collective divergence which follows it. Thereby, I know that the ancients travelled the path in unity.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 212-214 also contain echoes of DDJ41â€™s description of students on the path, in speaking of people travelling this path together.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These closing sentiments may be further appreciated in light of DDJ81, the closing sentiments of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Sages do not hoard</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Having helped others</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Oneself gains more</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Having given to others</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And does no harm</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And not oppose</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Similar to the Buddhist Boddhisatva tradition, the author of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">stresses that the â€œgreatest enlightenment of all enlightenmentâ€? should be pursued with the enlightenment of all in mind. As evidenced by our seemingly unlimited powers of communication and intelligence, it is natural for Humanity to work collectively. Though our survival instincts may lead to selfishness, all fulfilling life purposes ultimately involve service to others. Humans can acquire storehouses of wealth, and yet still feel that their lives lack purpose if their central goals are not directed towards serving Humanity. It would seem that this is linked to the nature and destiny of our place in the universe.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Like the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">emphasizes communal harmony, and national and international harmony, alongside personal inner-harmony. By clearing a path towards a more enlightened understanding of ourselves, these texts offer the possibility of a synergistic evolution of society, issuing forth as the collective expression of spiritually matured individuals.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage counsels the ruler, and shows him the way of peace, like the spirit counsels the heart-mind. <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Political metaphors for stabilizing the heart-mind give early Chinese teachings on mindfulness much of their essential character. <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     What the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">immediately reveals about the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, is that the Sage is not only a wise counsel to the nationâ€™s presiding authority, but is also within, guiding the ruler â€“ the heart-mind â€“ towards sovereignty over â€œall under Heavenâ€? and â€œthe myriad thingsâ€? â€“ ie., the senses, emotions, desires, stress, impulses, and anything else which must be stabilized in order to preserve inner unity. When these things are disordered, confusion reigns, and the sovereignty of the heart-mind is imperiled. The Sage is to the ruler what the spiritâ€™s illumination is upon the heart-mind. She brings clarity, perception, and peace to the ruler. To invite the Sage, the ruler must first become stable and orderly, kind and genuine.  Then the Sage will find it safe to convene with him, seeing that the ruler is capable of giving up tyrannical power and instead following Dao. The art of the heart-mind is not simply a way to find peace, but a way to bring forth the spiritual intelligence, the Sage.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">further provides an important example of mindfulness teachings in ancient China, appearing long before Buddhism arrived from India in 80 AD. While Buddhist mindfulness teachings may focus more directly on attention to inner phenomena (sensations, emotions, thoughts, etc.), both Buddhist teachings and the ancient Chinese â€œart of the heart-mindâ€? seek to lead students towards a clear perception of their inner state. As Lao Zi says in DDJ33:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know others, are wise</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know themselves, are clear-sighted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who overpower others, have strength</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who overpower themselves, have fortitude</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know contentment, are rich</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who exercise this fortitude, have will-power</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who do not lose their station, continue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who die but do not disappear, live long</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     XSS, lines 7-9, show that when the heart-mind is stirred-up, the eyes and ears no longer function as loyal servants of the heart-mind. As a political metaphor, this suggests the beginnings of usurpation, and so warns against letting the desires of the senses disturb, and thereby overthrow, the heart-mind. This is at the very basis of mindfulness practice in everyday life, and may be summed up as:  Maintain focus while not relinquishing â€œthe throne of the rulerâ€? (the heart-mind).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 1-11 may also provide some background for understanding DDJ12, which, in light of XSS7-9, appears to have implied â€œdesiringâ€? at the beginning of its first three lines</span> <span id="_ftnref109"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[109\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn109) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Desiring) the five colours blind(s) the eyes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Desiring) the five tones deafen(s) the ears</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Desiring) the five flavours numb(s) the mouth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The intensity of the hunt makes the mind go mad</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Goods which are difficult to obtain interfere with oneâ€™s journey</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, sages are guided by their stomachs</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And not by their eyes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Leaving that</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They take thi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In Chapter 10 of the Diamond Sutra (a passage which later became one of the most influential in Chinese Buddhism), a nearly identical admonition can be found, helping to unravel the expressions of the proto-Daoists:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, bodhisattvas and mahasattvas should give rise to a clear and clean mind. They should not linger on appearances arising in the mind. They should not linger on sounds, smells, sensations, or dharma (lit. laws) arising in the mind. They should, abiding nowhere, give rise to (the clear and clean) mind.</span> <span id="_ftnref110"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[110\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn110)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In a passage of great proximity to the meaning and (likely) the era of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, Xun Zi (313-238 BC) writes in his chapter â€œRemoving Obstaclesâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The mind is the ruler of the body, and the host of spiritual intelligence. It gives commands but does not take commands. It restricts itself, allows itself, takes from itself, overcomes itself, moves itself, and stops itself.  You can force someoneâ€™s mouth to be silent, you can force their body to scrunch up or stretch out, but you cannot force their mind to change their ideas. What it finds to be true, it accepts, and what it finds to be false, it rejects.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     For this reason I say: what the mind apprehends, allow it to do so without restraining it. Allow things to spontaneously appear to the mind in their breadth of diversity, with the extent of the mindâ€™s nature remaining not-two.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of Poetry</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">says:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Picking and gathering burdock roots</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The basket is not full yet the roots fall out</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I sigh for the man in my heart</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As I let it go to and fro</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     A basket is easy to fill, and burdock is easy to gather, but not when the mind is divided in every which way. This is why I say: A mind that branches out in many directions knows nothing; a mind that is not level is not acute; a mind that is divided is doubtful and confused. But for a mind with focused scrutiny, the myriad things can come together in its understanding; for in oneself is a unity that runs though all categories.</span> <span id="_ftnref111"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[111\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn111)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     It may be of value to understanding the Xin Shu and Nei Ye that Xun Zi describes the (heart-)mind as the host, or lord, of spiritual intelligence. If we are to understand the Sage as the spiritual intelligence, it may also help to understand that the Sage holds no executive power, nor goes where the powerful would try to control him. The ruler, as with the heart-mind, has the power to do as he wishes, but he cannot force the Sageâ€™s allegiance.  To earn that, he must show that he is capable of acquiescing to higher wisdom, of practicing kindness, of being content with frugality, and of transcending self-interest; further, he must show that he can unite with Dao and allow its power, De, to fill his sails. In this way, the ruler (the heart-mind) may rule with the expertise of the Sage (spiritual intelligence).</span> <span id="_ftnref112"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[112\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn112)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But when still, you naturally obtain it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage has control over his impulses, like the ruler has control over his ministers. He does not act rashly, but observes the time, thereby achieving maximum effect with minimal effort at opportune moments.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As lines 1-11 explain above, the desires of the senses give rise to impulses which may coerce and dethrone the heart-mind. Lines 12-19 explain that these impulses should not be given reign, as this would compel the heart-mind to â€œattempt to do the running for a horseâ€? and â€œthe flying for a bird.â€? Such efforts are both futile and dangerous. Instead, the heart-mind (ruler) must not be pushed forward, away from the â€œthrone position,â€? but rather observe these inclinations, â€˜letting the horse exhaust its strength â€“ letting the bird collapse its wings.â€™  Through this stillness, the throne of the heart-mind is naturally reclaimed.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Zhuang Zi expands on this teaching in chapter four, â€œThe Human World Todayâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">You have heard of flying with wings, but you have not yet heard of flying without wings. You have heard of knowing with knowledge, but you have not yet heard of knowing without knowledge. Look at the closed room. In an empty room, brightness blooms and good fortune stops to visit. If you do not also come to a stop, this is called sitting and racing about. If you allow the ears and eyes to penetrate within, while keeping the mindâ€™s knowledge outside, gods and spirits will naturally come to dwell with you. How much more will other people!  This is to transform the myriad things. It is the pivot of (legendary rulers) Yu and Shun, and that which Fuxi and Jiqu practiced to the end of their days. How much more should we all do the same!</span> <span id="_ftnref113"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[113\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn113) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Path is not far off, yet people are unable to reach it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If you sweep away and cleanse impurities, the spirit will remain settled.</span> <span id="_ftnref114"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[114\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn114)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">XSS22-23 might be further clarified by Heshang Gongâ€™s comments on DDJ11 (â€œThe surrounding clay makes a pot, and by its emptiness the vessel is usedâ€?).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 22-23 also reflect an idea common to Daoist meditation, and found in Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary on DDJ10. Note that Heshang Gongâ€™s comment here (below) also resembles the Buddhist mindfulness technique of impartially observing the mindâ€™s engagements.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Looking deeply, purify and eliminate</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">One should wash the heart-mind until it is clean and pure. The heart-mind lives in the fathomless depths of emptiness. Investigate. Know its myriad engagements. This is called â€œinvestigating the fathomless.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is said by some to show Buddhist influences, the proto-Daoist texts of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">show that Heshang Gong was, in fact, pointing out the early indigenous Chinese meditation traditions in Lao Ziâ€™s teachings.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The saying â€œthe Dao is not far off, yet people are unable to reach itâ€? (line 20) reflects similar statements in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">describing the ineffable quality of Dao. For example, DDJ14</span> <span id="_ftnref115"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[115\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn115) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">reads:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Greet it and you do not see its front</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Follow it and you do not see its rear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Hold to the ancient Dao and ride it until you possess the present</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Then you will have the power to know the ancient beginning </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œthe thread of Daoâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, however, â€œthe Dao is not far off, yet people are unable to reach itâ€? appears in context of lines 12-19 (above) which show how to attain the throne position of the heart-mind.  It is also followed by an illustration of how this position is lost in futile pursuits (see lines 24-27, below). Piecing these statements together, we see that Dao also refers to the state of inner unity and sovereignty, and that the method to attain this state is to sweep out the dust of the heart-mind (lines 22-23).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Dao, literally â€œthe Path,â€? should thus be understood not only as a process, but also as a place at which to arrive, or</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¾—</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">attain to.â€? Such a definition is significant to the lexicon of proto-daoist philosophy, especially in regards to â€œDe,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å¾·</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, Virtue,â€? as shown in the ancient</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">commentary:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Virtue is the abode of Dao.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When things attain (Virtue), they live.</span> <span id="_ftnref116"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[116\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn116) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Being alive, they can know the office of Daoâ€™s essence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, Virtue also means â€œattainment.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for this attainment, it is called â€œattaining the causality.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The effortlessness of this (causality) is called â€œDao.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The abode of Dao is called â€œVirtue.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, between Dao and Virtue, there is no space.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For this reason, it is said â€œthey are not separate.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The principle of this space is called â€œtheir abiding place.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 113-122)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who think they are clever often lack the virtue to invite success.  Because they think they are wise, they are oblivious to the truth.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Just as teachings on mindfulness advise focusing on the present moment and not getting caught up in the illusory creations of the mind, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">explains that engaging our intellects to attain stillness and wisdom will only lead us further from the all embracing emptiness of Dao. Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary suggests that Lao Zi alludes to this strategy of effortless attainment in chapter 27 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span> <span id="_ftnref118"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[118\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn118)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Excellent walking leaves no trail of footprints</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Excellent speech is without fault or blame</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Excellent counting does not use counting devices</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Excellent closing requires no bolts</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet the seal cannot be broken</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Excellent binding requires no rope to secure it</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">Yet cannot be unboundâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In lines 12 through to 29, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">discusses matters of 1) guarding stillness, 2) sweeping clean the heart-mind, 3) retaining spirit, 4) transcending wisdom, and 5) practicing non-action. In doing so, its author transmits the tradition of proto-Daoist self-cultivation in the same sequence as preserved in DDJ10:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Guard the fortress of your bodily spirits</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Embrace Oneness </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you do this without letting them flee?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Gather together the energy-breath and become soft</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the power of an infant</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Looking deeply</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Purify and eliminate</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you be without flaw?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Caring for the people and governing the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you be without effort?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heavenâ€™s gate opens and closes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you act the part of the female?</span> <span id="_ftnref119"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[119\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn119)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With your awareness shining on every corner</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you be without knowledge?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Giving them life and cultivating them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Giving them life yet not possessing them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Acting for them yet not expecting of them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Leading them forward but not managing them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This approach to true understanding is also found in DDJ11. In speaking of the space within an empty vessels, DDJ11 states â€œSo, substance is gained, and emptiness is used.â€? By emptying oneâ€™s heart-mind of negative emotions and attachments, one may use this spaciousness, or â€œempty vessel,â€? to attain Virtue. Virtue transforms things and brings about their completion and perfection. Thus, one uses â€œwhat is not there,â€? the emptiness of the heart-mind, to gain Virtue. Then, what is there (Virtue), may be used to bring about completion and perfection. This process, of Virtue fostering transformation, is further developed in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, especially lines 1-22, and the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Ling Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter eight (see commentary on NY1-22).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All people within the four seas would return to their commonalities and understand these rules.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Having learned rules of conduct, and not how to cultivate inner stillness and harmony, people often use these rules for self-serving purposes and become callous judges of othersâ€™ behaviour.  This has the opposite effect as teaching them to find inner stillness, from which they can empathize with, and truly care for the needs of, others.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The proto-Daoists are often regarded as the first anarchists, or otherwise the first to have written down a philosophy of anarchism. Both philosophies are, in fact, far more complex and multi-faceted than such comparisons take into account; however, there are some intrinsic similarities in the political facets that distinguished proto-Daoists and anarchists from their contemporaries. For Daoists, this political facet can be seen in their rejection of involuntary obedience to tradition, especially concerning obligations towards arbitrary hierarchies. The proto-Daoists felt that such obsession with authority was antagonistic to the development of both society and the individual. Mikhail Bakunin, an influential Russian anarchist, reflects this same ideology in tenets of his â€œRevolutionary Catechismâ€? (1866). You might note that, like most of the early Chinese philosophers, Bakunin also addresses the definitions of justice, duty, and virtue.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">II. Replacing the cult of God by</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">respect and love of humanity,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">we proclaim</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">human reason</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as the only criterion of truth;</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">human conscience</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as the basis of justice;</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">individual and collective freedom</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as the only source of order in society.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">III. Freedom is the absolute right of every adult man and woman to seek no other sanction for their acts than their own conscience and their own reason, being responsible first to themselves and then to the society which they have</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">voluntarily</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">accepted.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">...</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">V. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">freedom</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">of each is therefore realizable only in the equality of all. The realization of freedom through equality, in principle and in fact, is</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">justice.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">VI. If there is one fundamental principle of human morality,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">it is freedom</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. To respect the freedom of your fellowman</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">is duty;</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">to love, help, and serve him is</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">virtue.</span> <span id="_ftnref120"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[120\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn120)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reading these words from Bakunin, it is easy to see how many came to the conclusion that the proto-Daoists were also anarchists upon finding the following statements from Lao Zi in DDJ19:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quit sageliness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Abandon wisdom</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the people will benefit one hundred fold</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quit benevolence, abandon right-conduct</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the people will return to caring for their parents</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quit cleverness, abandon profit</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And robbers and thieves will not exist</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">These three</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Are only ornamental, and not satisfactory</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, we have the following:</span> <span id="_ftnref121"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[121\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn121)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Observe the natural state</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Embrace the unaltered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Minimize self-importance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And have few desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Zhuang Zi (Chuang Tzu) also illustrates the inadequacy of prescribed morality in many of his parables, including the following from his chapter entitled â€œHorses Hoovesâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yes, in the age of perfect virtue, men lived in common with birds and beasts, and were on terms of equality with all creatures, as forming one family â€“ how could they know among themselves the distinctions of superior men and small men? Equally without knowledge, they did not leave (the path of) their natural virtue; equally free from desires, they were in the state of pure simplicity. In that state of pure simplicity, the nature of the people was what it ought to be. But when the Sagely men appeared, limping and wheeling about in (the exercise of) benevolence, pressing along and standing on tiptoe in the doing of righteousness, then men universally began to be perplexed. (trans. Legge)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Re-reading the entire</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">through the lens of this key concept â€“ of returning to our spontaneous and intrinsic virtue rather than conforming to authorized prescriptions â€“ one could, advantageously, see its influence in nearly every verse.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>
