<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In their balance of emptiness and stillness, Heaven and Earth have lasted four and a half billion years. In this time, they have supported the lives of innumerable spiritual vessels. The Sage, therefore, takes Heaven and Earth as his teachers in the cultivation of life and longevity.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If we hope to regain our ancient intrinsic virtue, we would be remiss not to listen to the wisdom of our oldest living ancestors â€“ Heaven and Earth. From Heaven, the Daoists say, we can learn emptiness and non-attachment to self. From earth: stillness, silence, and groundedness. As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ends by stating:  â€œFor what is above, study Heaven. For what is below, study the Earth.â€? This can, in part, be understood to mean â€œmake your heart-mind empty, like Heaven, and your body stable, like the Earth.â€? By doing so, we can truly transcend the need for moral dictates and even free the mind of the confounding limits of human knowledge. The ancient commentary on the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(beginning at line 60, below) comments on line 39, â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The temple</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">refers to the heart-mind. The heart-mind is the abode of wisdom. Therefore it is called â€˜the temple.â€™  To purify it is to get rid of liking and rejectingâ€? (XSS, lines 161â€“164).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Zhuang Zi describes the master who has shed these limitations to his or her self-actualization in the following story from chapter 19, The Total Comprehension of Life:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Artisan Chui made things round with more accuracy than a compass, for his fingers followed the transformation of things without investigating them in his mind. Thus, his spirit tower (heart-mind) was unified and unfettered. The foot is forgotten when the shoe fits properly. The waist is forgotten when the belt fits properly. Knowledge forgets right and wrong when the heart-mind fits properly. There is no inward alteration, nor outward following when the confluence of affairs is fitting. Once fitting, and there is no longer any sense of not-fitting, forget both fitting and not-fitting.</span> <span id="_ftnref122"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[122\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn122) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lao Zi explains the path to this state, similar to what is today often called â€œthe flow state,â€? with the following from DDJ48:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of learning requires daily accumulation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reducing and reducing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Until arriving at effortlessness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Effortless, yet without inactionâ€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though having peculiar forms and strange abilities, he does not follow the myriad things from their incongruity to their coherence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">48</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">  </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ•…å?¯ä»¥ç‚ºå¤©ä¸‹å§‹ã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, he can fathom the beginning of all under Heaven.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing that even Heaven and Earth have an origin, he looks to the oneness of all things. Though seeming to have arisen separately, they all draw from the same source.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">   </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The term â€œnames</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å?? ming)â€? contains many connotations in early Chinese philosophy, including those shared in English, such as</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">appellation</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">reputation</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, but also</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">concept</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">fact</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">definition</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Lines 43-48 show a connection between the pursuits of the Chinese sage and the Western philosopher in their search for truth â€“ for understanding how things work and thus how they should be defined. In understanding this pursuit, we also see how the Chinese sage arrives at â€œthe namelessâ€? â€“ the eternal which is without any final state and thus without definition, yet from which all things arise. In the Daoist meditation of â€œsitting and forgettingâ€? (zuowang), one leaves all definitions until arriving at clarity, dwelling in emptiness, going back to where no distinctions have yet arisen, where there are no â€œnamesâ€? but simply the undifferentiated Oneness. Heshang Gong remarks on this outlook in his commentary on DDJ10:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œEmbrace Oneness. Can you do this without letting (your bodily spirits) flee?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People who can embrace Oneness, and not let it leave them, extend their lives. In Oneness, Dao began to situate life by the supreme harmony of vital energy-breath. Therefore it is said:  â€œOneness covered the world with names.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heaven attained Oneness and became clear; Earth attained Oneness and became serene; lords and kings attained Oneness and became upright and peace-loving. Going within, it is mind; going outwards, it is actions; in covering all with its blessing, it is Virtue.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">All the names together are One</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Referring to Oneness, it is said:  â€œIn a unified consciousness, there is no division.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     From this Oneness, the Sage attains greater clarity of mind and perception. As lines 12-19 and line 45 explain, in this stillness, one should simply observe phenomena without interfering. In doing (or â€˜not-doingâ€™) so, they can truly see phenomena for what they are, and avoid becoming subject to, or caught up in, them.</span> <span id="_ftnref123"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[123\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn123) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  As explained throughout these texts, this can bring about the tranquil sovereignty of the heart-mind over the senses, and thus the nourishing of life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 47-48 explain that it is not by being caught up in the external appearances, or differences, of things that the Sage finds â€œthe beginning of all under Heaven,â€? but instead by returning to the nameless â€“ their common beginning.     </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This teaching also appears in DDJ47,</span> <span id="_ftnref124"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[124\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn124) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and DDJ14 (below):</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By looking, it is not seen. It is known as Clear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By listening, it is not heard. It is known as Inaudible</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What cannot be obtained when seized is known as Infinitesimal</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">These three things cannot be inspected</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And are merged into one</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Above, it is not bright</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Below, it is not dark</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Immeasurable and unnameable</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is again nothing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œhaving no form or appearanceâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without a materialized image</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œabsent-mindedâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Greet it and you do not see its front</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Follow it and you do not see its rear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Hold to the ancient Dao and ride it until you possess the present</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Then you will have the power to know the ancient beginning </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œthe thread of Daoâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the junzi does not dwell on what he likes, nor is he coerced by what he dislikes.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Tranquil, pleasant, and effortless, he abandons wisdom, and it abides in him as a result.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Remains in the state of not knowing;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">59</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">   </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é?œå› ä¹‹é?“ä¹Ÿã€‚</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the Dao of tranquil means.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Maintaining contentment, the Sage is not drawn into danger.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The proto-Daoistsâ€™ focus on preserving and nourishing life led them to re-assess the value of common pursuits, finding that so many of them had the opposite intended effect. Seeking to be above others often makes them despise you; fame is often followed by disgrace; storing up treasures invites thieves; succulent foods often damage oneâ€™s health. This realization guides much of the Daoist lifestyle, and is intimated by Lao Zi in DDJ75:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  The people are careless towards death</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Because they seek fullness of life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This causes carelessness towards death</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So then, only those without regard for their lives</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Will strive for fullness of life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therein resides the virtue of valuing life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Such a realization is also profoundly important to Zen Buddhism, which teaches students to meditate on the temporality of the body, and the interdependence between mind and external objects. While also helping students to see the underlying reality of life, this practice reduces their attachment to false values and meaningless pursuits.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 51-52 describe this non-attachment by showing that the junzi</span> <span id="_ftnref125"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[125\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn125) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">does not dwell on gain and loss, likes and dislikes, nor on wisdom â€“ on knowing and not knowing. In this way, the junzi can remain â€œtranquil, pleasant, and effortless,â€? while moving unobstructedly through the snares of life. This practice of remaining in a learned obliviousness to oneâ€™s own likes and dislikes ushers the junzi into an awareness of the present, and helps them adapt appropriately to the time (see line 55).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To better understand what the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">means by â€œthe ruler who has Dao remains in the state of not knowing,â€? we can also look at an influential passage from the Zhuang Zi on â€œheart-mind fastingâ€? (xin zhai), a term synonymous with â€œpurifying the heart-mindâ€? (xin shu):</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yan Hui said: â€œâ€¦  By doing what otherâ€™s do, they have no basis to blame me. This is called being a fellow disciple. Maintaining the ways of antiquity is to be a disciple of antiquity. Though my words of instruction may point out the rulerâ€™s errors, they will be the words of antiquity and not my own. As such, though being direct, they will not be insulting. This is called being a disciple of the ancients. Will this suffice?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucius replied:  â€œMost certainly not!  You have too many conditions and policies. You plan to go to \[the tyrannical ruler of Wei\] having yet to learn anything about him. Though your plan is firm, you will only avoid transgression. Stopping at that, how can you successfully convert him?  You are only using your mind as the teacher.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yan Hui said:  â€œI have no way to proceed. May I be so bold as to ask the method?â€? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucius replied:  â€œFasting. I will tell you how, but having the method and putting it into action â€“ is this easy?  If you act as though it is easy, radiant Heaven will not find you suited to the task.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yan Hui said:  â€œMy family is poor. Weâ€™ve drunk no alcohol, nor eaten pungent vegetables for several months. Could this be considered fasting?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucius replied:  â€œThis is fasting in preparation to offer sacrifice. It is not the fasting of the heart-mind.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yan Hui said:  â€œMay I be so bold as to ask about the fasting of the heart-mind?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucius replied:</span> <span id="_ftnref126"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[126\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn126) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  â€œYou must be of singular focus. Do not listen with the ears, but listen with the heart-mind; do not listen with the heart-mind, but listen with the breath. Listening (then) stops in the ears, and the heart-mind stops in its verifications. As for the breath, it is the emptiness which receives all things, and it is Dao which brings (all things) towards emptiness.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Emptiness</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is the fasting of the heart-mind.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref127"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[127\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn127)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While heart-mind fasting is an integral part of Daoist sitting practice, it is also integral to the Daoist way of being in the world, or â€œbeing in the moment.â€? By emptying the mind of expectations and predeterminations, one can then perceive and adapt to reality. By following the breath, as students are taught in Taiji and Qigong (Tai Chi and Chi Kung), oneâ€™s body and mind-intent draw in and push forward with no dissociation. Listening at the level of the heart-mind, and at the level of inter-being where oneâ€™s very breath is in communion with their surroundings, allows one to purify the heart-mind, and accord with Dao in the all embracing emptiness. As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">describes, such openness allows one to be in the world with wisdom, equanimity, and effortless responsiveness. Doing so also requires a transcendence of doubt and of oneâ€™s impulses to wield control. Rather, they must learn to observe from a state of equanimity. This is shown in lines 49-59, which explain that our likes and dislikes, just as they are used to wield control over a population through rewards and punishments, wield control over our equanimity and ability to travel gracefully through life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The metaphor of likes and dislikes creating rewards and punishments also translates into advice for inner cultivation. A common admonishment by Daoist teachers is that students will progress quicker if they give their energy to the present, to what they are doing at the time, rather than to hopes and dreams of higher levels and achievements. These aspirations, noble as they may be, hold the power to distract and lead one away from actualization in the present, just as desires and fears provide a handle by which others can lead them away from their best interests.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, the ruler who has Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Remains in the state of not knowing.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">He responds to things as though by coincidence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the Dao of tranquil means. (XSS, lines 56-59)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To rule their own heart and mind, the Daoist is as though oblivious to rewards and loss, but rather, cherishes the benefits of living by Dao. Lao Zi expressed these sentiments with his natural eloquence, in chapter 20 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Stop learning</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And there will be no grief</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is reluctant acceptance so different from rejection?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What is the difference between good and evil?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People in a fearful place cannot be without fear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Uncultivated!  They have not been centered!</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The crowd is joyous and buoyant</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As though having caught a massive beast </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Or celebrating spring rites</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I alone am like the clearness of still water</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Alas, in this way, making no predictions</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Nor making myself predictable</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Like a newborn baby</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Not yet able to make these distinctions</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Roaming!  As though having no home to return to</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The people in the crowd all have more than they need</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But I alone am as one who has lost everything</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I have the mind of a simpleton, indeed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Clouded and muddy!</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is customary for people to have clear and cutting perception</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I alone am as though in a twilight of understanding</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is customary for people to be fascinated</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I alone am as though distant and forlorn</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quick!  I am like the ocean</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Drifting!  As though without any place to stop</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The multitudes of people all have purpose</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet I alone seem stubborn</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And unsophisticated</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I alone seem strange to others</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">For I cherish the nourishment of the mother</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By not thinking of rewards and punishments or benefits and losses during  their stillness practice, students allow the natural process, Dao, to unfold.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

## <span id="_Toc507075975"><span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Ancient Commentary Section of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">appearing in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">:</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">These words do not deny the ruler of his power.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is simply that his power should not meddle in what is truly the domain of those below him.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The ruler is established in Yin. Yin is found in stillness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quiet and still, it does not change.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is with names that sages arrange the myriad things.</span> <span id="_ftnref155"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[155\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn155)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Of people, there are those who are firmly established,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Sage is without these (categories).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Being without them, he is unusual amongst the myriad things.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unusual because he is empty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When people are coerced by what they dislike, they lose what they like.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Intimidated by what they like, they forget (and thus endure) what they dislike.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said: </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">(The junzi is) not intimidated</span> <span id="_ftnref156"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[156\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn156) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">by what he likes, nor coerced by what he dislikes.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the presence of what is disliked, he does not neglect logic.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the presence of what is desired, he does not have excessive emotions.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œThe junzi is tranquil, pleasant, and effortless,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">201</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">   </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">åŽ»æ™ºèˆ‡æ•…ã€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">He abandons wisdom, and it abides in him as a result.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is to say that he is empty, and in the original unaltered state.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(XSX), while not referring to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">or</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, bears many resemblances to these texts, suggesting a larger tradition of teachings and practices in which these texts were situated. As is often said of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">appears to have been written for rulers, while providing universal wisdom applicable to all. Its teachings, therefore, likely grew in consensus amongst a community of sages, before being preserved in writing for the Sovereign by one or more members of this community. Having found consensus, the practices and worldviews in these texts would also be transmitted verbally to nephews, siblings, scholars, and the like, accumulating various experiences and developing into longer treatises. This seems to have been the case in the development of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, a process which likely began long before any of these texts were committed to writing.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">shares a number of passages and expressions with the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, leading some to conclude that the XSX was based on this text. While plausible, this theory does not account for the unique directions the XSX takes before and after these shared sayings, nor the unique and calculated sequences in which these sayings appear in the XSX. The inclusion of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">may, otherwise, be due to it appearing in many duplicates as a self-contained book when Liu Xiang consolidated the many duplicates found in the 564 book bundles that he pared down into the 86 books of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was likely an expansion of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, including additional teachings of the proto-daoist internal cultivation tradition, and therefore included as a separate book. This would make the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">one of the first documents of this tradition.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The first twenty lines of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">present a clear description of the Daoist approach to cultivating virtues. Not by adjusting their external behavior, but by settling themselves internally and pacifying their desires do people cultivate a true and lasting inner virtue. A comparison can be seen in lines 14â€“17 between breath filling the body and conduct filling the world. When one is full of positive qi, they express this outwardly with positive conduct, filling the world with social harmony and contributing to the realization of the great peace of Dao in the world. Added to this teaching of inner attainment outwardly expressing itself, is the technique of aligning the body to bring about internal alignment and balance. Just as one can bring peace and order to their nation by bringing peace and order to themselves, they can facilitate internal peace and order by achieving external peace and order (alignment) in the body.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 18-20, which are entirely unique to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, further demonstrate what it means to follow Heaven and Earth. Similar to lines 38-40 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, we see here that to be â€œabove, like Heaven, and below, like Earthâ€? involves transcendence of the self. Heaven is not aware of its Heaven-ness, and Earth is not aware of its Earth-ness. They have transcended this notion of self. In their stillness, sages also transcend their notion of self-ness. As explained in line 206 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:  â€œBe unified and without division. This is called â€˜knowing Dao.â€™â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The notion of transcending the self is prominent in Buddhism, where the selfâ€™s absence of independent existence is described thoroughly to help one overcome their attachment to the â€œillusion of self.â€? The proto-Daoist texts take a different approach to a similar end, convincing one to overcome attachment to self by showing the freedom that can be known by doing so.  Chapter seven of the Dao De Jing states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven has longevity, Earth has continuit</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">y</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ã€€</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven and Earth have the power of longevity and continuity because they do not live for themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is how they can live for so long</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages leave themselves behind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And they end up in front</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They do not cater to themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet they persist</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is it not because they are without selfishness and wickedness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That they are able to fulfill themselves?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ13 adds:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What does it mean to say â€œAppreciate the great worrying</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That both (favour and disgrace) cause to your person?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The reason I have great worries is because I have a self</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If I did not have a self, what worries would I have?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Finally, DDJ33 states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know others, are wise</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know themselves, are clear-sighted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who overpower others, have strength</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who overpower themselves, have fortitude</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know contentment, are rich</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who exercise this fortitude, have will-power</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who do not lose their station, continue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who die but do not disappear, live long</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The last line of DDJ33 is often considered a reference to the Daoist notion of spiritual immortality; however, with this common thread of transcending the self, it may also suggest that those who overcome the petty concerns of the ego can live longer and achieve lasting accomplishments.</span> <span id="_ftnref169"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[169\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn169)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">     In the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Huainan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">(139 BC), another compendium of Daoist thought which, like the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">, was initiated by an ascendant of Liu Bang, founder of the Han Dynasty, we find a continuation of teachings found throughout the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">â€™s proto-Daoist texts. In chapter one of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Huainan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">, appear instructions for attaining â€œinner Virtue,â€? spiritual intelligence, and the constant accompaniment of Dao. Though the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">are never quoted in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Huainan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">, common themes throughout these texts help one to uncover and clarify their essential underlying motifs. Not wishing to deprive readers of making these connections for themselves, the following excerpt, from the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Huainan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">, chapter one, is provided below without annotation.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Now, those who use their ears and eyes to hear and observe strain their bodies to understand correctly. Those who use knowledge and deliberation to govern correctly abuse the mind and achieve nothing. Therefore, sages use a single measurement, complying with what has been well established. They do not alter its acceptability; they do not change its regularity. Thus, they can determine what accords to the level, knowing what is crooked by what is just.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Euphoria and anger are deviations from Dao;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Anguish and sorrow are losses of Intrinsic Virtue. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Likes and dislikes overtax the mind;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cravings and desires disturb Pure Nature.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Intense anger ruins the yin;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Intense euphoria collapses the yang.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Weakened qi renders one mute;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Fear and terror causes insanity.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If one is anxious, sorrowful, and frequently angry, </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sickness will accumulate.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If likes and dislikes grow numerous,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Misfortunes will also follow.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, when the mind is neither anxious nor jubilant, Intrinsic Virtue is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind is far reaching yet unchanging, tranquility is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When cravings and desires do not burden the mind, emptiness is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind is without likes and dislikes, equanimity is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind is not scattered about on things, purity is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If the mind can succeed in these five (refinements), it will break through to spiritual intelligence.  To break through to spiritual intelligence is to attain what lies within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, using the internal to control the external,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Your many endeavours will not fail.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If, internally, you can attain it,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Externally, you can harvest it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With this inner attainment</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸­ä¹‹å¾—</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å‰‡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">),</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The five major organs will be peaceful;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thoughts and worries will be stabilized.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The tendons will be strong, and your strength will be powerful;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Your ears and eyes will be acute and clear.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though relaxed in your efforts, you will not be wayward</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though firm and strong, you will not bring regret.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There is nothing you will overshoot</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And nothing you will fall short of.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dwelling in the small, you will not be cramped;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dwelling in the large, you will not be extravagant.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Your yang-spirits (hun) will not be agitated;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Your shen-spirit will not be distracted.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Calm and collected, quiet and still,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">You will be amongst the world like an owl.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Great Way is level and smooth.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though it may leave a person, it is never far away.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Seeking it nearby,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though moving ahead, you can continually return to it;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As it presses you, you can be responsive;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As you feel it, you can move;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When things are impressive, they do not deplete you;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though things change, you remain without form or image.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When you give (Dao) free reign and roam with it to the furthest reaches</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">You will be like its echo and shadow.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Climbing up high or descending into depths,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">You will not lose your grip.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When walking through dangers and traversing narrow paths</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">You will not lose this mysterious companion.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If you can be like this, its Virtue will not retreat. As the myriad things scatter and blend together, you can follow their shifts and transformations, listening to the world as though it were a wind at your back moving you swiftly onwards. This is called â€œrefined Virtue.â€? With refined Virtue, there is true happiness.</span> <span id="_ftnref170"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[170\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn170)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages hold to the basis</span> <span id="_ftnref171"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[171\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn171) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and cherish it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">27</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">   </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è€³ç›®ç«¯ï¼ŒçŸ¥é? ä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è­‰</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; letter-spacing:-1pt">28</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">  </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">èƒ½å°ˆä¹Žï¼Ÿèƒ½ä¸€ä¹Žï¼Ÿ </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you stop it?  Can you bring it to a halt? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you do this, not by asking others, but by achieving this within yourself?</span> <span id="_ftnref172"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[172\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn172)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, here as well, carries sentences similar to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(NY), its focus is uniquely centered on inner and outer unity â€“ on inner peace resulting in social harmony. This topic begins in the preceding lines (see XSX 14â€“20), which segue into a discussion of unity by stating:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All things uphold their names and come together.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages hold to the basis,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and cherish it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The world is then orderly and peaceful.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This unity requires a return to the state of mind that precedes distinctions or â€˜namesâ€™. Line 26 states â€œConsolidate the intent.  Unify the heart-mind.â€? As shown later in both the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(line 114) and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(line 167), intent (</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">yi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) precedes words and thus the distinction of â€˜namesâ€™. By consolidating intent, the heart-mind finds the Oneness of â€œthe beginningâ€? mentioned in line 27. Such an understanding will be helpful when encountering lines 32-47, below, which also speak to unification, and the transcendence of thought, leading to wisdom.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    Heshang Gong speaks of the originating Oneness in his comments on DDJ10:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Embrace Oneness. Can you do this without letting (the bodily spirits) flee?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People who can embrace Oneness and not let it leave them, extend their lives. In Oneness, Dao began to situate life by the supreme harmony of vital energy-breath. Therefore it is said:  â€œOneness covered the world with names.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heaven attained Oneness and became clear. Earth attained Oneness and became serene. Lords and kings attained Oneness and became upright and peace-loving. Going within, it is mind; going outwards, it is actions; in covering all with its blessing, it is Virtue.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">All the names together are One.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Referring to Oneness, it is said:  â€œIn a unified consciousness, there is no division (or doubt).â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œGather together the energy-breath and become softâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Gather and embrace the vital energy-breath within. Then it will not be chaotic and the body will become soft and pliant.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œThis is the power of an infantâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Have the power of an infant. Be, internally, without a thought or worry, and externally, without official duties. Then the vital spirits will not leave.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">      Line 22, â€œSages hold to the basis,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and cherish it,â€? can be further explained by reading</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 203â€“212, which define â€œthe</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å›  basis (cause, reason).â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œHe responds, but does not initiate; moves but does not possess.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œthe basis.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The basis is to reside in oneâ€™s own, while according with other things.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(The junzi) responds to feelings, yet does not initiate them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following the principle, he moves (things), but does not possess (them).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œIf one is excessively headstrong, they will err when adapting to changes.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If headstrong, one cannot be empty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If not empty, one becomes the same as other â€œthings.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With change and transformation, there is growth. With growth, there is bound to be confusion.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, the treasure of Dao is the basis (of responding and not initiating; moving yet not possessing). On this basis rests ability. This is called usefulness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">      Lines 26-31 could be variously interpreted, either as consolidating the thoughts and minds of the people to create a unified and familial nation, or otherwise as consolidating oneâ€™s own thoughts and mind so as to attain clarity, peace, and perception. Lines 32-47 confirm the latter as the ultimate significance of these verses.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     A connection between thoughts and the beginning of peril is made clear in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 103â€“104, with the statement â€œInvariably, mental formations will create excessive knowledge, even at the expense of oneâ€™s life.â€? Similar statements about divination also appear in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">62-63: </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Not by the day or the month, but by how affairs follow (Dao), and not by prophesy or divination, but by how cautiously one follows (Dao), can you know their fortune or misfortune.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And in DDJ38:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And speak as though they know how to recognize what is coming</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Here again, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">bears great similarity to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, though also differs significantly in meaning. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(lines 235-262) speaks of unification as a way to extend and preserve life, whereas the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is unique in lines 39-42 where it gives attention to wisely managing political affairs, as per the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s double entendres for the nation and the individual. This dual focus continues in the XSX until line 64.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">further elaborates on the meaning of inner unification by connecting it with the cessation of thoughts (lines 32-36) in the process of refining qi (energy-breath), furthering its earlier instructions to consolidate the intention and unify the heart-mind (XSX, line 26) so as to make the consciousness â€œunified and without (doubt or) divisionâ€? (BX, line 206), and thereby eliminate scattered thoughts (see XSS, line 41).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This â€˜technique of the heart-mind (xin shu)â€™ extends itself to managing affairs by fostering decisiveness, certitude, and focus in endeavours, honing the strength of the mind to eliminate inner distractions.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 41-42 make a comparison between guarding the power of the heart-mind, and guarding the power of a ruler. In both cases, to ensure that only those meriting positions of influence attain them, the Sovereign must not be confused or agitated.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Understanding the teachings in these verses helps one to understand the backdrop of tradition in which the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was written, and to see with greater clarity the implications of its metaphors. Consider, for example, the above teachings on the cessation of thought, along with lines 43-47, in regards to DDJ28:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ Return to Wuji, Supreme Nothingness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing praise, hold onto reproof</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And be a valley under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Being a valley under Heaven, Virtue will always fulfill you</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Return to your unaltered substance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unaltered wood is shaped into vessels</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages make use of this model</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When acting in positions of leadership</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thereby, the greatest establishment is undivided</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When line 46 speaks of uniting the lights of the sun and moon, this evokes the meaning of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ˜Ž</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ming.  Ming is translated as â€œenlightenment,â€? yet means more literally â€œclear vision.â€? It is written by combining the characters for</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ—¥ sun and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æœˆ moon. This could also be understood as suggesting that the junzi embraces the yin and yang energies of the sun and moon, and the emptiness and stillness of Heaven and Earth. The practice of â€œingesting the essence of the sun and moonâ€? became a part of Daoist visualization meditations closer to the 3</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">rd</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">century AD, but as we see, may find its beginnings in proto-Daoism.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 46-47 also show underlying currents of thought evident in DDJ25:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  Dao is immense, Heaven is immense</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Earth is immense, and the Emperor is also immense</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">From the periphery to the center</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There exists the Four Immensities</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the Emperor represents their unification</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Man is regulated by Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Earth is regulated by Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven is regulated by Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao is regulated by its own spontaneous nature</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Contrasting lines 43-64 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(beginning in the previous section) with lines 105-121 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">helps to reveal some of the more esoteric language within the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. For example, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">reads in lines 115-121:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the orderliness of the heart-mind reaches to the very center</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Orderly words leave the mouth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And orderly affairs increase amongst the people</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As such, all under Heaven will be orderly!</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When one word is grasped, all under heaven fits together</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When one word settles (in the heart), all under Heaven cooperates</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is the meaning of â€˜serving the greater good.â€™</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Contrasting this excerpt with lines 54-64 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, â€œone wordâ€? can then be understood as referring to â€œDaoâ€? in the lexicon of these writers, noting this difference in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, line 61. Further, â€œserving the greater goodâ€? can be understood as the prevalence of Dao, rather than disorder being brought about by â€œthe collectivity of those who seek to take charge, and control the system for their own profitsâ€? (line 63). â€œThe greater goodâ€? (gong,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å…¬</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) also means â€œpublic interest, impartial, unselfishâ€? as opposed to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.1rem">ç§?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">private, selfish,â€? and is said to lead one towards Dao in DDJ16:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ Know how to embrace eternality</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This embrace shows the way of impartiality</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(å…¬</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The way of impartiality</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(å…¬</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) shows the way of a king</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The way of a king shows the way of Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The way of Heaven shows the way of Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The way of Dao shows the way of longevity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And for the body to be without peril</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     A number of corresponding ideas on the use of force, abuses of power, and what is â€œnot Daoâ€? (see XSX, line 64), can be found by comparing XSX48-64 with DDJ30:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for those who use Dao to counsel the king</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is not by weapons that they have power in the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such activities are reciprocated</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Where troops gather, thorns and brambles appear </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following war, there is sure to be famine and misfortune</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Large armies are sure to bring sadness in the future</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim well, and then stop</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Do not dare to abuse power</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not boast</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not attack again</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not become arrogant</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not claim all the credit</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Achieve your aim, but do not abuse power</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Things thrive in their prime and then become aged</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œnot Daoâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What is â€œnot Daoâ€? ends prematurely</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     It may appear that the author of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(lines 105-121) condensed lines 43-64 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">so as to focus more on the subject of internal cultivation, or that the author of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">expanded on the words of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">; however, this is to assume that both texts were not simply based on the mutual influence of earlier teachings.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 65-69 provide an early example of Chinese writings on immortality. This illustration of â€˜stillness in motionâ€™ appears before a description of the physical form becoming more durable as a result of â€œaligning and quietingâ€? oneself (XSX70â€“73). XSX67-69,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸?åŒ– (They) do not change.. they are not transformed,â€? therefore, departs from earlier notions of immortality which referred only to the words and deeds of a person living on in perpetuity.</span> <span id="_ftnref178"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[178\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn178)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 65-69 also continue the trend of connecting longevity with the elusive qualities of Dao, a tenet which likely influenced DDJ35:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 80-99 provide a rich example of the proto-Daoistsâ€™ esteem for warm-heartedness. With a â€œgolden heart,â€? one is even protected from external harm, and may forgo rewards and punishments. Such sentiments are also echoed in DDJ50:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I have heard that those who are good at absorbing life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Travel the land without encountering rhinoceros or tigers</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That they walk into groups of soldiers</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without requiring armour, or soldiers, for protection</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The rhinoceros has no place to thrust its horn</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The tiger has no place to grab with its claw</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the soldier has nowhere to place his weapon</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Most of lines 80-99 appears in lines 216-230 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, though with some significant differences. Line 80â€™s â€œa golden heart withinâ€? appears in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">as</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å…¨å¿ƒåœ¨ä¸­</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">(though) the heart-mind remains within</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,â€? exchanging</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é‡‘ goldenâ€? for</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å…¨ maintainingâ€? by omitting two strokes from the character.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é‡‘å¿ƒ Golden heartâ€? is repeated in line 89 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, fitting the imagery in line 90â€™s â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">illuminate</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">like the sun and moon</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,â€? while the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s terminology has instead </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¿ƒæ°£ä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">å½¢</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ˜Žæ–¼æ—¥æœˆ the manifestations of the heart-mindâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">energy-breath</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">illuminate like the sun and moon.â€? This might suggest that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">developed from a â€˜corruptedâ€™ copy of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, where</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">é‡‘ goldenâ€? was written as</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å…¨ maintaining,â€? forcing the editor to make sense of this mistaken terminology and so explain it further down as â€œenergy-breath of the heart-mind.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 80-99 also tie in to lines 109-119 which speak of intention preceding words, explaining in part why â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">unspoken words are heard like drums of thunder, while the golden heart illuminates like the sun and moon.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€?  Similarly, lines 92-95 tie into lines 109-112. Cultivating positive intention would thus appear to be part of the reason behind the proceeding lines which advocate music, courtesy, respect, and internal quiet as ways to alleviate emotions that lead to distress and a deterioration or depletion of life energy. This deterioration can also pollute oneâ€™s intent.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The above comment, that euphoria, pleasure, sorrow, and anger endanger oneâ€™s cultivation of pure nature, is analogous to DDJ50, especially in light of Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œTo depart from life is to enter deathâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When emotions and desires leave the five internal organs, the hun-spirit (in the liver, governing anger) becomes calm, and the po-spirit (in the lungs, governing sorrow) becomes settled. Vitality then flourishes.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When emotions and desires go deep into the consciousness of the heart</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">èƒ¸</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è‡†</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), vital essence is over-exerted, and the spirit becomes confused. This causes death.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThe companions of life are thirteen, The companions of death are thirteenâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lao Tzu is saying that (the path to) life and death are both governed by thirteen things: the nine bodily apertures and four closures.</span> <span id="_ftnref183"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[183\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn183) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  To nourish life, the eyes should not observe frantically, the ears should not listen frantically, the nose should not smell frantically, the mouth should not speak or taste frantically, the hands should not grasp frantically, the feet should not walk frantically, and the vital spirits should not be frantically engrossed. For death, it is the opposite of this.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œIn their way of living, people are ensnared by way of (these) thirteenâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People know to seek life; however, in doing so, they instead bring about death by these thirteen things.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œWhy is this so?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Asking why death arrives this way.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œBecause they seek a life of excessâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who die by seeking life try to make a living in order to support an excessive lifestyle. Defying Dao and disobeying Heaven, their frantic behaviour causes them to lose the true path.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While Heshang Gong speaks to the ways by which people are ensnared, ie. by over-indulgence in, and reliance on, the senses, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">speaks to the next stages of this ensnarement, specifically the pleasure and joy, or sorrow and anger determined by whether or not the desires of the senses are fulfilled.  Thus, Lao Zi and Heshang Gong caution against over-stimulation, while the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also offers methods to ease the symptoms of this over-stimulation, cultivate positive intention, and regain the stability that allows a return to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">xìng</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€“ pure-nature.  </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 100-108 resemble lines 85-95 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, with the exceptions that:</span>

1.  <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, â€œeuphoria, pleasure, sorrow, and angerâ€? are replaced with â€œeuphoria, anger, sadness, and worry.â€? The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also makes a similar statement in line 27, but lists â€œsorrow, pleasure, euphoria, anger, desire, and avarice.â€?</span>
2.  <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, poetry (rather than music) is prescribed for anger, while music is prescribed for sadness.</span>
3.  <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">adds the line â€œto maintain respect, nothing compares to silenceâ€?</span>
4.  <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also adds a final line â€œpure nature will then be firmly established.â€?</span>
