<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 109-126 speak to the essential role of intention in cultivating life energy.  Purifying intention is both an aim and effect of becoming internally peaceful and practicing the â€œart of the heart-mind.â€? As the Guigu Zi</span> <span id="_ftnref190"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[190\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn190) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Genuine intention must begin with the heart-mind technique (xin shu). Seek, through non-doing, stable tranquility of the five internal organs, and harmony throughout the six bowels.  When the vital-essence, spirit (shen), yang-spirits (hun), and yin-spirits (po) are steadfastly guarded and unmoving, you can internalize your gaze and return your listening; settle your will and contemplation on cosmic emptiness, and attend to the spiritâ€™s leaving and returning.     </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     With genuine intention, oneâ€™s energy becomes more positive and life nourishing, allowing the eyes to sparkle and the demeanour to reflect peace, patience, and kindness. Emotional turmoil and overpowering desires suffocate this effect, making the breathing short and the mind narrow. Thus, cultivating energy is not simply filling up the body with fuel, but opening up the windows to the soul and letting fresh positive energy into your spirit. As said in lines 80-82:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A golden heart within cannot be hidden.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Externally, it is observed in the physical form</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And can be recognized in the appearance of the face.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 109-112 confirm that self-cultivation occurs, not only in seclusion, but should be ongoing in daily affairs. Further guidance for practicing â€˜the art of the heart-mindâ€™ in daily affairs can be found in DDJ8, which describes how to become an embodiment of water in all instances.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The highest excellence is like water</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The excellence of water benefits all things</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And does not fight against them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It dwells in the places that people detest</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">How close it is to Dao!</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in dwelling can be found in the Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in the heart can be found in its depths</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in giving can be found in benevolence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in speech can be found in sincerity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in aligning can be found in order</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in professionalism can be found in competence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Such excellence in action can be found in appropriate timing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Simply because it does not fight</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Water) has no enemy</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     By giving awareness to internal energy, thoughts about the past and future are outshined by the power of the present. Lines 113-123 describe a process of spontaneous energy cultivation that takes place upon reaching the inner stillness and silence of the heart-mind (see especially lines 120-123). Without specifically referring to this internal energy work, DDJ15 has often been interpreted as describing the same process:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their stillness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can make clouded water slowly become clear?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their serenity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can sustain this progress until life slowly arises?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-weight:bold"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">     As with the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">â€™s line 204 (â€œWithout soaring (into the sky), without spilling over, the destined life-force (ming) will be extendedâ€?), Lao Zi cautions moderation and balance in this work, by continuin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">g</span> <span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-weight:bold">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-weight:bold"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who maintain this Dao do not desire fullness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is because they are not full that they can remain covered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And not let what is new come to an end</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When this â€˜stillness-qigongâ€™ becomes internally active, energy circulates and nourishes where there is lacking. As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states in lines 208-215:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Invariably, Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is sure to enclose, sure to condense</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sure to expand, sure to open</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sure to strengthen, sure to solidify</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It preserves excellence (yet) does not dwell</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It removes excess and nourishes where there is weakness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Having known the furthest limits</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Return to Dao and Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heshang Gong also describes the nourishing power of inner harmony in his comments on DDJ55:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">When the mind is attuned to the breath, this is called â€˜powerfulâ€™</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind unifies in harmony and softness, spirit-energy flourishes within. The body then becomes pliant. Reverting to frantic actions, the harmonized energy-breath abandons equilibrium, and the body gradually becomes unyielding.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The depiction in XSX109-126, of a clear mind allowing for a reservoir of energy to develop and nourish the body, provides a backdrop by which to read DDJ5 and DDJ6 as a single stream of thought.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  The gate of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is it not like a bellows?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Empty yet not finished</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It moves, and again more is pushed forth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To speak countless words is worthless</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is not as good as guarding balance within</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Chapter Six)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be a valley to the spirit and you will not die</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called the Fathomless and the Female</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The gate to the Fathomless and the Female</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is called The Root of Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Soft and gentle</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is her way of existence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Do not draw on her use laboriously</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ends by emphasizing the importance of learning from the natural world. The saying â€œFor what is above, study the Heavens; for what is below, study the Earth,â€? sums up the statements in lines 109-123, and indicates the still-point in the Heavens which also exists in the heart-mind. From this still-point of the Heavens emanates the vital essence of life, much the same as from the still-point of the heart-mind emanates the thoughts and their subsequent phenomena. It would thus appear significant that the first matter addressed in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is that of this primordial essence and its manifestations.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heshang Gong says the following about this inner center in his commentary on DDJ1:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œ(This) mystery, ever more mystifyingâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Returning to the center of Heaven, there is another Heaven. It dispenses energy-breaths which can be potent or weak. Obtaining harmonious fertile fluid</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.1rem">å’Œæ»‹æ¶²</span> <span style=" font-size:1.1rem ;letter-spacing:0.27rem">)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">from its center, this gives birth to the worthy and wise; If one receives polluted, chaotic, and aberrant (energies), this gives birth to greed and licentiousness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œ(Is a) multitude of gates, all leading to the subtlety withinâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven can return to the Heaven within itself, and dispense energy-breaths which are either potent or weak. Eliminating strong emotions, abandoning desires, and guarding balance and harmony within:  this is called â€œknowing the gate-key to the door of Dao.â€?             </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heaven, therefore, nourishes life on earth as the heart-mind and spirit naturally promote essence in the lower body. According to Daoist alchemical theory, the body is supplied with energy that is stored in the â€˜lower dantienâ€™, located just below the navel, and generates vital essence in the kidneys and sexual organs. Following the analogy of Heaven and Earth, the primordial essence nourishes the physical essence of the body. When this primordial essence is distilled, like murky water, through stillness and silence, it generates wisdom, virtue, and longevity. Heshang Gong explains this process in his commentary on DDJ6:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven feeds people with the five energy-breaths. They go in through the nose, and are stored in the heart-mind. The five energy-breaths are refined to make the vital essence, shen-spirit, intelligence, clear vision (enlightenment), vocal expression, and the five intrinsic natures. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The transformation of this primordial essence proceeds to create virtue in an individual by means of the five intrinsic natures. The five intrinsic natures both support and rely on the health of the internal organs which, according to Daoist theory, correspond as follows: humanity</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä»? ren) in the liver; propriety</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç¤¼ li) in the heart; sincerity</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¿¡ xin) in the spleen; loyalty</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç¾© yi) in the lungs; and wisdom</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ™º zhi) in the kidneys. This accounts for the opening lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">which state that it is essence stored in the breast (the location of the mind according to the ancient Chinese) that makes a Sage. The breast contains the â€˜middle dantien (energy center)â€™ â€“ an area of development in Daoist internal cultivation usually given focus after the lower dantien has been firmly established.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Given the role of Heaven (the heart-mind), and its effect on Earth (the body), the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">shows the role of Earth (the body) in completing the process of refinement by cherishing the energy absorbed from the â€œcenter of the heart-mind.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, all that is collected internally (should be) regarded as a wellspring.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When this source is not exhausted, internally and externally, it circulates freely.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the source is not dried up, the four limbs will become firm and solid,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Enabling command of their functions, and keeping them fit and strong.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 120-123)</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This should not be mistaken to suggest an inert lifestyle, but simply one that is not over-taxing. Exercise that over-strains the body has a deleterious effect in later years. By contrast, relaxed movement, utilizing the bodyâ€™s natural structure and alignment, as is the case in Daoist exercises and martial arts, extends the bodyâ€™s longevity. Such movement also allows relaxation of the mind and disengagement of the emotions in the midst of physical activity. While Daoist martial arts (Taiji, Baguazhang, Xing Yi) and Qigong also develop agility, stamina, strength, and martial skill, the â€œstillness in movementâ€? cultivated through repeated foundational movements is their not-so-hidden treasure.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     By the statement â€œWhen this source is not exhausted, internally and externally, it circulates freely,â€? the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also refers to mental and emotional exhaustion, teaching moderation in such things, much as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">teaches about eating habits.</span> <span id="_ftnref191"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[191\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn191) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  Daoist self cultivation requires that one consider if maybe that extra serving wonâ€™t be missed; maybe thoughts latching onto every phenomena are unnecessary; maybe anger, fear, and disappointment can also be forgone. Making such choices is an important step in not exhausting the essence on which self cultivation relies, and in developing an inner environment conducive to this essence. By reflecting and accepting the great emptiness and clarity of the universe, in its total void of ego and independence from conceptual knowledge, those who â€œnourish lifeâ€? allow Dao to work unhindered in creating a mind like Heaven and body like Earth.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Just as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">may be a compilation, representing the oral and written teachings of many Daoist sages, perhaps inspired by Li Erâ€™s (Lao Ziâ€™s) early lectures, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">may be a compendium of earlier written and oral teachings focused on Daoist internal cultivation.</span> <span id="_ftnref195"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[195\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn195) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In its title,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å…§æ¥­</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nèi Yè</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,â€?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">nèi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">means â€œinner, internal,â€? and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">yè</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">means â€œprofession, vocation; work, endeavour.â€?  Thus, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">describes the internal work of the Sage, perhaps in contrast to his or her external work of fostering balance and harmony throughout â€œall under heaven.â€?  â€˜Nei yeâ€™ carries essentially the same meaning as the more modern term â€˜nei</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">gong</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(internal work)â€™, translated as â€˜internal cultivationâ€™ and referring, as well, to the practice of life-energy transmutation.  While the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">provides guidance on leadership, politics, cosmogony, nature, and self-cultivation, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is a more concise and direct self-training manual for those requiring the illumination demanded of an advisor to world-altering decision makers.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Daoist internal cultivation relies especially on â€œthree treasures.â€? These three are essence (jing), energy-breath (qi), and spirit (shen). The process of transformation in this cultivation consists of transmuting jing into qi, qi into shen, and then shen into emptiness. In the pursuit of physical, energetic, and spiritual immortality, this path of transformation continues further still.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As the proto-Daoist texts in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">show, the practice of energetic transmutation through stillness was already taking shape in the 4</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">th</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">century BC. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begins with an explanation of such transformations, while appearing to differ slightly from later explanations by suggesting that jing-essence transforms qi, rather than transforms</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">into</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">qi (see lines 9-18). The difference here relies on the fact that the beginning of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">refers to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">original</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">essence (yuan jing) of creation, rather than the essence of bodily substance. This original essence provides every living thing with its character, or DNA if you will. As original essence is â€˜unpackedâ€™, it gives rise to the earthly jing, said to reside in the kidneys and internal reproductive organs, as well as to qi and shen (spirit).</span> <span id="_ftnref196"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[196\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn196) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">shows, yuan jing naturally expresses itself when the mind and body are not obstructed and obscured by emotions. Generally as a result of desire and its consequential emotions, the mind cannot give free expression to yuan jing and so yuan jingâ€™s full realization as qi, spirit, nature (xing) and destiny (ming) is limited. As one practices the art of the heart-mind, the process of internal cultivation clears away the limitations to a full expression of our heavenly endowments, and frees up spiritual resources needed to embrace our heaven-endowed potential.</span> <span id="_ftnref197"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[197\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn197)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen (The Yellow Emperorâ€™s Canon of Internal Medicine, Plain Questions)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which shows a deep connection to these early traditions, speaks to this natural potential in its first chapter where we find a depiction of the simplicity that allows people to enjoy these natural benefits:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the sages of high antiquity taught those below, they all told them of the evil that seeks out depletion, of the thieving winds (that cause it), of what to avoid in particular seasons, and that the spacious emptiness of calm cheerfulness</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ?¬</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æƒ”</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) is filled with genuine qi.</span> <span id="_ftnref198"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[198\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn198) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With spiritual vitality (jing-shen) protected within, what illness approaches? Thereby, the will is firmly established and desires are few; the heart-mind is peaceful and without fear. Though the body works hard, it is not fatigued, and the qi is compliant. Each person follows their wishes, and everyone achieves their goal.</span> <span id="_ftnref199"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[199\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn199) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, they enjoy their food, have the clothes they need, take pleasure in customs, and neither those of high or low station have longings. The people were therefore called natural.  Cravings and desires did not strain their eyes, excess and wickedness did not confuse their hearts and minds. They were not afraid of being considered foolish, wise, competent, or incompetent. Thus, they were as one with Dao. Thereby they could all live to one hundred years and neither their movements nor their activities would decline. Their virtue remained intact, and so they were not at risk.</span> <span id="_ftnref200"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[200\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn200)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Zhuang Zi illustrates this naturalness in his chapter â€œFixed Ideasâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said: If the body is over-worked and does not rest, it becomes worn out; if the spirit is employed without pause, it becomes over-worked; and when over-worked, it becomes exhausted. It is the nature of water that when free from other substances, it is clear, and when it is calm, it is level; but if it is collected, obstructed, and not allowed to flow, it cannot maintain its clarity.  It is a reflection of Heavenâ€™s virtue.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Thus it is said: To be pure, genuine, and uncontaminated; to be calm, unified, and stable; to be content and not impositioning; to move according to the phases of Heaven: this is the way to nourish the spirit.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Now, if one has a sword from Gan or Yue, he hides it in a protective case and does not dare use it, for he considers it a most valuable treasure. But the spiritual vitality (jing-shen) travels in all directions, flowing this way and that without limit. Above, it reaches the Heavens; below, it circles the Earth. It transforms and nourishes all things, and cannot be equated with any image. Its name is â€œOne with Divinity.â€? The Dao of pure naturalness is the only way the correctly protect the spirit.  Protected as such, it will not be lost, for the spirit will become unified. Unified, (yuan) jing will rejoin in symbiosis with Heaven. There is a saying in the hinterlands which states that â€œthe multitudes concern themselves with profit; noble scholars concern themselves with reputation; aristocrats increase their ambitions; sages treasure essence.â€? Thus, to be natural is to be uncontaminated; to be pure is to not diminish the spirit.   One who can encapsulate naturalness and purity is called a Genuine Person (Zhen Ren).</span> <span id="_ftnref201"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[201\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn201)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The concept of a â€œGenuine Personâ€? is analogous to the common understanding of a â€œreal man,â€? though with some more specific qualifications. While the terms Genuine Person (also translated as â€œTrue Manâ€?) and â€˜real manâ€™ both suggest courage and confidence, the Genuine Person is courageous without being violent, courageously themselves yet respectful of others, self-expressive but peaceful, self-assured yet humble, natural and spontaneous but not inappropriate. It is because they hold to the level and smooth path of Dao that they can move in any direction without going off course.</span> <span id="_ftnref202"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[202\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn202) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It also goes without saying that the Genuine Person need not be male, but simply genuine.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To fully understand the implications of the terms Genuine Person and Sage, we may look again to the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huang Di Nei Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Su Wen</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter one:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Huang Di said: I have heard that in high antiquity there were Genuine Persons who would hold onto the leading hand of Heaven and Earth, and the hand of yin and yang, exhale and inhale qi essence, stand for themselves and guard their spirit. Their muscles and flesh were as one. Thereby, they could enjoy a lifespan undetermined by Heaven and Earth for they had no specific time to come to an end. This was their way of living in the Dao.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In middle antiquity were the Perfected Persons, who by their natural Virtue could accord fully with Daoâ€¦ They can also be counted as Genuine Persons.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Next were the Sages who dwelled in the harmony of Heaven and Earth and accorded with the principles of the eight winds. Their cravings and desires were suited to the era and local customs, and they had no hatred or anger in their hearts. In their activities they had no desire to avoid the world. In their dress and manner, they had no desire to be elevated and admired by popular people. Externally, they did not over-exert their bodies with endeavours; internally, they did not worry and speculate in their thoughts. They considered enjoying tranquility to be the highest application of oneself, and self-realization to be achievement. Physically, they did not deteriorate, and their spiritual vitality did not dissipate.  (As with the Genuine Persons), they too could live for 100 years.</span> <span id="_ftnref203"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[203\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn203)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These early discourses on health preservation indicate that the key to not only preventing illness, but realizing our human spiritual potential, is found in protecting our spiritual vitality from the contamination of contrivances to our essential nature. This free expression enlivens our vitality, as evidenced by the preceding context of Huang Diâ€™s description of Genuine Persons, which was an inquiry into how a man of advanced years can continue to be fertile.  This background of preserving naturalness and spontaneity helps to bring out the underlying thread of such guidance as it weaves throughout the practices found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 1-22 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">contain a slightly different description of the beginnings of life than in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huang Di Nei Jing, Ling Shu Jing (The Yellow Emperorâ€™s Canon of Internal Medicine, Classic of the Spiritual Hinge)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, likely written or compiled a century or two after the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. The early development of these ideas in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">are nonetheless faintly detectable in chapter eight of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Ling Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Qi Bo replied:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which Heaven gives an individual is De (intrinsic virtue). That which Earth gives an individual is qi (energy-breath). When De and qi intermingle, there is life. From life, what then comes into existence is called jing (essence).  When the two jing (of Heaven and Earth) combine and grasp each other, we have what is called shen (spirit). What follows the departures and arrivals of shen is called hun (yang spirits). What stays with the departures and arrivals of jing is called po (yin spirits). That which relies on things is called the heart-mind (xin). What the heart-mind recalls is called intention (yi, focus, idea).  When the intention remains in a particular place, this is called will (zhi). What comes from the will as it processes and transforms is called thought (si). When thought travels a great distance (as though in search of its) beloved, this is called contemplation (lu). When contemplation arrives at its location, this is called wisdom (zhi).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Thus, wisdom nurtures life, for one must submit to the four seasons, make alterations according to cold and heat, harmonize euphoria and anger so that they abide peacefully, and moderate yin and yang to balance hard and soft.  In this way, excessive imbalances will not arrive, and an extensive lifespan will be continually observed.</span> <span id="_ftnref204"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[204\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn204)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In their commentary on chapter eight of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Ling Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, Claude Larre and Elisabeth Rochat de la Vallée point out that, like chapter 50 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Ling Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also delineates 13 facets of life which develop in the process of forming a human life, the same facets which degenerate in the process of death.</span> <span id="_ftnref205"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[205\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn205) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lao Zi states in chapter 50,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To depart from life is to enter death</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The companions of life are thirteen</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The companions of death are thirteen</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In their way of living, people approach death-traps</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By way of (these) thirteen</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Why is this so?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Because they seek a life of excess</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These 13 facets in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Ling Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">are: Virtue (from Heaven), qi (from Earth), life</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(ç”Ÿ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), jing (essence), shen (spirit), hun, po, the heart-mind, intention, will, thought, contemplation, and wisdom (competence,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ™º</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     A shared tradition behind DDJ50 and LSJ8 may be evidenced by the fact that DDJ50 is followed by DDJ51â€™s description of De, a description which supports the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Ling Shu Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s role for De in the creation of life. Chapter 51 of the Dao De Jing states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao actuates them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Virtue takes care of them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Power completes them</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å‹¢æˆ?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao actuates them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Virtue takes care of them, extends their lifespans</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Teaches them, completes them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Tests them, raises them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And brings them back (to their pure natures)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Actuates them but does not possess them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sets them in motion but does not expect of them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Extends their lives without ruling and controlling</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called Fathomless Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As Heshang Gong comments on DDJ51, De equates to Oneness, which may be understood as the aligning and balancing power of Dao,</span> <span id="_ftnref206"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[206\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn206) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">described in chapter 22 of the Dao De Jing:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which is flexible is preserved</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which is bent is straightened</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which is empty is filled</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which is broken is repaired</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which is lacking acquires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That which is excessive becomes confused</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sage embraces Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So as to bring the world into alignment</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     And in DDJ39:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the beginning was the attainment of Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven attained Oneness and became clear</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Earth attained Oneness and became serene</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Gods attained Oneness and became spiritually powerful</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Valleys attained Oneness and became full</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The myriad things attained Oneness and were born</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lords and kings attained Oneness and all under Heaven became loyal</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A full picture of jing-qi-shen transformation in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts could be drawn by combining the descriptions of jing and qi transformation in NY1-20 with the description of jing to shen transformation in XSS90-97:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What people occupy themselves with today is jing-essence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Getting rid of desires should be the priority.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">From this follows quiet stillness;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Quiet stillness brings about jing-essence;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">From jing essence, singularity is established.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Singularity brings about illumination;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Illumination brings about spirit;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for spirit, this is reaching the treasure.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">refers here to jing-essence as it appears in the body. Chapter 21 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">offers additional perspective on the jing-essence referred to in the beginning of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€“ that of a universal essence which, similar to the earthly jing-essence in the body, is described as the most basic nourishment of life energy. Refining this basic nourishment into its more pure original substance is at the foundation of Daoist internal alchemy (Nei Dan). As shown in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Guan Zi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">texts, and in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, this transformation takes place through what might be called a distillation of the heart-mind. This distillation purifies worldly contrivances in the heart-mind and brings about the â€œpure essence.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ21:    </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Openness is Virtueâ€™s form</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is ancient and it is modern</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Its attributes do not leave</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">How am I able to know that the multitudes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Began according to this nature of beginnings?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By this</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">   </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 23-38, above, may be well illustrated by a popular Zen parable:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">A learned scholar named Huike approached</span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Boddhidharma and said, â€œMy mind is disturbed, please pacify it for me.â€? Boddhidharma responded, â€œBring me your mind and I will pacify it for you.â€? Upon reflection, Huike responded â€œHaving sought it, I can no longer find it,â€? to which Boddhidharma said â€œThere you go then, I have pacified it.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In mindfulness practice, students learn to observe inner and outer reality without judgement, grasping, or expectation. This alone can calm the mind as influences, such as emotions and thoughts, when observed, often dissolve like snowflakes caught in the hand.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     NY23-25 provide an important ancient Chinese psychological insight, which is that the mind works spontaneously. Thoughts do not arise out of effort, but</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">responsively</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. This is why when Huike sought for his mind he could no longer find it. Concentration and study may give rise to thoughts and ideas, but those thoughts arise â€œof themselves.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref211"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[211\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn211) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The mind does not construct these thoughts, but simply follows them along their respective paths as they rise up and garner the attention of the mind. Thus, clearing the mind does not consist of actively clearing the mind of thoughts, but of learning to stop following them along their journey. To do this, one must first become aware of the thoughts that carry them along, and eventually learn to just observe them. Simply observing them and letting them dissipate, one eventually finds they are no longer in the company of so many thoughts, and can thus relax in the openness that appears in their absence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 23-38 also help to clarify DDJ47 when contrasted with its images of seeking externally what can only be attained within oneself:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao might be interpreted as the state of balance and harmony. <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">Perhaps the most revealing word in lines 39-50 is also one of the most often edited in translations of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">. Line 43, â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal; font-style:italic">Strategic!  No one hears its voice</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">â€? is usually found, today, with â€œmou</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è¬€</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">, strategic,â€? replaced with â€œmo</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ¼ </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:normal">, desert; indifferent,â€? and translated as â€œsilent.â€? However, è¬€ strategic also fits here in the sense that strategy implies something undisclosed and deceptive. As DDJ36, which describes the effectiveness of unforeseen strategies, states:  â€œThe stateâ€™s sharp instruments should not be revealed.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     NY86-87 also use</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è¬€ strategiesâ€? in the sense of something hidden and underlying: â€œPleasure, anger, obtaining, and giving are the underlying motivations</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(è¬€</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) o</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">f</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">humanity.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The description of Dao as strategic compliments lines 49-50, â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yet its sequence of development, we call â€˜Dao,â€™</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€? a statement supported by Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary on DDJ21:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œHow am I able to know that the multitudes began according to this nature of beginnings?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(In other words) â€œHow can I know that the myriad things followed Dao to be infused with energy-breath?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œBy thisâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œThisâ€? refers to â€œthe present.â€? In this very moment, the myriad things all receive the Daoâ€™s vital energy-breath in order to live, to move, to stand up, and to rise to their places. If not by a Path (Dao), this could not have happened.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">      Without giving undue weight to this line, it could be noted that, whereas the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">can be read as concealing a great deal of subtle government strategy, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">can be read as concealing a similar portion of subtle martial strategy. In either case, many insights into Dao and the heart-mind of human beings appear to have come from contemplating the path towards a peaceful society.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 51-54 show how Dao may be attained, and maintained, even by people who have never heard of Dao. Holding onto a natural simplicity and tranquility becomes a rather obvious priority for anyone trying to recover their health. The proto-Daoists, however, taught that doing so was not just a matter of health, but also of success, luck, and destiny (lines 55-58, and 69-73). In the same way that this inner harmony nourishes and repairs the body,</span> <span id="_ftnref214"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[214\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn214) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">bringing the organs and circulations to an ideal balance, it will also bring an individual into balance with their exterior world, effecting a harmonious, organic, relationship between external elements and between those elements and the individual.</span> <span id="_ftnref215"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[215\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn215) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  This is evident in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(lines 55-58, and 69-73), and in DDJ37:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">The Dao is always effortless yet without inaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">When lords and kings can guard this within</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">The myriad things eventually transform themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Transforming, yet desiring to do so intentionally</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">I pacify this desire with the simplicity of namelessness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">The simplicity of the nameless removes all desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">When the tranquility of desirelessness is established</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">The world stabilizes itself</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also shows, this harmony cannot be attained impatiently, or fabricated with ingenuity. This is not to say that people should not work tirelessly, however. The Duke of Zhouâ€™s comment on the first line of the first hexagram (Heaven) in the Yi Jing (I Ching) states â€œHeaven moves with vitality. The junzi therefore sturdies himself to ceaseless activity.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref216"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[216\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn216) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  It is simply a matter of doing so with an inner tranquility and harmony. As Heshang Gong comments on DDJ23:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Men should conduct affairs like the Dao, in peace and stillness. They should not conduct affairs like gusting winds and violent rainstorms.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 65-78 venture to describe the indescribable, Dao, while at the same time acknowledging the ineffable and intangible qualities that make it â€œunnameableâ€? in the Daoist sense of being indistinguishable from reality as a whole. Though the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">makes constant reference to the influence of Dao throughout Heaven, Earth, and Humanity, as with the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, it ultimately heeds the opening statement of chapter one: â€œThe dao which can be told is not the eternal Dao. The name which can be named is not the eternal name.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     More similarities can be seen here in regards to DDJ21. Line 74, â€œDao is without root and without stem; without leaves and without flowersâ€? is comparable to DDJ21â€™s: â€œIt is ancient and it is modern. Its attributes (names) do not leave.â€? <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">   </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The â€œseasons of Heavenâ€? change, yet are constant in their cycles. The â€œextensions (lit. â€œbranches,â€? see line 85) of Earthâ€? transform, yet are constant in their types. Therefore, sages move and adapt as necessary, but are constant in their inner alignment and stillness. The ability to outwardly adapt while remaining inwardly stable is of great importance in proto-Daoist texts, which show that, by guarding inner balance while being outwardly flexible, dangerous straits in life can be successfully navigated</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In a comment, attributed to Confucius, on the Yi Jingâ€™s water hexagram (Kan), we find:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">again reflects the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">here were the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This pure essence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is the pure essence of energy-breath.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The way of energy-breath is to flourish.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Flourishing, it becomes thoughts;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thoughts become knowledge;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">After knowledge, it stops.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Invariably, mental formulations</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Will supersede knowledge even at the expense of oneâ€™s life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Su Wen, chapter 39, explains this phenomenon with further details:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The hundred diseases are generated by qi.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When one is angry, their qi rises</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When euphoric, their qi relaxes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When sad, their qi dissipates</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When fearful, their qi descends</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When cold, their qi collects</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When over-heated, their qi leaks out</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When startled, their qi is chaotic</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When exhausted, their qi is wasted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When pensive, their qi is knotted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When one is pensive, the heart-mind occupies a location</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And the shen-spirit keeps returning to a location</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The aligned qi is halted and does not circulate</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, qi is knotted</span> <span id="_ftnref225"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[225\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn225)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">We find the method to untangle these knots in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which suggests detaching ourselves from the frantic chases of the mind and returning to inner unity. By following the guidance in lines 91-92, (â€œIf you can be aligned, you can be silent. Then you can be settled.)â€? one may realize what Lao Zi speaks of in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter 56:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who know, do not speak</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who speak, do not know</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Close your ports</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Shut your gates</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dull your points</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Separate your tangles</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Soften your glare</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be like ashes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is to say</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œBe one with the sacredâ€?â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While Oneness carries a number of metaphysical connotations, lines 91-114 speak to its more immediate application in being of a unified and undivided consciousness. By keeping the heart-mind settled, focus is not easily agitated and dissipated, allowing the energy-breath and heart-mind to remain centered and reach the destination of their focus.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As Heshang Gong comments on DDJ10:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œGather together the energy-breath and become softâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Gather and embrace the vital energy-breath within. Then it will not be chaotic and the body will become soft and pliant.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œThis is the power of an infantâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Have the power of an infant. Be, internally, without a thought or worry, and externally, without official duties. Then the vital spirits will not leave.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œLooking deeply, purify and eliminateâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">One should wash the heart-mind until it is clean and pure. The heart-mind lives in the fathomless depths of emptiness. Investigate. Know its myriad engagements. This is called â€œinvestigating the fathomless.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Like NY105-114, Heshang Gong explains in DDJ14 that by holding Oneness we are able to become the active, rather than reactive, party in our own lives.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Hold to the ancient Dao and ride it until you possess the present</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages hold and embrace the ancient Dao which gave birth to Oneness and allowed them to commandeer things. Understand the present by holding onto Oneness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">carries a similar passage to NY100-106, but follows with the statement "Therefore, all that is collected internally (should be) regarded as a wellspring. When this source is not exhausted, internally and externally, it circulates freely.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref226"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[226\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn226) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  Further,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 37-38, read:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸€æ°£èƒ½è®Šæ›°ç²¾ã€‚ </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unified energy-breath can bring transformation. This is called â€œessence.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸€äº‹èƒ½è®Šæ›°æ™ºã€‚ </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unified endeavours can bring transformation. This is called â€œwisdom.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">rather than, in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, line 105:</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸€ç‰©èƒ½</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">åŒ–</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è¬‚ä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç¥ž</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">; </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With Oneness, things can be transformed. We call this spirit.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ä¸€äº‹èƒ½</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">è®Š</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è¬‚ä¹‹æ™ºã€‚ </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With Oneness, situations can be changed. We call this wisdom</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     These differences suggest, not simply a suppression of thoughts, but a transmutation of the energy that becomes thoughts (see NY99-104). By aligning the posture</span> <span id="_ftnref227"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[227\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn227) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and remaining internally still and clear, this energy, normally occupied by wandering thoughts, can be returned to the resonance of intention, awareness</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ„? yi), associated in Daoist medical theory with the unifying earth element of the spleen.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Following the closing statement of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€œFor what is above, study the Heavens; for what is below, study the Earth,â€? this method could be described as â€œby the power of stillness, making clouded water slowly clarify / By the power of serenity, making life slowly ariseâ€? (DDJ15). Further, b</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">y</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">clearing clouds (thoughts) from the sky (heart-mind), the light of the sun (spirit) can nourish the earth (body).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 107-109 illustrate how those adept at the heart-mind method (xin shu/xin fa) can bring about change without losing their inner Oneness and spirit. This is described further in the following lines (below), especially 129-150 which speak of spiritual intelligence.  This spiritual intelligence is maintained by following the directions in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">of not being swayed by emotions and fears, but rather, staying balanced in both breath and wisdom. This ability is cultivated in the practice of Tai Ji (Tai Chi), which teaches the continuous flow of breath and movement, and thereby a calm rhythm of breathing while transforming the obstacles (opponents) in front of oneself. Doing so allows the free flow of intuitive response in the application of learned skills.  Thus, neither the power of oneâ€™s breath, nor their ability, is diminished by adapting to the circumstances requiring change.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">speaks of â€˜order,â€™ this should not be understood as a fixed, rigid, and stultifying order, but a natural one in which things find comfort in their true elements.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As such, Lao Ziâ€™s method of government can be seen as developing directly from an early tradition of attaining inner power through non-interference and stillness. As he states in DDJ48:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of learning requires daily accumulation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of Dao requires daily reduction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reducing and reducing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Until arriving at effortlessness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Effortless, yet without inaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Conquering all under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is best done without the endeavour to do so</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Perpetually, this endeavour will continue without satisfaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Even when all under Heaven has been conquered</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     And in DDJ29:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The wish to possess all under Heaven, and control it</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I see this has no end</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The world is an instrument of the gods</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It cannot be controlled</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who try, spoil it</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who grasp, lose</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Chinese traditions of cultivating inner peace may very well have developed out of purification rituals meant to prepare a supplicant for making offerings to deities and spirits. These rituals date back well beyond the time of Confucius, who makes many references to obtaining the favour of shen ming, or â€˜spiritual lights.â€™ The description here of power and stability, preserved by the residence of an inner spirit (see line 135), coincides closely with Heshang Gongâ€™s references to the shen ming and the protection they provide to those who follow the way of natural simplicity. See, for example, his following comments on DDJ7:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">All people love (sages) like their own mothers and fathers. The spiritual lights (shen ming)</span> <span id="_ftnref232"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[232\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn232) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">protect them like a newborn child. Thus, they always remain.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages act with love towards people, and are protected by the spiritual lights. Is this not because they are fair, upright, and without selfishness?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     On the other hand, as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">appears to be doing here, Heshang Gong more commonly uses the term shen ming to refer to something cultivated; for example, in his comments on DDJ12:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThus, sages are guided by their stomachsâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By guarding the five intrinsic natures,</span> <span id="_ftnref233"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[233\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn233) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">abandoning the six emotions, and uniting the qi of concentration,</span> <span id="_ftnref234"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[234\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn234) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">spiritual intelligence (shen ming) is fostered.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This idea of cultivating shen ming may not be entirely disconnected from the concept of these spiritual entities, however, as evidenced in Heshang Gongâ€™s comments in DDJ16:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThe way of impartiality shows the way of a kingâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Impartial, honourable, and unselfish, one can become king of all under Heaven. By governing and aligning the body, form is unified. Countless spiritual lights then assemble in the body.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThe way of a king shows the way of Heavenâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Being a king, here, means that Virtue will gather spiritual lights and take you through the Heavens.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     It appears that the author (or authors) of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was likely aware of this understanding of shen ming, and its relevance to oneâ€™s own spirit and cultivation (see line 135). Heshang Gong, and the author(s) of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, do not so much advocate communion with the shen ming, as authors of Confucian texts did, but rather advocate embodying their power within oneself. This can be seen in NY1-8 and 235-253 (below). Perhaps one of the reasons for this departure is the proto-Daoistsâ€™ tendency towards co-existent self-reliance, in contrast to the interdependence more characteristic of Confucian mores.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     What the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">more directly refers to here is â€˜spiritual intelligenceâ€™, the ultimate state of spiritual and mental clarity, unimpaired by imbalances that may result from psycho-physical tensions, emotions, and the ultimate cause of emotions: craving. The anger of not getting what we feel we deserve, the euphoria of getting it, and the sorrow of losing it can be transcended through the art of the heart-mind.  By eradicating cravings, expectations, driving emotions, mental constructs, and limited cognitive knowledge of time and space, one can allow the illumination of the spirit to enter the emptiness of the heart-mind. This is further elucidated in chapter one of the Huainan Zi, which complements the instructions of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">quite helpfully when compared with the discussion of order and alignment in NY115-128, and then the refinements needed to bring forth spiritual illumination discussed in NY129-150:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Now, those who use their ears and eyes to hear and observe strain their bodies to understand correctly. Those who use knowledge and deliberation to govern correctly abuse the mind and achieve nothing. Therefore, sages use a single measurement, complying with what has been well established. They do not alter its acceptability; they do not change its regularity. Thus, they can determine what accords to the level, knowing what is crooked by what is just.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Euphoria and anger are deviations from Dao;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Anguish and sorrow are losses of Intrinsic Virtue. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Likes and dislikes overtax the mind;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Cravings and desires disturb Pure Nature.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Intense anger ruins the yin;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Intense euphoria collapses the yang.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Weakened qi renders one mute;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Fear and terror causes insanity.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If one is anxious, sorrowful, and frequently angry, </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sickness will accumulate.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If likes and dislikes grow numerous,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Misfortunes will also follow.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, when the mind is neither anxious nor jubilant, Intrinsic Virtue is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind is far reaching yet unchanging, tranquility is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When cravings and desires do not burden the mind, emptiness is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind is without likes and dislikes, equanimity is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the mind is not scattered about on things, purity is refined.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If the mind can succeed in these five (refinements), it will break through to spiritual intelligence.  To break through to spiritual intelligence is to attain what lies within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, using the internal to control the external,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Your many endeavours will not fail.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If, internally, you can attain it,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Externally, you can harvest it.</span> <span id="_ftnref235"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[235\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn235)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 151-173 ask the reader to consider the seeds of emotion, thoughts, and action, created by the heart-mind. A peaceful heart-mind sprouts peaceful emotions, thoughts and actions. An agitated heart-mind sprouts agitated emotions, thoughts and actions. Thus, the state of our environment is shaped by our heart-mind, and the seeds of emotion, thought, and action that it creates.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 160â€“163 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">resemble lines 109â€“112 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which illustrate this point somewhat more directly, in saying:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When is there no benefit from my affairs? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When there is no benefit in my heart-mind.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When is there no peace where I reside? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When there is no peace in my heart-mind</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While both texts reflect the opening lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">with this sentiment, they are somewhat more methodical in their techniques, and so go on to provide directions for looking deeply into the â€œheart of the heart-mindâ€? where one can delve into the soil of intention (yi), uproot the weeds of agitation and rumination, and thereby foster seeds of inner and outer harmony. This technique begins in lines 122-128 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which approximate to the opening lines of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, providing a physical complement to the art of the heart-mind:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the bodily form is not aligned,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Virtue does not approach;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the center is not tranquil,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The heart-mind is not orderly.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When the bodily form is aligned, it absorbs Virtue.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heavenâ€™s benevolent generosity and Earthâ€™s balancing righteousness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Then naturally arrive in abundance.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(NY122-128)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lao Zi expands on the process of cleansing the heart-mind in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter three:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, the Sageâ€™s government</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Empties the mind and enriches the stomach</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Softens the will and strengthens the bones</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">People then remain uncontrived and without desires</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">While the scheming do not dare to act</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Act by not acting</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And everything will fall into place</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In Daoist meditation, focus is put on the lower energy reservoir under the naval (lower dantien), while the heart and mind release the constraints of thinking and emotion. The meditator does not try to control the course of nature (ie., softens the will), but allows an inner alignment to naturally come about. This reverses the effects of stress-response and helps the body and mind to return to balance, allowing nutrients to be properly absorbed and circulated (strengthens the bones). Heshang Gong comments on the line â€œstrengthens the bonesâ€?: â€œHe cherishes his vital essence and takes seriously what was bestowed upon him. Thus, his bone marrow is full, and his bones are strong.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When the mind and breath have naturally settled and become peaceful, and the energy of thoughts is about to arise, one can become aware of the subtle resonance of thought that is about to arise and gently direct it to the lower dantien, or to the bone marrow. This allows the mind to remain silent and undistracted, and the intent to direct energy back into the bodyâ€™s reservoirs, described in the following lines (NY174-184). If the mind becomes distracted and clouded by thoughts, the intent is deferred, allowing thoughts to become chaotic, which in turn causes the intent to be directed by limited patterns of the mind. Emotion, stress, and confusion may then disturb the harmonious balance (order) of the heart-mind and deplete vital energy.  Therefore, to preserve this harmonious balance, it is best to stay unified in awareness, and â€œwithout (doubt or) division.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Rumination is understood in Chinese medicine as a superficial, or pathological, expression of the spleenâ€™s earth energy. On observation, one may find that their thoughts are an instinctual attempt to reconnect to the grounded earth energy of the spleen, which is actually found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">yi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, intention (also associated with the spleen). As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">shows, by returning to the original open awareness that lies underneath the thoughts, one can restore balance, clear, away the clouds of thought, and thereby uncover the heart of the heart-mind. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>
