<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The â€œabyss of energy-breath,â€? â€œwellspringâ€? and â€œflood of harmony and peacefulnessâ€? in lines 174-178 may indicate a shared oral tradition with Meng Ziâ€™s (Menciusâ€™) teaching on â€œflooding qiâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(Meng Zi replied), 'It is difficult to describe it. This is qi: It is exceedingly great, and exceedingly strong. Being nourished by rectitude, and sustaining no injury, it fills up all between heaven and earth. This is qi: It is the mate and assistant of righteousness and reason. Without it, man is in a state of starvation. It is produced by the accumulation of righteous deeds; it is not to be obtained by incidental acts of righteousness. If the mind does not feel (satisfied with oneâ€™s) conduct, the nature becomes starved. I therefore said, "Gao has never understood righteousness, because he makes it something external." There must be the constant practice of this righteousness, but without the object of thereby nourishing the qi. Let not the mind forget its work, but let there be no assisting the growth of that nature. Let us not be like the man of Song. There was a man of Song, who was grieved that his growing corn was not longer, and so he pulled it up. Having done this, he returned home, looking very stupid, and said to his people, "I am tired today. I have been helping the corn to grow long." His son ran to look at it, and found the corn all withered. There are few in the world who do not deal with their qi as if they were assisting the corn to grow long. Some indeed consider it of no benefit to them, and let it alone â€“ they do not weed their corn. They who assist it to grow long, pull out their corn. What they do is not only of no benefit to the nature, but it also injures it.â€™</span> <span id="_ftnref241"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[241\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn241)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Though Meng Zi has a moral cultivation as the base of his qi cultivation, the influence of Daoist cultivation practices are evident in his advocacy for allowing to nature what nature does best.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Such descriptions of â€œabyss,â€? â€œwellspringâ€? and â€œfloodâ€? in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">lines 74â€“191 are also reminiscent of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">è°·</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">valley in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapters six</span> <span id="_ftnref242"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[242\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn242) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and 28. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ28:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing the male, guard the female</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And be a valley under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be a valley under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And Virtue will never flee</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But will return to her infant son</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing the white, guard the black</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And be a guide for the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be a guide for the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And Virtue will remain without wavering</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Return to Wuji, Supreme Nothingness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing glory, hold fast to humiliation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And be a valley under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Being a valley under Heaven, Virtue will always fulfill you</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Return to your unaltered substance</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unaltered wood is shaped into vessels</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sages make use of this model</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When acting in positions of leadership</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, the greatest establishment is undivided</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Seeing the similarity in the teachings of DDJ28 and the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the metaphor of â€˜the state as the selfâ€™  can be understood in Lao Ziâ€™s words â€œthe greatest establishment is undividedâ€? as referring to the same types of unification described in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     From a Chinese medical perspective, lines 174-191 also follow the creation cycle of the five elemental phases. This begins with the notion that life energy is rooted in the jing (vital essence) of the kidneys:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When pure and vital essence remains, life-energy spontaneously emerges.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">One is then externally peaceful and radiant,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Concealing this surging wellspring within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A flood of harmony and peacefulness,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It becomes an abyss of energy-breath. (NY174-178)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The water phase of kidney-jing gives rise to the wood phase of the liver, expressed in the muscles and the forward yang-energy of growth and determination.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If this abyss does not dry up,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The four limbs solidify; (NY179-180)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The wood phase gives rise to the fire phase of the heart-mind, which may be associated with the â€œnine orificesâ€? in line 182. Though the ears, eyes, nostrils, mouth, urethra and anus are associated with various particular phases, the â€œfree and unblockedâ€? state of the headâ€™s orifices suggests consciousness, and the heart-mind. This connection is also made evident in the opening lines of the Xin Shu Shang: â€œThe heart-mind holds the throne of the ruler. The nine apertures hold offices of various public servants. When the heart-mind remains with Dao, the nine apertures act reasonably.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If this wellspring is not exhausted,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The nine bodily orifices are free and unblocked.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">One can then absorb</span> <span id="_ftnref243"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[243\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn243) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">all of Heaven and Earth,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Covering the four seas. (NY181-184)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The fire phase gives rise to the earth phase, associated with the spleen, the absorption of the stomach, and intention.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Within, oneâ€™s intention is not vacillating;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Externally, they are without affliction and calamity.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Their heart-mind is maintained, within,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And their body is maintained, externally. (NY185-188)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This shows the progressive transformations that take place as life-energy reaches through oneâ€™s being. The only phase not yet touched on in these lines is the metal-phase, associated with the lungs and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">skin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Suffice it to say, when oneâ€™s intention is not vacillating, their breath may become more natural, deep, and full. Lines 192-193 (below) begin by referring to the healthy glow of the skin that follows the practice of aligning and quieting oneself, mentioned earlier in lines 91-114.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">NY216-234 provide an early clarification of the Daoistâ€™s approach to social harmony, and may support their rejection of the perceived</span> <span id="_ftnref252"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[252\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn252) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Confucian focus on cultivating external conduct:  If oneâ€™s energy is not balanced and harmonious, it cannot be hidden by external conduct.</span> <span id="_ftnref253"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[253\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn253) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  Thus, it is deemed more beneficial to cultivate â€œinternal virtue,â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref254"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[254\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn254) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">reclaiming essence and original nature, rather than external behaviours and actions. These lines also profess the superiority of Daoist methods over Legalist methods of government (see especially lines 229-230).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The approach to successful governing found in NY229-234 is central to Daoist advice given to rulers, and helps to contextualize DDJ13:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦  What does it mean to say â€œAppreciate the great worrying</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That (favour and disgrace) cause to your person?â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The reason I have great worries is because I have a self</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If I did not have a self, what worries would I have?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, those who (govern) the self as the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And cherish it as such</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">On them the world can rely</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who (govern) the self as the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And love it as such</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To them the world can be entrusted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     DDJ13 can be read as advising that a ruler ought not rely on othersâ€™ opinions of them, but simply care for and cultivate oneself and the world as though they were one and the same thing. Thereby, they will not be seduced by pursuits for glory and fame at the expense of both the nation and their own body. Similarly, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">counsels that cultivating internal harmony and vitality should be the first priority of a ruler.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Zhuang Zi also advises this approach in his chapter â€œRetiring to Non-attachment (chapter 11)â€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I have heard of retiring to non-attachment; I have not heard of ruling all under Heaven. As for retiring, it is for fear of corrupting the pure nature of all under Heaven. As for non-attachment, it is for fear that the intrinsic virtue of all under Heaven will shift. When all under Heaven does not corrupt their pure nature, nor shift their intrinsic virtue, then order has been attained! </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     \[...\]  Thus, even the greatness of all under heaven would not suffice for rewards and punishments. Since the time of the three dynasties, there has been nothing but clamour over the business of rewards and punishments. What leisure have they had to find peace in the reality of their pure nature and destiny?   Their enjoyment of clear vision?  Just debauching in lust. Their enjoyment of hearing?  Just debauching in sounds. Their enjoyment of benevolence?  Just throwing their intrinsic virtue into disorder. Their enjoyment of righteousness?  Just opposing common sense. Their enjoyment of ceremonies?  Simply an exhibition of skills. Their enjoyment of music?  Simply exhibitions of lewdness. Their enjoyment of wisdom?  Simply an exhibition of craft. Their enjoyment of knowledge?  Just expositions of fault.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     If all under Heaven were to find peace in the reality of their pure natures and destinies, it would make no difference if these eight things existed or disappeared. When all under heaven does not find peace in the reality of their pure natures and destinies, these eight things begin to warp and swell, throwing all under Heaven into chaos. When all under Heaven begins to revere and insist on them, how extensively are all under Heaven mislead!   Then they do not simply partake and move on, but will fast before speaking of them, they will kneel when presenting them, they will sing praises of them and dance about. What can I do once it has gone this far?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Therefore if the junzi cannot resist engaging in administration of the world, there is nothing better than to do nothing. Doing nothing, he can then find peace in the reality of his nature and destiny. Therefore, valuing his body as he values the world, to him the world can be entrusted. Having love for his body as he has love for the world, on him, the world can rely. Therefore, if the junzi can contain and not indulge his five senses, nor bring out his intelligence and perception, he will be still as a corpse yet displaying a dragon, quiet as an abyss yet with a voice like thunder. His spiritâ€™s movements will be entrained with Heaven. Though at ease and without action, myriads of things will accumulate around him. (Following this, he will ask) â€œWhat leisure do I have to govern the world?â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref255"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[255\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn255)

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     To understand the implications of consolidating qi and becoming â€œspirit-like,â€? it helps to understand</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ling</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ling qi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the cultivation of which is the focus of lines 327-353, below. It is</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ling</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, spiritual potency, that spirits are said to consist of, and so to consolidate qi and become spirit like is to cultivate this ling qi. The above precautions concerning thought correlate to the following lines, 254-266, which show how thinking, a major source of stagnation due to knotted qi in Chinese medicine, can bring one out of the natural balance that fosters inner potency. Ling also carries the meaning of the efficacy of Dao. As Dao is sometimes referred to as a carpenterâ€™s level or chalk-line, showing what is just and what is crooked,</span> <span id="_ftnref259"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[259\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn259) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">to move away from Dao would bring the loss of this efficacy, and thereby misfortune (see line 240). To be careful of excessive thought is to remain close to this guiding line and avoid illnesses and calamities before they arrive (see 327-353). Remaining close to Dao in such a way, one does not â€œwait until thirsty to dig a well.â€? As Qi Bo explains in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Jing, Su Wen</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter two:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As for Dao, the sages practice it; the foolish decorate themselves with it.  To accord with yin and yang leads to life; to oppose them leads to death. To accord with yin and yang leads to order; to oppose them leads to chaosâ€¦ Therefore, sages did not establish order to stop illness, they established order before illness arose. They did not establish order to stop chaos, they established order before chaos arose. To provide medicine after illness is already affixed, or instill order after chaos has already ensued, this is like digging a well after one is already thirsty, or fashioning weapons after war has already begun.</span> <span id="_ftnref260"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[260\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn260) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 235-253 may also help to show the early teachings behind DDJ10, especially in regards to inner consolidation, and freeing the mind of inner dialogue.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ10:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Guard the fortress of your bodily spirits</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Purify and eliminate</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you be without flaw?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Caring for the people and governing the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you be without effort?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you act the part of the female?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">NY254-258 could be read as a cause and effect progression from over thinking through to death, explaining the general Daoist attitude towards superfluous knowledge. Thus, â€œthinking and searching lead to knowledge,â€? beginning this downward spiral. This may also be hinted at in NY238-240:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you, without divining by yarrow stalks,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Know what is fortunate and what is perilous?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can you stop (peril from arriving)?  Can you make it cease?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Reading NY254-258, it can be understood that thinking and searching give rise to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">knowledge</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">which leads to inaction, or â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">sluggishness and idleness</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€? which give rise to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">anxiety</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. This anxiety then leads to fear-based</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">aggression and arrogance</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the consequences of which bring a great deal of</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">anger</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">into oneâ€™s environment. This environment of conflict leads to deeper</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">anxiety, constrained qi,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and thus</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">illness</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, which leads to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">death</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. How does one reverse this escalation of illness? â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">If one does not make premature determinations, the life-force will later re-establish itself</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€? (lines 261-262). This caution is corroborated by Classical Chinese medical theories of knotted qi, brought about by over-thinking, and the constraint (yu,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">é¬±</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) of qi that this knotting will produce. Constrained qi, according to the famed Chinese physician Zhu Danxi (1281-1358), is the root of all pathological changes.</span> <span id="_ftnref265"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[265\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn265) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This understanding was also illustrated in Zhuang Zi, chapter 15:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is the nature of water that when free from other substances, it is clear, and when it is calm, it is level; but if it is collected</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(é¬±</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), obstructed</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(é–‰</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), and not allowed to flow, it cannot maintain its clarity.  It is a reflection of Heavenâ€™s virtue.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Thus it is said: To be pure, genuine, and uncontaminated; to be calm, unified, and stable; to be content and not impositioning; to move according to the phases of Heaven: this is the way to nourish the spirit.</span> <span id="_ftnref266"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[266\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn266)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     A helpful strategy to avoid over-thinking, and the consequent knotting and constraint of qi, can be found in the Tibetan Buddhist teaching, â€œTilopaâ€™s Six Nailsâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Donâ€™t recall. (Let go of what has passed.)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Donâ€™t imagine. (Let go of what may come.)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Donâ€™t think. (Let go of what is happening now.)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Donâ€™t examine. (Donâ€™t try to figure anything out.)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Donâ€™t control. (Donâ€™t try to make anything happen.)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Rest. (Relax, right now, and rest.)</span> <span id="_ftnref267"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[267\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn267)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 267-284 speak to the effect of inner balance and harmony in fostering life and health. Western medicine differentiates between physical health and mental and emotional health, prescribing various doctors for physiological or psychological issues. Chinese medicine, however, unifies the health of the body and the mind, both because of their mutual influence, and because they both determine any single individualâ€™s experience of health and vitality. Excessive anger, sadness, euphoria, fear, and worry can easily destabilize a personâ€™s life and deny them the basic enjoyment of life and vitality. Thus, a personâ€™s mental-emotional experience is treated as an important indicator of the overall balance of their system, much like imbalances may also be revealed through the skin, hair, or fingernails. According to Chinese medicine, emotional imbalances can signal potential imbalances in specific internal organs that those emotions affect or arise from. For example, excessive anger may indicate â€œfullnessâ€? of liver, and excessive fear may indicate â€œemptinessâ€? of the liver.</span> <span id="_ftnref271"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[271\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn271) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though the intricacies of the mind-body system in Chinese medicine were likely developed somewhat later than the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">provides a glimpse into early discussions of the importance of emotional balance for guarding the vitality of mind, body, and spirit. We can see how understandings of the emotionsâ€™ impact on health developed over about two hundred years by comparing the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s teachings on emotional balance with The Yellow Emperors Classic of Internal Medicine (Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen),</span> <span id="_ftnref272"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[272\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn272) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">chapter five:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven has four seasons and five elemental phases. (The former) brings about birth, growth, gathering, and storing. (The later) brings about cold, heat, dryness, dampness, and wind.  People have five storehouses (organs) which transform the five qi,</span> <span id="_ftnref273"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[273\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn273) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">giving rise to euphoria, anger, thought (rumination),</span> <span id="_ftnref274"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[274\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn274) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">sorrow, and fear. Thus, euphoria and anger harm the qi, while cold and heat harm the body. Violent anger harms the yin, while violent euphoria harms the yang. Weakened qi moves upwards; filling the vessels, it leaves the body. If euphoria and anger are unrestrained, and cold and heat are excessive, life lacks solidity.</span> <span id="_ftnref275"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[275\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn275)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">shows in lines 267-284, a harmonious balance of Heavenly and Earthly essences brings about life,</span> <span id="_ftnref276"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[276\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn276) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and the inner balance of emotions preserves it. The result is that one becomes peaceful and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">zheng</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(correctly aligned and balanced) in their breast. Referring to â€œthe breast,â€? the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">makes a number of indications, the breast being the place where (yuan) jing collects and develops a Sage (see NY 1-8), also the place of the heart which governs the inner kingdom, and the lungs which â€œhold the office of the grand tutor; they bring forth order and moderation.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref277"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[277\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn277) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As such, we could also infer zheng qi â€“ the properly aligned and balanced qi that prevents â€œthieving windsâ€? from harming the body.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While NY267-284 teach the ancient Chinese art of the heart-mind, they also show how to reclaim what became known in the late 1990s as emotional intelligence (EQ). Emotional intelligence refers to oneâ€™s capacity to recognize their own emotions and mitigate the negative effect of these emotions in their lives. Such negative effects might include limitations on impulse control, on oneâ€™s ability to differentiate sense and reality, and on self-actualization. An interpersonal component of emotional intelligence also exists, which involves empathy and recognizing how and why others are experiencing emotions. Reference to the interpersonal and empathetic side of EQ can be found in NY192-207:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When people can align and quiet themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In the great clarity, they are reflected</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">With the great illumination, they observe</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Being respectful and careful, they are without error</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Daily refreshing their virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They know every place under Heaven</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wherever there is deficiency in the four directions</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They reverently supply</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œinternal attainment.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     For returning from a state of emotional turmoil, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">counsels limiting sense stimulation and refraining from euphoria and anger until the emotions are again balanced and â€œupright (aligned)â€?  (see lines 276â€“284). â€œBalanced and alignedâ€? illustrates a state of peacefulness, presence, and awareness: a state of calm preparedness, uninfluenced by the erratic tendencies of anger and euphoria.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Correlations to EQ in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begin, especially, in lines 216-228, which demonstrate the effective consequences of not being aware of oneâ€™s own emotions when interacting with other people.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Though the heart-mind remains within </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It cannot be hidden and concealed</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The harmony of the body reveals it</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is seen in the skinâ€™s colour</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Welcoming others with an energy-breath of goodness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is like embracing them with the affection of brothers and sisters;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Welcoming others with an energy-breath of wickedness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is like injuring them with a soldierâ€™s spear.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Itâ€™s wordless tone</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Strikes like thunder</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The manifestations of the heart-mindâ€™s energy-breath</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Illuminate like the sun and moon</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And are perceived as though by oneâ€™s own mother and father</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In summary, knowing oneâ€™s own emotions, and finding inner peace, one can develop empathy and not let their emotions get in the way of a harmonious inter-being.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">NY285-296 may show an early example of medical treatments of the emotions based on five elemental phase theories later found in the Huang Di Nei Jing.  The five elemental phases are influenced by each other according to creative, destructive, and dominating relationships.  For example, the generating cycle entails that:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">wood is the origin of fire</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">fire is the origin of earth (ash)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">earth is the origin of metal</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">metal is the origin of water</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">water is the origin of wood </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The reverse of this cycle is destructive: </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">wood depletes water</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">water depletes metal</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">metal depletes earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">earth puts out fire</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">fire depletes wood. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The dominating cycle entails that each elemental phase dominates the one after the one which follows it in the creative cycle â€“ the â€œgrandchild.â€? So:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wood is dominated by metal</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Metal is dominated by fire</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Fire is dominated by water</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Water is dominated by earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Earth is dominated by wood</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In NY285-296 we find :</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Invariably, peopleâ€™s lives</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Require balance and alignment.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What causes them to lose this</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is surely euphoria, anger, sadness, and worry.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To put an end to anger, nothing compares to poetry;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">\[Early poetry usually described sentimental longing (sadness). Sadness is associated with the lungs and metal.  Anger is associated with the liver and wood. Metal dominates wood.\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To dispel sadness, nothing compares to music;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">\[Music is associated with pleasure, fire, and the heart.  Fire dominates metal.\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To moderate music, nothing compares to courtesy;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">\[Courtesy requires adapting to others, and may entail fear, which are both associated with water and the kidneys.  Water dominates fire.\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To maintain courtesy, nothing compares to respect;</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">\[Respect requires calm, presence, thoughtfulness, and the unity of considering all as one, associated with earth and the spleen.  Earth dominates water.\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To maintain respect (earth), nothing compares to silence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">\[Silence may again be associated with earth. These lines sought the way to dispel anger (associated with wood), and so do not finish with a wood-based solution, not wishing to dominate earth. Further, earth generates metal which was the original solution for anger. The dominating cycle is used to bring order, from which a positive generating cycle can resume, where wood maintains the yang spirits (hun), fire maintains the shen-spirit, earth maintains the intention (yi), metal maintains the yin spirits (po), and water maintains the will (zhi) .\]</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Internally silent, and externally respectful,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">One can return to their pure nature.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Pure nature is thereby greatly established.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lines 285-296 also carry what appears to be a Confucian influence; however, the practice and teaching of poetry, music, courtesy, and respect were long a part of the Zhou-influenced education that Confucius received prior to becoming a teacher, himself, and making such education vastly more accessible. The principles of music are known to have existed in China for centuries before Confuciusâ€™ teachings, with one of the surviving bronze bells, played by ensembles to make harmony and melody, dating</span> <span id="_ftnref279"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[279\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn279) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">to approximately 900 BC. As we can see in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of Music</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Yue Ji</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Book of Rites</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Li Ji</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), much of the early Chinese arts were developed to teach a sort of minimalism that allowed one to appreciate beauty, without stimulating desire in such a way that satisfaction would be elusive. This aesthetic is also highly evident in the traditional Chinese methods of tea ceremony (gong fu cha) where tea is brewed lightly and appreciated with cups that hold only three savoured sips. Minimalist calligraphy scrolls, earthen teaware, and the spacious sounds of a guqin radiate a beauty that can only be found in the meeting of simplicity and harmony. Practicing the arts in this way, a balance of sense, emotion, and rectitude is preserved:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€¦ In the ceremonies of the great sacrifices, the dark-coloured liquor took precedence, and on the stands were uncooked fish, while the grand soup had no condiments: there was much flavour left undeveloped. Thus we see that the ancient kings, in their institution of ceremonies and music, did not seek how fully they could satisfy the desires of the appetite and of the ears and eyes; but they intended to teach the people to regulate their likings and dislikings, and to bring them back to the normal course of humanity</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem">å??äººé?“ä¹‹</span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem ;letter-spacing:0.23rem">æ­£</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     It belongs to the nature of man, as from Heaven, to be still at his birth. His activity shows itself as he is acted on by external things, and develops the desires incident to his nature. Things come to him more and more, and his knowledge is increased. Then arise the manifestations of liking and disliking. When these are not regulated by anything within, and growing knowledge leads more astray without, he cannot come back to himself, and his Heavenly principle is extinguished.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Now there is no end of the things by which man is affected; and when his likings and dislikings are not subject to regulation (from within), he is changed into the nature of things as they come before him; that is, he stifles the voice of Heavenly principle within, and gives the utmost indulgence to the desires by which men may be possessed. On this we have the rebellious and deceitful heart, with licentious and violent disorder. The strong press upon the weak; the many are cruel to the few; the knowing impose upon the dull; the bold make it bitter for the timid; the diseased are not nursed; the old and young, orphans and solitaries are neglected â€“ such is the great disorder that ensues.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Therefore the ancient kings, when they instituted their ceremonies and music, regulated them by consideration of the requirements of humanity.</span> <span id="_ftnref280"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[280\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn280)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     From the Confucian point of view, music is a model of the necessary qualities of good character and the ideal art to bring them about. Participation in musical ensembles makes immediately apparent the necessity for courtesy and respect. If a member of the ensemble takes it upon themselves to indulge their whims and dismiss their role in subordination to the greater cause, the quality of music will quickly deteriorate and bring shame to all involved. Listening to and respecting the other musicians as equals, allowing them their space, and contributing the appropriate amount of oneâ€™s own input, all determine the quality of music, and potential for a cooperative group of people to benefit from their interaction. This also teaches the benefits of humility â€“ as Lao Zi states in DDJ81 â€œhaving helped others, oneself gains more.â€? Interacting with others through this collective harmony and cooperation will surely enrich all involved, and help return them to the simplicity of their pure nature, as the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">points out in lines 292-296.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">NY297-316 contradicts a common misconception about Daoism and proto-Daoism which purports that their philosophies would advocate indulgence before limiting oneâ€™s whims, mistakenly believing that limiting whim is limiting nature. To the contrary, indulging in whims is viewed as extreme behaviour leading to imbalance and confusion. As the proto-Daoist texts show, it is through balance and harmony that pure nature is realized. Thus, strategies to avoid extremes may also be employed in Daoist self-cultivation. Strategies for moderation can also be seen earlier in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, applied to the emotions, in lines 285-296. So, cultivating awareness and moderation of oneâ€™s  emotions, while taking command of impulses, should not be seen as an unnatural or un-Daoist thing to do. Of course, at a certain level, one might transcend these emotions and impulses, and thereby any need to moderate them. For those still seeking such a level of attainment, however, techniques may be relied upon as important components of self-cultivation. Another example of self-moderation is taking an upright posture to aid in inner stabilization, regarded in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(BX201-203) as a necessary technique for people who have unavoidably become caught up in the busyness of society.</span> <span id="_ftnref282"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[282\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn282)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Regardless, while techniques are sometimes necessary, it should not be forgotten that Daoists still cherish simplicity. As Heshang Gong comments on DDJ27, the best method is not complicated, and the work of seeking balance and harmony does not take place only in isolation: </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œExcellent walking leaves no trail of footprintsâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Those who are excellent at walking the Dao seek it in themselves, and do not go down to the hall or out of the gates. Thus, they leave no trail of footprints.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€¦</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œExcellent counting does not use counting devicesâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Those who are excellent at finding a strategy to attain Dao simply guard Oneness within and do not shift from it. Their strategies are not numerous, and so they do not use counting devices to know them all.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œExcellent closing requires no bolts yet the seal cannot be brokenâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">For excellence in the way of sealing off desires and strong emotions, guard the vital spirits within and do not be like gates and doors. Locked bolts can be opened.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">â€œExcellent binding requires no rope to secure it, yet cannot be unboundâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Achieve excellence by tying Dao into your usual affairs. Then you can tie it to your heart. This will then not be like ropes and cords, which can be untied.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€™s suggestion that â€œknowledge flourishesâ€? when food intake is regulated, is supported by a November 2014 article in the Journal of Neuroscience, which states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Recent findings .. provide a window into the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which exercise and IERs \[intermittent energy restrictions/fasting\] bolster brainpower, protect neurons against injury and neurodegenerative disorders, and improve systemic energy metabolism and function of the autonomic nervous system.</span> <span id="_ftnref283"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[283\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn283) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">         </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A similar teaching to NY317-326 can be found in XSX1-20, which also suggests that a pleasant feeling of qi is greatly beneficial:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">When the body is not aligned, Virtue does not approach.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">When the center is not pure and clear, the heart-mind is not stable.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">An aligned body is adorned with Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">And the myriad things attain completion.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">When these wings (of Virtue and the heart-mind) naturally come together,</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">The spirit knows no limits.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Illuminated, itâ€™s comprehension of the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Spans throughout the four directions.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Therefore it is said:  â€œWhen things do not confuse the senses,</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">And the senses do not confuse the heart-mind</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">This is called â€˜inner Virtueâ€™.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Thereby, the energy of intention is settled;</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Having (settled), it returns to alignment.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Energy-breath then fills the body,</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">And oneâ€™s conduct is righteous and upright.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">If this fullness (of energy-breath) is not pleasant, the heart-mind does not benefit.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">If oneâ€™s conduct is not upright, the people will not be provided for.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Therefore, Sages resemble Heaven during such times. They are without thought of self when sitting above all.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">They resemble Earth during such times. They are without thought of self when supporting all.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">As for thought of self, it puts the world in chaos.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Another excerpt worth contrasting here is</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 51-59:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Therefore, the junzi does not dwell on what he likes, nor is he coerced by what he dislikes.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Tranquil, pleasant, and effortless, he abandons wisdom, and it abides in him as a result.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">He responds, but does not initiate;</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Moves but does not possess.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">If one is excessively headstrong, they will err when adapting to changes.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Thus, the ruler who has Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Remains as though without any knowledge.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">He responds to things as though by coincidence.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">This is the Dao of tranquil means.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    </span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It should be understood, that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">is not simply a manual for improving oneâ€™s emotional state, cultivating better interpersonal relationships, and thereby improving oneâ€™s sense of overall wellbeing. While it may have remained limited to these elements were it fully entrenched in Confucianism, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">was born of the proto-Daoist culture found in the 4</span> <span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">th</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">century B.C., and so largely concerns the cultivation of humanityâ€™s Heaven-endowed life force, pure nature, jing, qi, shen, intrinsic virtue, inner and outer reflections of Heaven and Earth, and of course, aligning all of these things with their origin:  Dao.  Ancient China was a world of mysticism, spirits, ghosts, gods, divine power, rituals, and spiritual influence that could predict and change the future. Though modern readers may leave these elements of the text behind, the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">should not be misrepresented as simply a manual for emotional regulation. In actuality, this facet holds the means to the textâ€™s higher goals of Daoist internal cultivation, energy transmutation, and spiritual awakening.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     In speaking of attracting the spontaneous approach of good fortune, lines 327-353 reflect another concept that might be easily absorbed by modern terminology, where â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">the law of attraction</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€? describes what was called</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ganying</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ„Ÿæ‡‰ â€œfeeling response,â€? often translated as â€œresonance response,â€? in ancient China. Ganying is the phenomenon of mutual attraction that exists between things of the same type, much as a ruler who is chaotic in his heart-mind will bring chaos to his realm. This principle was likely observed while playing the imperial bells when bells of the same tonal frequency would mysteriously resonate after only one of them had been struck.</span> <span id="_ftnref291"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[291\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn291)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The earliest explanation of this principle is found in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">æ–‡è¨€ Wen Yan commentary (from the â€œ10 Wingsâ€?) on the Yi Jing (I Ching) chapter one (Qian), line five.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What is the meaning of the words under the fifth yang line, â€œA dragon is flying through the sky â€“ it will be advantageous to see a great man?â€? The Master said:  â€œIdentical notes resonate together; identical energies seek each other; water drifts towards what is wet; fire approaches what is dry; clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger; the Sage comes forth and all things look to him; what originates in heaven is drawn towards what is above; what originates in the earth is drawn towards what is below. So does everything follow its kind.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref292"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[292\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn292) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heshang Gong helps to illustrate that DDJ23 speaks to the same principle as in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€“ that anger and frustration hinder good fortune. In doing so, he also illustrates that this occurrence comes about through the spontaneous attraction of identical types. Note that he also repeats much of the Wenyan commentary, above:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThose who are one with Dao, Dao is also happy to have themâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who encounter Dao, and are one with it, Dao is also happy to have them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThose who are one with Virtue, Virtue is also happy to have themâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who encounter Virtue, and are one with it, Virtue is also happy to have them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThose who are one with loss, loss is also happy to have themâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who encounter loss, and are one with it, loss is also happy to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">lose</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œWhere faith and trust is not satisfactoryâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Rulers who do not sufficiently trust those below them are not trusted by those below them.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">â€œThere will be no faith and trustâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This explains that things which are of the same type return to each other. Identical notes resonate together; identical energies seek each other; clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger; water drifts towards what is wet; fire approaches what it is dry. This is the spontaneous nature of types.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heshang Gongâ€™s comment â€œThose who encounter loss, and are one with it, loss is also happy to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">lose</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">them,â€? suggests that by not dwelling on loss in frustration and thereby internalizing it, loss will eventually detach itself. The beginning lines of DDJ23 (see below) seem to refer to this dwelling on loss, and bringing it up again and again rather than letting it go. By, instead, watering the seeds of Dao and Virtue, Dao and Virtue can take root and reach throughout oneâ€™s life. The closing lines of DDJ23 explain that one must have faith and trust in Dao and Virtue so that they can restore themselves in oneâ€™s life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">DDJ23:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To speak rarely is natural</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Gusting wind does not last in the early morning </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Sudden rainstorms do not last all day</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who acts in this way?  Heaven and Earth</span>\
<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If Heaven and Earth cannot continue in such a way</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">What then, should be the case for men?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They should follow the method of Dao!</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(To be a person of) Dao, be one with Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(To be a person of) Virtue, be one with Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(To be a person of) loss, be one with loss</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are one with Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao is also happy to have them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are one with Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Virtue is also happy to have them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who are one with loss</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Loss is also happy to have them</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Where faith and trust is not satisfactory</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There will be no faith and trust</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     So, this silent faith â€“ that returning to tranquility will draw harmony into oneâ€™s circumstances â€“ is connected to the strategy in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">for attracting good fortune</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">lines 337-353).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lines 337-353 also illustrate an important concept, translated here as â€œmagical qiâ€?:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ling qi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. Ling takes on a number of definitions including the efficacy of spirits and the potency of Dao. Attained in a similar way to the spiritual vitality (jing-shen</span> <span id="_ftnref293"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[293\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn293) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) and genuine qi (zhen qi) referred to in Zhuang Ziâ€™s chapter 15 and chapter one of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span id="_ftnref294"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[294\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn294) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ling qi â€œfills the spacious emptiness of calm cheerfulnessâ€?</span> <span id="_ftnref295"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[295\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn295) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and is nourished by â€œthe Dao of pure naturalness.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref296"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[296\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn296) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">recognizes a similar basis for accommodating these vital energies in speaking of a happiness</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(æ­¡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">huan</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) that is neither pleasure</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(æ¨‚</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">le</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), nor euphoria</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(å–œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">xi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), but the sort of joy and happiness that accompanies the fulfillment and enjoyment of life. While pleasure, euphoria, lust, and attachment may simply result in sluggishness and idleness, leading to anxiety (see line 255) and further emotional obstacles to oneâ€™s full expression of Dao, this is the happiness of self-expression and living out oneâ€™s destiny (ming).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The place that the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">gives to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">huan</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(happiness,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ­¡</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), here, as distinct from pleasure and euphoria, is later subsumed in Chinese medicine by</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">le</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(pleasure,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">æ¨‚</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">), translated as joy and differentiated from euphoria as a pleasant and harmonious happiness, like a thriving symphony of fulfillment and connectedness, rather than the erratic, oblivious, impulsiveness of elation and euphoria.</span> <span id="_ftnref297"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[297\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn297) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This sense of fulfillment, of inner and outer harmony, like one is part of a beautiful symphony between nature and destiny, Heaven, Earth, and Humanity, and all the many interweaving facets of life, is akin to the state of a nation that the great sages of antiquity could bring about and disappear within. It assures the smooth functioning of the nationâ€™s many facets, and makes it nearly impossible to attack, let alone defeat, for even opposing soldiers would come to its defence. As Lao Zi said in chapter 67, by upholding kindness and moderation, and refraining from putting oneself ahead of all others, the nation remains secure in perpetuity. This allows one to become part of the symphony of life, and not upset its harmony by allowing the desires to close oneâ€™s ears, ensnaring them in a life lived, instead, only for self-gratification.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">points out, the thriving energy of this perfect symphony brings about</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ling qi</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, the energy of spiritual potency. Ling qi, in turn, brings about health, and protection from both inner and outer afflictions,</span> <span id="_ftnref298"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[298\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn298) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">whether by nourishing the mind and spiritual intelligence or though its symbiotic relationship with the Heavenly phases.</span> <span id="_ftnref299"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[299\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn299) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When ling qi enters â€œthe spacious emptiness of calm cheerfulnessâ€? it restores and assures an internal balance</span> <span id="_ftnref300"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[300\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn300) <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">that is free of anxiety, sorrow, anger, euphoria, attachment, lust, and confusion (see</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">lines 327-340), thereby further protecting people from foolish, erratic, actions and the emotional turmoil that upsets the internal organs and their harmonious exchanges or â€œcommunications.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref301"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[301\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn301)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">are filled with guidance on returning to the state of inner calm and faith (xin), as are the Buddhist excerpts quoted in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">.  Finding a quiet place to sit and practice the â€˜art of the heart-mindâ€™ is an accessible means to accomplish this, for most people at some point during their day. Once caught up in the frantic pace of modern life, however, it is important to remember that stress does not increase our effectiveness, and that focus and calm are more conducive to efficiency and competency. If we canâ€™t afford to slow down our bodies, we can at least slow down our breath and, thereby, our heart-rates, making them both peaceful and even until we can find a way to enjoy our place in life as we are living it in the given moment, stressful as it may seem at the time. This will assist in bringing about an inner stillness that improves our responses to whatever requires presence and attention. In doing so, we reclaim self-determination and further discover Lao Ziâ€™s words from DDJ47, â€œWithout going out the door, know all under Heaven. Without glancing out the window, see Heavenâ€™s Way. The further out one goes, the less they know.â€? Seeking peace and transformation in ourselves â€“ cultivating ourselves and our world from within rather than seeking to change everyone and everything around us â€“ our internal-cultivation will express itself as external-cultivation as it improves our relationships and communications with the people and world around us.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When is there no benefit from my affairs? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When there is no benefit in my heart-mind.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When is there no peace where I reside? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When there is no peace in my heart-mind.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">(Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, lines 109-112)</span>
