# <span id="_Toc507075981"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">A Meditation, inspired by the material in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This meditation is one way in which the material in</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">can be adapted for practice.  It includes techniques that I have encountered on my own journey of Daoist and Buddhist teachings and practices, and is not meant to represent or replace teachings of a Daoist lineage teacher.  If you have the good fortune of personal study with such an instructor, I would advise to continue with their instructions, or otherwise, present them with this meditation and ask if it would benefit what you are learning before changing your practice. Please also see the disclaimer at the beginning of this book.  It is recommended to read over the instructions below, in full, before beginning.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     If you are new to meditation, the first several sessions should be devoted to simply learning to sit, or even lie down, and do nothing without any simultaneous activities such as listening to music, reading, watching television, talking to someone, driking, eating, etc.  This, in itself, is difficult for most people who are not experienced meditators, and so you must first find comfort in simply doing nothing for 10 minutes.  When this is accomplished, in the next session do nothing for 15 minutes.  Then the next time for 20 minutes, then 25 minutes, and then 30 minutes.  Only when you are comfortable just â€œstaring at the wall,â€? or doing nothing, for 30 minutes, should you begin with the following techniques.  For this preliminary meditation, you are free to ponder whatever you like.  The goal is simply learning how to do nothing, comfortably.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     There is one activity that can done during this stage of â€œdoing nothingâ€? to help prepare for meditation: put your right hand on your chest and your left hand on your stomach. As you breathe, breathe into your diaphragm so that only your left hand (stomach) moves up and down, with your chest relaxed and not moving. When this can be done naturally and effortlessly (which may take minutes or weeks), allow your breath to subtly fill your entire torso, with your stomach, by far, having the most noticeable movement.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Please note that the â€œpreparationâ€? and â€œclosingâ€? sections of this meditation can be followed as though part of a guided meditation.  The â€œtechniquesâ€? section, however, is meant to be read and absorbed beforehand, and simply taken into consideration following the â€œpreparationâ€? stage.  It is not meant as a step by step guide in the same way that the preparation and closing are.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem; font-weight:bold">Preparation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The following meditation can be done while sitting on a folded and rolled-up towel, or firm cushion, in cross-legged, half-lotus, or full-lotus position.  It can also be done while sitting near the edge of a medium-height chair with your feet flat on the floor.  Begin by placing your hands on your thighs, and finding your posture.  Your back should be straight, yet relaxed â€“ finding that position where the muscles, structural alignment, and circulations return to their effortless functions.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     After sitting in this balance for a moment, thank the spirits of your current environment for allowing your practice to be fulfilling, by clasping your right fist in your left hand and giving a gesture of thanks, salutation, and respect in front of your bowed forehead.  After bringing your hands down, circle them up to the sides and, using your intent, gather heaven-qi down in front of you, over and through your body, and into the earth.  Bring down this heaven-qi three times.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">      Now, in a similar motion as when gathering heaven-qi, gather the qi to the lower dantien.  Circle your arms from your sides to gather qi in front of you, and place your hands over your lower dantien: place your right palm over the lower-dantien, about 2.5 inches below the navel, and place your left palm over your right hand, lining up the lao-gong points at the center of the palms with the dantien.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Finally, circle the torso from the waist in a clockwise or counter-clockwise direction, three times, and then in the opposite direction three more times.  Next, gently bend the torso forward and then back to alignment three times.  Lastly, take three deep breaths, beginning with an exhalation to clear the lungs of carbon-dioxide.  Following the third inhalation, meditation begins.  </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">As the saying goes, â€œit takes 20 minutes before water starts to boil.â€? Do not expect immediate immersion.  Allow the mind to sit, undisturbed.  Let it relax and find balance, just as you did earlier with the body. Put your awareness to the centering oneness that resides behind your mind, and allow everything to settle until your will and intention becomes genuine. This, in itself, is enough to guide your entire meditation session; however, the following guidelines are also helpful to bring you back to this point.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem; font-weight:bold">Techniques</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Quieting the mind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">A common and helpful technique to calm the mind and abide in openness is to count your breaths from one to ten, counting on the exhale of each breath. When you get to 10, start again from one. By the second (or third) round do not engage any thoughts between the numbers. The only word you should create in your mind is the number of the breath, and maybe an internal â€œahhhhâ€? or â€œmmmmm.â€? To take the place of thoughts, you can also allow the mind to open up to the sounds of your environment, and to a general awareness of where you are at the present moment, just being where you are while looking straight ahead at a chosen spot on the floor. Your central focus should not be disturbed by sounds, but simply aware of how sound-and-silence passes through your consciousness without any disturbance, like clouds passing through the sky: â€œAbiding nowhere, let the mind arise.â€? As you go deeper into internal silence, all of this may disappear as well.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The big exception to this exercise, especially for those new to it, is as follows: Consider thoughts as nouns and verbs. Thoughts will spontaneously pass through your mind and occur to you â€“ consider these as nouns. The trick is not to follow these thoughts and turn them into verbs â€“ thinking. As the mind clears, like the sun shining through a clearing sky, things will occur to you; they will become apparent; you will have realizations. This is fine. Just let the realization pass through your mind, like you would watch a cloud pass through the sky, and then move back into the open clarity of not-thinking. If you begin to add to, and expand on, this realization, rather than moving back to open clarity, this is the thinking. When you notice this happen, begin again from 1. If thoughts rise up in your mind but you then return to open clarity (not-thinking) before the next number, continue counting your breaths up to 10, and then begin from 1 again. After some time, these spontaneous thoughts will stop rising up and you will simply abide in the present moment. Without thoughts, where else can you be but in the present, right there, staring at the floor, or gazing internally â€“ pure awareness. Continuing to practice like this, as your mind occupies itself with experience rather than thoughts, you can eventually stop counting, like a space shuttle releasing its rocket boosters. When you realize your mind has gone off track again, simply begin again from 1, or focus on the breath as though every breath is the first breath.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Body and self as the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Lao Zi says</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who (govern) the self as the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And cherish it as such</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">On them the world can rely</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Those who (govern) the self as the world</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And love it as such</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">To them the world can be entrusted</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     This means to love oneself as all things and all things as oneself, yet it also means to first bring order to oneself before trying to bring order the world.  Much as in the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, Lao Ziâ€™s</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">teaches the way of governing the body according to the same principles by which the Sage governs the nation. This is largely the focus of Heshang Gongâ€™s commentary. Consider this in light of the Sageâ€™s method of non-doing and non-interference, and the application of these methods in meditation. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Chapter 37 of the Dao De Jing states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Dao is always effortless yet without inaction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When lords and kings can guard this within</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The myriad things eventually transform themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Transforming, yet desiring to do so intentionally</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I pacify this desire with the simplicity of the nameless</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begins by stating:  â€œIn the body, the heart-mind is the throne of the emperor.â€? From his throne, the emperor brings peace and harmonious stability (order) to the nation and its people, just as the heart-mind effortlessly brings harmonious order to the domain of the body and self, governing through â€œnon-action.â€? As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Xia</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">and</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">suggest, the stability of the heart-mind can be effected by bringing peace and alignment to the body. As this peace and alignment of the body can effect the same in the heart-mind, the heart-mind can effect this peace and alignment throughout oneâ€™s entire being. Cultivate quiet stillness, both externally and internally, to bring order â€œwithout doing.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œFor what is above, study the heavens.  For what is below, study the earth.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is said that when the nation is peaceful and harmonious, the heavens will bestow natural abundance through harmonious weather and seasons. The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">begins by explaining:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is invariably the essence of things that gives them life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Below, it gives birth to the five grains</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Above, it aligns the stars</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Circulating between Heaven and Earth</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">We call them ghosts and spirits</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Collected within the bosom</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">We call them Sages</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Heshang Gong comments on Lao Ziâ€™s â€œchapter oneâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Returning to the center of Heaven, there is another Heaven.  It dispenses energy-breaths which can be potent or weak.  Obtaining harmonious fertile fluid from its center, this gives birth to the worthy and wise. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">    When peace and harmony endure, the heavens bless the nation with jing â€“ life energy. This mirrors the operations of the mind and body:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their stillness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can make clouded water slowly become clear?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their serenity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can long sustain this progress, until life slowly arises?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(DDJ15)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     With a clear mind, the clouds of thought part, and the sun-energy (attention) of the mind and spirit can shine on the Earth (lower dantien), and nourish it. Just as the primordial jing is needed to fertilize the fields, it is also needed to develop the body and self.  Invite it.  Open the heart-mind and intention to it.    </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Thoughts may rise up, like steam forming clouds. Allow the energy of these thick clouds to rain down into the Earth (dantien).  Just forget everything, and let everything settle like earth and gravity. Eventually, clarity will return. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Wu Wei</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dao De Jing, chapter seven states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven has longevity, Earth has continuit</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">y</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ã€€</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Heaven and Earth have the power of longevity and continuity because they do not live for themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is how they can live for so long</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Therefore, sages leave themselves behind</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And they end up in front</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">They do not cater to themselves</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Yet they persist</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Is it not because they are without selfishness and wickedness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">That they are able to fulfill themselves?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Chapter seven of the Dao De Jing is one of the best, yet least understood, descriptions of wu wei.  Wei</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(ç‚º</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">) can be translated as effort, and so wu wei as â€œeffortless.â€? In Daoism, this effort is meant in contrast to â€œzi ranâ€? â€“ the spontaneity of nature. Heshang Gong comments on DDJ1, â€œThe path that can be told is not the Eternal Pathâ€?:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">It is not the Path of natural spontaneity (zi ran) and long life. The Eternal Path nourishes the spirit with effortlessness (wu wei). Taking no initiative, it brings peace to the people.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     As can be understood from DDJ7, wu wei is action taken from the ego, rather than the action of Dao. Learning wu wei is to recognize and reject egoic interference in what Dao is better able to take care of. This is why Daoist texts warn against emotions such as euphoria, anger, pleasure, sorrow, and fear â€“ because they make it almost impossible to act from Dao rather than from ego. Training in Daoist meditation teaches the cultivation of this power, showing the way to handle worldly obstructions the same way as we do our own emotional obstructions â€“ without wei. This cultivation is therefore also intrinsically a cultivation of effortless virtue as we learn how to act from Dao, the greater principle, rather than the limitations of our own desires. These egoic impulses hamper our ability to act in ways that will foster a harmonious inter-being with the world, and so cultivating wu wei in our behaviour may even seem, from the outside, an effort to cultivate â€œmoral behaviour.â€? This is not the case, however, as the resulting â€œmoralityâ€? is as natural to wu wei as sweetness is to a pear.  DDJ65 speaks to this simultaneously internal and external cultivation:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The ancient masters who aligned society with Dao</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Did not do so by enlightening the people</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">But rather, fostered their simplicity </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Difficulty in governing people</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Comes from a wealth of wisdom</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Hence, when knowledge is used to govern the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This results in thievery from the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Not using knowledge to govern the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Blesses the nation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Understand the broader application of these two principles</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">There is an infinite understanding</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Which can be found in these principles</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called Fathomless Virtue</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Fathomless Virtue, profound and far-reaching</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following it, things return back to their nature</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Arriving at great submission</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The Bai Xin also speaks to this in saying:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing oneself is called â€œinvestigatingâ€? (jì);</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing others is called â€œhelping across the riverâ€? (jÄ«).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By knowing what is frivolous and what is necessary, one can bring the world into unison.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Internally, solidifying oneself into a unified whole, one may lengthen their lifespan.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Discussing the application of this principle reveals the way to rule all under Heaven.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(BX163-167)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This principle can also be found DDJ48:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of learning requires daily accumulation</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The pursuit of Dao requires daily reduction</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Reducing and reducing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Until arriving at effortlessness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Effortless, yet without inaction</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">(</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">ç„¡ç‚ºè€Œç„¡ä¸?</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">ç‚º</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Reduce excessive taxes</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Consider the Daoist governmental practice of eliminating excessive taxes. Do not ask of the body.  Let it be.  Let the jing waters absorb into it.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œDo not rely on rewards and punishmentsâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Not thinking also relates to Daoist warnings against relying on rewards and punishments. Do not think about the potential benefits and losses of sitting practice.  Rather, allow the natural process to unfold. While Virtue,</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¾· De,â€? is synonymous with</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€œ</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">å¾— de, attainment,â€? this attainment is of Dao and zi ran â€“ the simplicity of nature. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œWhen achievement is attained, the Sage withdrawsâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When all is well, the Sage does nothing; when the body is enriched, thoughts may cease to arise.  These thoughts no longer need to direct the ruler â€“ the heart-mind, though a little thought here and a little thought there may be helpful to steer the kingdom back to this state of self-sustaining harmony.  Once this state is arrived at, allow</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">â€“ allow nature to flow along undisturbed.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     When thoughts stop, oneness with the present can arrive. The mind is not scattered, and thoughts of future and past return to present awareness.  â€œMing/enlightenmentâ€? most often refers to â€œclear sightednessâ€? â€“ a clear awareness of the present in relation to the future and past. Oneness in awareness brings comfort and balance, or having a place in given circumstances rather than resisting them. Oneness in the self becomes oneness in, and with, a personâ€™s environment and circumstances, both internally and externally.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Zen employs the method of looking at the floor to stay present in the immediate, and not travel through the mind. This is also a helpful technique for when closing the eyes results in rumination.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">Unity and Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Unify the will by eliminating the distractions of desire.  This unity contains no thought, no division of the mind-will-consciousness on distractions, yet still contains flexibility.  This is like the solid yang line within the water trigram, surrounded by two yin lines.  Allow flexibility so that the one yang can develop.  Though force should not be used, this is still a test and conditioning of will and resolve.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Bai Xin</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Without soaring (into the sky), without spilling over, the destined life-force (ming) will be extended.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Harmonize by returning to the center, and both body and pure nature (xing) will be preserved.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Be unified and without (doubt or) division.  This is called â€œknowing Dao.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Wishing to be enveloped by it, you must unify to the furthest extent, and solidify that which is protected within.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(BX 204-207)</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     While there seems to be a difference between the resolve of being â€œwithout division,â€? and recognizing that â€œall is not-twoâ€? (see</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Xin Ming</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">in introduction), these two forms of unity are intimately connected.  As mentioned in the introduction to</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, â€œfaith-mindâ€? in the title of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Xin Ming</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">also means confidence mind â€“ â€œno (doubt or) division.â€?  There is confidence and resoluteness in realizing that all is â€œnot two.â€? For example, our troubles and our joys are â€œnot two.â€?  This is that and that is this.  Practicing inner unity helps to see the world this way.  This unity is both a way of seeing the world and a way of being, yet these are also â€œnot two.â€? The</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Nei Ye</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">states â€œyour thinking about it will not reach comprehension.â€? Knowing, knowing, knowing is too much.  Know â€œnot two.â€?</span> <span id="_ftnref302"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[302\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn302)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œThose who know others are wise, those who know themselves are clear sighted.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Bai Xin, lines 198-200 state:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">By rejecting what is close and chasing after what is far, how can one but squander their power? </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus it is said:  â€œDesiring to take care of myself, I must first know my true inner state, and become acquainted with the universe by examining within myself.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">In this way, one can know the image, thereby knowing the tendencies of their true inner state.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Knowing the tendencies of their true inner state, they will know how to nourish life.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     We can begin to cultivate a deeper awareness of both ourselves and our environment using the same technique: â€œabiding nowhere, let the mind arise.â€? Close your eyes and, without any attachment to what is there, notice the sounds and silence.  As the Buddha taught, note their 4 stages of existence in the mind:  1)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">arising:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">the sound arrives; 2)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">abiding:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  the sound remains; 3)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">declining:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">the sound is passing; 4)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ceasing:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">the sound has ceased.  Note these sounds without attaching any judgments of good or bad to them.  Just passively observe them without straying from the basis â€“ your balance in the center within. As the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Xin Shu Shang</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">commentary states in lines 203-221:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œHe responds, but does not initiate; moves but does not possess.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œthe basis.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The basis is to reside in oneâ€™s own, while according with other things.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">(The junzi) responds to feelings, yet does not initiate them. </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Following the principle, he moves (things), but does not possess (them).</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œIf one is excessively headstrong, they will err when adapting to changes.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If headstrong, one cannot be empty.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">If not empty, one becomes the same as other â€œthings.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">With change and transformation, there is growth. With growth, there is bound to be confusion.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, the treasure of Dao is the basis (of responding and not initiating; moving yet not possessing). On this basis rests ability.   This is called usefulness.</span> <span id="_ftnref303"></span> [<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[303\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftn303)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">The junzi remains in the state</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œof not knowing.</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold ;letter-spacing:0.25rem">â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œarriving at emptiness.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-weight:bold">â€œResponding to things as though by coincidence.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called â€œadapting to the seasonâ€? â€“</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Like a shadow taking the shape of a form,</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Or an echo responding to a sound.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Thus, when things reach them, (the junzi) respond.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When these things move on, (the junzi) remain in place.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This means (the junzi) reverts back to emptiness.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     After practicing this outer observation, and being able to do so passively and without disturbance, put the mind to your feelings and thoughts.  Note their 4 four stages of existence in the same way as you observed the sounds â€“ without any attachment to what is there, and without any judgments of good or bad. Note 1)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">arising:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  a feeling is arising; 2)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">abiding:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">a feeling is present and abiding; 3)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">declining</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">: the feeling is diminishing and ceasing; 4)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">ceasing:</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">  the feeling is no longer present in any way whatsoever. Now, apply this same practice of observance to your thoughts, noticing when a thought arises, when thinking is present, when your thinking is wrapping up, and when those thoughts have disappeared.  When they have disappeared, abide in that space of openness and emptiness.  Lao Zi speaks of this silence in chapter 16 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Arrive at supreme emptiness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Embrace deep silence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Myriad creatures arise together</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">I thereby observe them return</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">So many things blossoming</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">And each returns back to its roots</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Returning to the roots is called silence</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">This is called returning to eternal life</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Continue abiding in silence until you feel the session of sitting has reached its saturation point, remembering</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, chapter 15:</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their stillness</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can make clouded water slowly become clear?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Who, by the power of their serenity</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Can long sustain this progress, until life slowly arises?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.2rem; font-weight:bold">Closing</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">When you feel the saturation point of the session has been reached, gently open your eyes (if they were closed) and place your palms on your thighs. Now again, â€œabiding nowhere, let the mind arise.â€? The mind, like an empty cup, can also be defined by what is inside of it. Without actively listening or being drawn towards any sounds, allow them to pass in and out of your awareness.  Do not hold onto them, do not seek or grasp them, but let them pass through the clear awareness of your mind.  Notice that you can be aware of far more things, and that your awareness can stretch much further, when it is not seeking to be aware of anything in particular.  â€œAbiding nowhere, let the mind arise.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Now, in the same way, see what is in your environment.  Do not get stuck looking at anything, but allow things to passively come into your visual awareness.  If you are inside, stand up and look out the window.  Allow your visual awareness to awaken to the things and movements in your environment.  These two exercises, of audio and visual awareness, need not last more than 15-30 seconds each, as they are only preparing you to be more centered and receptive as you go about your day, transitioning you from internal awareness to both internal and external awareness. By the same token, there is no reason they canâ€™t be practiced in silence for several minutes or more.</span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">     Lastly, thank the teachers that have helped to guide, support, and protect you in life. Clasping your left hand over your right fist at the level of your brow, making the same gesture as earlier, thank your teachers on the earthly plane.  Beginning again to make a second gesture slightly higher than the first, thank your teachers on the spiritual plane (for example, guardian angels, Lao Zi, The Buddha, etc).  Making a third gesture, somewhat higher than the second, thank the universe, the Dao. After bringing your hands down, circle them up to the sides and bring heaven-qi down through you and into the earth.  Bring down this heaven-qi three times.  After the third time, bring your hands around the front and gather qi as you place your right hand over the dantien and your left hand over top of the right.  Hold the qi like this for a brief moment.  Then, without bringing your hands very high (keeping them more or less around the waist, and only at your sides), bring heaven-qi down to the earth three times, beginning your step into the world at the end of the third time.</span>

# <span id="_Toc507075982"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">Bibliography</span></span>

# <span id="_Toc507075988"><span style=" font-size:1.3rem; font-weight:bold">ABOUT THE AUTHOR</span></span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem">Dan G. Reid taught himself how to read Classical Chinese with the help of textbooks, online tools, and internet forums. Dan also studies and practices sitting meditation, Qigong, internal martial arts (Xingyi, Baguazhang, Taji Chuan), and is a multi-instrumentalist and poet. His first published translation was</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Heshang Gong Commentary on Lao Ziâ€™s Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">, followed by</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem; font-style:italic">The Thread of Dao: Unraveling Early Daoist Oral Traditions in Guan Ziâ€™s Purifying the Heart-Mind (Bai Xin), Art of the Heart-Mind (Xin Shu), and Internal Cultivation (Nei Ye)</span> <span style=" font-size:1.0rem">. In 2018, Dan began studying Chinese physiotherapy, herbalism, moxibustion, and massage (Tui Na) to become a Registered Massage Therapist using ancient Chinese modalities, allowing him to apply and further his studies in Classical Chinese Medicine.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">If you enjoyed this book and would like to leave a review, please</span> [<span style=" font-size:0.92rem; text-decoration:underline; color:#0000ff">click here</span>](https://www.amazon.com/Thread-Dao-Unraveling-traditions-Cultivation-ebook/dp/B078J7XRBX/ref=pd_rhf_dp_p_img_8?_encoding=UTF8&psc=1&refRID=6TH75VEBQVBWXCH17WFD) <span style=" font-size:0.92rem">.</span>

<div>

</div>

\
[<span style=" font-size:1.0rem; text-decoration:underline; color:#0000ff">The Ho-Shang Kung Commentary on Lao Tzuâ€™s Tao Te Ching</span>](https://www.amazon.com/Ho-Shang-Kung-Commentary-Ching-Revised-ebook/dp/B018UUARJK/ref=asap_bc?ie=UTF8)

<span style=" font-size:1.0rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">â€œIn my own use of the DDJ as a Daoist practice scripture it was very important to clearly see how this DDJ commentary is a guide for key Daoist concepts like emptiness, wuwei, stillness, speaking few words, yielding, the quiet dragon, and more.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">     As a Daoist priest and founder of a Daoist lineage, American Dragon Gate Lineage, I highly recommend this translation by Reid and have actually made it required study for my priests-in-training.â€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">-</span> <span style="font:7.0pt 'Times New Roman'">    </span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Shifu Michael J. Rinaldini, Daoist Abbot and founder of the American Dragon Gate Lineage of Quanzhen Daoism. Author of</span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">A Daoist Practice Journal:  Come Laugh With Me</span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem">; and</span> <span style=" font-size:0.92rem; font-style:italic">A Daoist Practice Journal, Book 2:  Circle Walking, Qigong & Daoist Cultivation</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">Central to Taoism, Zen Buddhism, and neo-Confucianism, the Tao Te Ching may be the single most influential Eastern philosophical text of the last 2300 years. Ho-Shang Kung (circa 100 AD) clarifies the language and metaphors of the Tao Te Ching, while offering a Sage's insights into how they may be applied to the cultivation of wisdom, vitality, longevity, harmonious leadership, and Taoist virtues such as naturalness, sincerity, and ease.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">     With an intimate understanding of the culture and history within Lao Tzu's verses, Ho-Shang Kung's commentary has played an indispensable role in deepening the understanding of the Tao Te Ching for mystics, philosophers, and scholars alike.</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.92rem">     Guided by Ho-Shang Kung's commentary and linguistic analysis, Dan G. Reid provides a translation which is both eloquent, and exceptionally faithful to the Chinese text. With an audience of scholars and Taoist practitioners in mind, a Classical Chinese reading guide is provided, and the Chinese text appears alongside the commentary. Dan G. Reid's translation of the Tao Te Ching also appears separately for focused study.</span>

</div>

<div id="_ftn48" style="-aw-footnote-isauto:1">

[<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[48\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftnref48) <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The description of â€œonenessâ€? in this chapter, as it relates to power and transcending doubt, offers insight into the oral traditions behind chapter 39 of the</span> <span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-style:italic">Dao De Jing</span> <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">. DDJ39 reads:</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">In the beginning was the attainment of Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Heaven attained Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">And became clear</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Earth attained Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">And became serene</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Gods attained Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">And became spiritually powerful (ling)</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Valleys attained Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">And became full</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The myriad things attained Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">And were born</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Lords and kings attained Oneness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">And all under Heaven became loyal</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Then occurred the following</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Heaven, lacking the cause of its clarity</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Began to tremble and split open</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Earth, lacking the cause of its serenity</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Became fearful and began to gush forth</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The gods, lacking the cause of their spiritual power</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Became fearful and stopped moving</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The valley, lacking the cause of its fullness</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Became fearful and began to drain</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The myriad things, lacking the cause of their life</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Became fearful and began to die out</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The lords and kings, lacking the cause of their being praised and elevated</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-weight:normal">Became fearful and began to fall</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Therefore, value the lowest and treat it as the root source</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Elevate the low and treat it as the foundation</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">This is why lords and kings call themselves orphans, widows, and â€œno hub-of-the-wheelâ€?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Is this not treating the lowest as the root source?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Is it not?</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Thus, they are sent several palanquins without a palanquin</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Have no desires for fine jade</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Nor for cheap necklaces and stones</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-weight:normal">(Translated by Dan G. Reid)</span>

<span style=" font-size:0.83rem"> </span>

</div>

[<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[61\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftnref61) <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Buddhism arrived in China from India in 80 AD.</span>

<div id="_ftn62" style="-aw-footnote-isauto:1">

[<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[62\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftnref62) <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The Buddha was born and raised in southern Nepal as Siddhartha Gautama.  His year of birth is uncertain, but is said to be as early as 563 BC, and as late as 400 BC.  The factual dates of Daoist timelines are also debated, but may go back to the oracle shamans of the Xia Dynasty (c.2000 BC).  Either way, these teachings first existed in China, in indigenous sources, for centuries before Buddhism arrived there in 80 AD.</span>

</div>

<div id="_ftn63" style="-aw-footnote-isauto:1">

[<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[63\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftnref63) <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">Translated by Dan G. Reid</span>

</div>

<div id="_ftn64" style="-aw-footnote-isauto:1">

[<span style=" font-size:0.67rem; vertical-align:super">\[64\]</span>](text00000.html#_ftnref64) <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">The Quan Zhen School of Daoism (founded circa 1167 AD) has long integrated seemingly Buddhist philosophies and practices into its own.  As shown throughout</span> <span style=" font-size:0.83rem; font-style:italic">Thread of Dao</span> <span style=" font-size:0.83rem">, many of these philosophies and practices existed in China for centuries, before Buddhism arrived there in 80AD, though it may have been their popularity in Buddhism which brought them to the attention of the Quan Zhen Patriarchs.  A modern example of this:  Quan Zhen Abbot Michael Rinaldini, founder of the American Dragon Gate Sect, teaches use of the â€˜break-through questionâ€™ (called a hou-tou in Zen) â€œWhat is not-two?â€?  He uses this hou-tou to help students, and the Daoist priests that he trains, with Daoist zuowang (â€œsitting and forgettingâ€?) meditation. </span>
